units.tr: Life is short, but art is long [ὁ βίος βραχὺς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή]. We thought it worthwhile to print this little treatise and make it public, taken as far as possible from his writings, since it has been awaited for so long with eager longing by very many. It is by the most excellent and distinguished Mr. Florentius Schuyl, Doctor of Medicine, the most diligent public professor of the Institutes and of Botany in this most flourishing Academy of Leiden. Only the part on fevers remains. It was indeed to be wished that he had brought this little book to completion, and that so great a man, enjoying the bloom and vigour of his age, had been spared the death that brings no tears, so that more of the fruits of study for frail mankind—

units.tr: Just indignation has forced from me a refutation of this most impudent little book. For who could bear with equanimity a man who is a physician in name and profession only, and who, for no other reason than that Sylvius has generously and frankly shared his Practice with the learned world, declares in plain words, in a published pamphlet, that Sylvius is nothing but filth to him, and who sets out to carp at the veteran Practitioner? And he does so so abusively that he is not ashamed to call a most distinguished man, one who has deserved very well of medical science, an outstanding error-maker, not only wandering but also

Ibid., p. 4. patimur manes, optimus ille, qui minimis premitur. Neither Sylvius nor anyone who loves truth refuses a candid admonition. But who can bear a man who does not know what it is to understand, who does not even think beyond his crude senses, who still delights in that coarse and murky proposition, long since rejected by lovers of truth, in this noonday of the sciences: There is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses; who openly scorns chymistry, a notable instrument of medical truth, and dismisses its experts as a barbarous tribe and dusty fellows; who, finally, prefers to be carried about on the shoulders of others, like a wooden puppet moved by alien sinews, rather than trust his own judgement? Who, I say, can bear that this disgrace of the most humane Gallic nation should so clumsily wield its rustic censor's rod against things it understands no better than what befits an honourable man;

Pag. 77. 3 Pag. 80. ceat; tàm incondito garritu & dissoluto furore omni modestiâ posthabitâ Sacras Musas interstrepere; calumniis tàm impudenter proscindere Inclytæ Academiæ Lugduno-Batavæ Professorem Medicæ Praxeos Primarium, Virum experientissimum, indefessâ diligentia de studiosa Juventute optimè merentem. Ego certè putavi tantillum me debere honori Facultatis Medicæ atque existimationi Collegæ conjunctissimi, ut hominis audaciæ obviam irem, demonstraturus jejunum hunc Medicum in Philosophia, Medicina, Hippocrate itidem & bonis auctoribus planè hospitem, Sylvium non modò nusquam refutasse, sed ne verosimile quidem argumentum illi objecisse: & quod seriò notatum velim, ipsum Sylvio nunquam contradixisse, quin Hippocrati pariter aliisque Veteribus turpiter contradixerit; illudque præstitisse ut veritatis amantes dubitaturi sint, fitne le Vasseur indoctior, an impudentior.
units.tr: 1. p. 11. 2. p. 77. 3. p. 80. befits an honourable man; who, setting all modesty aside, should bellow against the Sacred Muses with such uncouth chatter and wild rage; who should so shamelessly tear with calumny at the Professor of Medical Practice, the foremost man of the famous Academy of Leiden, a most experienced man who deserves well of studious youth by his tireless diligence? I, for my part, thought I owed a little to the honour of the Faculty of Medicine and to the reputation of my most intimate colleague, so that I should meet this man's boldness, intending to show that this unlearned physician, a stranger to philosophy, to medicine, and likewise to Hippocrates and the good authors, has not only nowhere refuted Sylvius but has not even put forward a plausible argument against him. And let me seriously note this: he never contradicted Sylvius without shamefully contradicting Hippocrates and the other Ancients equally; and he has so managed it that lovers of truth will be in doubt whether le Vasseur is the more ignorant or the more shameless.

units.la: Præfatio, ut inde ordiar, quam per ingeniosam profopopœian Bibliopola bellulo isti opusculo præfixisse fingitur, præter calumnias hoc unicè Lectori inculcat, quasi id ex Titulo non satis constaret, litem intentari Triumvirali humori Sylvii, in quo eo loco nihil carpit, præterquam quòd Sylvius è rebus (personis dicere voluit) Imperii ad res agrotantium Triumviratùs nomen audaculè traduxerit. Grande videlicet crimen, nec nisi famâ aut vitâ piandum ! Sylvius dicere ausus fuit esse in Intestinis humorum Triumviratum; & nota quantâ cum modestiâ hoc nomine usus fuerit Praxeos suæ pag. 93. Si, inquit, terminis Helmontianis impunè uti licet. Sed veniam tibi non concedit, conjunctissime Collega, hic importunus Censor. Cave & tibi Hippocrates, qui lib. de Flat. iv. 9. ausus fuisti æra vocare μέγιστον δυνάστην maximum Dominum; nec veritus fuisti Aph. 5. S. III. asserere Austrum & Aquilonem δωδεκάδεα imperium sive Dominatum tenere: & Lib. de Corde, ut infinita alia huc facientia taceam, ipsâ imperandi voce •ἐχέν abuteris. Sed verò quàm frequens apud Medicos est mentio prædominii humorum, qualitatum, temperamentorum, &c. Nec quisquam adeò in Medicina hospes est, qui nesciat partes humani corporis dispesci in Principes, penès quas est imperium, & subditas, quibus relicta est obsequii gloria. Hinc apud quosdam cor, apud alios cerebrum passim Regis, Principis & Gubernatoris nomine exornatur. quâ de re si perorantem audivisset disertum Laurentium vel ullum bonum Authorem cum judicio legisset, phrases ab imperio ad rem Medicam traductæ, apud omnes omninò Medicos usitatissimæ, tàm novæ aut duræ non apparuissent vitiligatori. Apud Chymicos nicos denique, Paracelsum præferim & Helmontium, vocem Archiei centies occurrere, atque hunc de Duûm Viratu totos Tractatus scripsis-se, neminem, uti opinor, fugit, præter unicum Doctorem Le Vasseur, cui hic modus loquendi ut ut omnious, quotquot de re Medicâ commentati sunt, familiaris, prorsus novus, inauditus & insolens videtur.
units.tr: The Preface, to begin there, which is pretended to have been prefixed to this pretty little work by the bookseller through a clever prosopopoeia, does nothing but press upon the reader, besides slanders, the charge that a suit is brought against the Triumviral humour of Sylvius, in which passage he finds fault with nothing except that Sylvius has boldly transferred the name of Triumvirate from the affairs (he meant to say persons) of the empire to the affairs of the sick. A great crime indeed, and one to be expiated only with fame or life! Sylvius dared to say that there is a Triumvirate in the intestines of the humours; and note with what modesty he used this name in his Practice, page 93: If, he says, one may use Helmontian terms with impunity. But this troublesome Censor does not grant you pardon, most intimate colleague. Beware, Hippocrates too, who in the book On Airs ventured to call the air the greatest lord [μέγιστον δυνάστην], maximum Dominum; and you did not hesitate in Aphorism 5, section 3, to assert that the South and North winds hold dominion or lordship [δωδεκάδεα]; and in the book On the Heart, to say nothing of the infinite other passages that bear on this, you misuse the very word for ruling imperandi [ἐχέν]. But how frequent among physicians is the mention of the predominance of humours, qualities, temperaments, and so on! Nor is anyone so much a stranger to medicine as not to know that the parts of the human body are divided into princes, in whom dominion resides, and subjects, to whom the glory of obedience is left. Hence in some authors the heart, in others the brain, is everywhere adorned with the name of King, Prince, or Governor. If he had heard the eloquent Laurentius speak on this matter, or had read any good author with judgment, the phrases transferred from government to medical matters, most common among all physicians, would not have appeared so new or harsh to this fault-finder. Finally, among the Chymists, especially Paracelsus and Helmont, the word Archeus occurs a hundred times, and I think no one is unaware that Helmont wrote whole treatises on the Triumvirate of the Two; yet this mode of speaking, familiar as it is to all who have written on medical matters, seems quite new, unheard of, and strange to Doctor le Vasseur alone.

units.la: Deinde, ne solus videatur insanire, Lectori persuadere satagit Antesignanum Sylvianæ sententiæ oforem, atque futilis sui Libelli proxœnetam esse D. Petrum Augustinum Rompfium, qui (nota stupendam hominis arrogantiam) teste Doctore Le Vasseur de se ipso, neminem in rerum natura invenire potuit, præter hunc Sapientum Octavum, qui Sylvii fundamenta subrueret solidius. Verba, scilicet, Bibliopolæ Libellum Le Vasseur commendantis sic sonant: Petrus Augustinus Rompsius Auctori, videlicet Le VasVasseur, benevolentiæ adeò jure conjunctus est, ut eo noster, ad ea, quæ in Sylvium animo volvebat, datâ epistolâ liberè profundenda nullum commodioremesse judicaret amicum. LeVasseur grávem futurum D.Rompsio,(quod (quod scilicet exoptare videtur pag. 88. ne non, quod ipse contraxit, odium in alium derivet, & in malis socium habeat) ut eo etiam nomine, Literarum amantes ipsi Le Vasseur irascantur, quòd D. Rompsium tanti stuporis & malitiæ insimulaverit, quasi illius nugas & calumnias non probasset modo, sed & in scenam produxisset, fuissetque totius illius Tragœdiæ choragus. Quamvis autem sententia D. Rompsii, Judicis ab ipso Le Vasseur assumpti, pag. 88. quâ calumniarum damnatur, refutando infrunito isti libello abundè sufficiat, publici tamen interest palàm resciri, quousque Doctor le Vasseur in Sylvium, Rompsium & veritatem fuerit injurius.
units.tr: Then, lest he seem to be the only one raving, he takes pains to persuade the reader that the champion of the Sylvian opinion, and the go-between of his trifling pamphlet, is Mr. Petrus Augustinus Rompsius, who (note the man's amazing arrogance), according to Doctor le Vasseur's own testimony about himself, could find no one in nature except this Eighth of the Wise to undermine the foundations of Sylvius more solidly. The words of the bookseller commending Le Vasseur's pamphlet run thus: Petrus Augustinus Rompsius is so closely joined to the Author, that is, Le Vasseur, by the right of goodwill, that he judged our friend, when he was to pour forth freely by letter what he had in mind against Sylvius, to have no more suitable friend. A sound commodity commends itself, clearly. Cato more rightly says: Nor praise yourself, etc. And so Le Vasseur, on this occasion, cites two witnesses favouring his opinion: the bookseller, whose testimony, being supposititious, is to be given little weight, since he deals only in books; and Mr. Rompsius. But no one would easily be persuaded that a man of most polished judgment was ever pleased with a piece written so crudely. Indeed Mr. Rompsius wished himself to be excused to Mr. Sylvius through Mr. Angillius, a man distinguished by singular learning and integrity of life, and he himself excused himself to me, saying that the slanderous pamphlet of Doctor le Vasseur could in no way be approved by him. So far is it from being the case that, because of Doctor le Vasseur's absurdities, Rompsius will be burdened (which, namely, he seems to wish, page 88, so that the hatred he has incurred may not be turned upon another and so that he may have a partner in misfortune), that, on that account too, lovers of letters should be angry with Le Vasseur himself, because he has charged Rompsius with such stupidity and malice, as if he had not merely approved his trifles and slanders but had brought them onto the stage and been the leader of that whole tragedy. Although, indeed, the opinion of Rompsius, the judge whom Le Vasseur himself has taken up, page 88, by which the slanders are condemned, is quite enough to refute this unwise pamphlet, it is nonetheless in the public interest to learn openly how far Doctor le Vasseur has done wrong to Sylvius, to Rompsius, and to the truth.

units.la: Paginæ igitur 1. 2. 3. 4. nihil prorsus continent præter stupendam vanitate turgentis animi impotentiam, quâ, sine ulla prorsus probatione, clamitat, Sylvium tyrannidem affectare, Medicinæ fundamenta funditus subruere, totamque Medicinam perituram nisi ille, novus scilicet Atlas, eam sustineat. at vero quia inde nihil infertur praeterquam Sylvium talem nullâ prorsus adductâ ratione dici ab impotenti le Vasseur, atque hic αὐτόπτης hactenus non fuit habitus: imo quia ipse sinistrum & exorbitantem suum impetum enixè excusatum cupit, quia, uti confitetur pag. 88. lin. 16. 20. & 21. scribendi æstro perculsus atque maniâ, velut Enthusiasta, malo videlicet & calumniandi spiritu abreptus, sibi satis scrupulosè cavere non potuit, ne cogar maledicta maledictis repellere omnes illius calumnias tanquam à furibundo & maleferiato prosectas, ne afflicto addatur afflictio, pro non dictis habebo.
units.tr: The pages 1, 2, 3 and 4 therefore contain absolutely nothing but the astonishing impotence of a swollen mind, which, without any proof whatever, cries out that Sylvius aims at tyranny and undermines the foundations of Medicine from the ground up, and that all of Medicine will perish unless he, a new Atlas forsooth, holds it up. But since nothing follows from this except that the impotent Le Vasseur calls Sylvius such without offering any reason, and since this man has not hitherto been regarded as an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης]; indeed, since he himself eagerly wishes to excuse his own sinister and extravagant onslaught, because, as he confesses on p. 88, lines 16, 20 and 21, he was struck by the frenzy and mania of writing, like an Enthusiast, carried away by an evil and slanderous spirit, and could not take sufficiently scrupulous care of himself, I shall not be forced to answer insults with insults. Lest affliction be added to the afflicted, I shall count all his calumnies as having been spoken by a raving and maddened man, and so as unsaid.

units.la: Paulò igitur propius ad rem accedere videtur pagina quintâ; Sylvius, inquit, factus de Spargyrico Medicus, idem semper in Medicina garrit, (quàm insulsè!) quod in Chymia profitebatur: Salia fixa, volatilia, acida, spiritus, ef- fervescentiam, &c. quasi in his solis Medicina, quanta quanta est, resideret. Quasi vero hæc Sylvius ex Hippocrate non potuisset hausisse. Sed hac de re paulò post, unde manifestum fiet non quidem in his solis, quod Sylvio, reclamante Veritate, assuere annititur Versutus orator, sed in his præcipuè Medicinam consistere. Sylvio igitur objicere non erubescit peculiarem Chymiæ cognitionem, quod multis locis ingeminat; quasi illud semel effutivisse non sufficeret, atque piaculum esset novisse naturæ penetralia, callere Anatomiam, quâ abditi naturæ recessus referantur: corporum principia explicantur: quâ remotis scoriis aquæ, spiritus, olea, acida & salia tùm fixa tùm volatilia, uti & composita medicamina minus fastidiosa & maximè efficacia conficiuntur: quâ denique omnium δυναμέων, ut loquitur Hippocrates, sive potentiarum & facultatum ratio indagatur, uti ipse vel invitus fatetur pag. 62. Hâc arte si vel leviter tinctus fuisset, tàm insulsè nunquam in Sylvium insurrexisset.
units.tr: Page 5 seems to come somewhat closer to the matter: Sylvius, he says, having become a physician from a Spagyrist, always prattles the same things about Medicine (how foolishly!) that he professed in Chemistry: fixed and volatile salts, acids, spirits, effervescence, and so on, as if Medicine, whatever its extent, resided in these alone. As if Sylvius could not have drawn these things from Hippocrates! But on this matter more shortly, from which it will become plain that the crafty orator is striving to fasten on Sylvius, while Truth protests, not these alone, but that Medicine consists chiefly in these. He is not ashamed to object to Sylvius his particular knowledge of Chemistry, which he repeats in many places, as if it were not enough to have blurted it out once, and as if it were a sin to know the inner recesses of nature, to be skilled in Anatomy, by which the hidden retreats of nature are laid open and the principles of bodies explained; by which, the dregs being removed, water, spirits, oils, acids and salts, both fixed and volatile, as well as composite medicines that are less offensive and most effective, are prepared; by which, finally, the account of all the δυνάμεων [powers], as Hippocrates calls them, that is, of powers and faculties, is investigated, as he himself confesses, though unwillingly, on p. 62. Had he been even slightly tinged with this art, he would never have risen so foolishly against Sylvius.

units.la: Quod autem addit Sylvium ingeminare Salia fixa, volatilia, acida, spiritus, effervescentiam, si vel mica salis vel tantillum purioris spiritûs in ipso fuisset, hæc Sylvio non exprobrasset.
units.tr: As for his claim that Sylvius keeps repeating fixed and volatile salts, acids, spirits, effervescence: if there were even a grain of salt or a little purer spirit in him, he would not have reproached Sylvius with these things.

units.la: Etenim salsum, acidum, spiritus atque effervescentiam principes esse Sanitatis & Morborum causas discere debuisset, si non ex Chymicis, à quorum nominibus abhorret, saltèm ex Hippocrate, qui ut variis in locis, ita & data opera toto libro de Veteri Medicina totus in eo est, ut probet, accuratam horum omnium cognitionem, primariam Medicæ artis columnam esse, inquiens Text. xxiv. Nihil utilius neque magis necessarium, quàm hæc cognovisse, quod & probè & convenienti ratione investigantes juxtà hominis naturam hæc primi inventores
units.tr: For he ought to have learned that salt, acid, spirits and effervescence are the chief causes of health and of disease, if not from the Chemists, whose names he abhors, then at least from Hippocrates. Hippocrates, as in various places, so also deliberately throughout the whole book On Ancient Medicine, sets out to prove that accurate knowledge of all these things is the primary pillar of the medical art, saying in Text. xxiv: Nothing is more useful or more necessary than to have known these things, which the first discoverers, investigating them rightly and in a suitable manner according to the nature of man,

units.la: invenerunt judicaveruntque artem dignam, quæ Deo adscriberetur, quemadmodum etiam esse receptum. Cùm enim plebei quique facilè agnoverint Calidum & frigidum, humidum &siccum, ignorantes verò illorum causas, salia, acida, spiritus, olea, effervescentiam, &c. sæpius hominibus nocuerint quàm profuerint; à Deo doctos existimat illos, qui non tàm laborant circà calidum, frigidum, humidum & siccum, &c. quàm circa ipsorum causas, non enim calidum est, quod magnam vim habet, sed ipsum acerbum & fluidum, & alia, quæ à me relata sunt, ut inquit Hippocrates l.c. Text. xxvi. 21. Dixerat autem antea Text. xxiv. 20. ἔνι γὰρ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ πικρὸν, καὶ ἁλμυρὸν, καὶ γλυκὺ, καὶ ὀξὺ, καὶ στρυφνὸν, καὶ ταλαδαιγὸν, καὶ ἀλλὰ μυρία παντοίας δυνάμιας ἔχοντα, πολλῶς τε καὶ ἰσχυρά. Inest enim in homine & amarum & salsum, & dulce & acidum, & acerbum & fluidum, & alia infinita, omnigenas facultates habentia, copiamque
units.tr: discovered and judged to be an art worthy of being ascribed to God, as is also the accepted view. For although ordinary people can readily recognise the hot and cold, the moist and dry, yet, ignorant of their causes, salts, acids, spirits, oils, effervescence and so on have more often harmed men than helped them; so he thinks those are taught by God who labour not so much over the hot, cold, moist and dry, and so on, as over their causes: for it is not the hot that has great power, but the bitter and the fluid, and the other things I have related, as Hippocrates says in the same place, Text. xxvi. 21. Earlier, in Text. xxiv. 20, he had said: [ἔνι γὰρ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ πικρὸν, καὶ ἁλμυρὸν, καὶ γλυκὺ, καὶ ὀξὺ, καὶ στρυφνὸν, καὶ ταλαδαιγὸν, καὶ ἀλλὰ μυρία παντοίας δυνάμιας ἔχοντα, πολλῶς τε καὶ ἰσχυρά.] For there is in man both bitter and salt, sweet and sour, sharp and fluid, and countless other things, having faculties of every kind, many and strong, and with supply

units.la: quæ que ac robur. Unde hæc passim κατ' ἐξοχὴν facultates & potentias vocat. lib. iv. de morb. v. 8. lib. de Vet. Med. Text. xxiv. 28. ibid. Text. xxx. 14. & xxxiii. 17. & xxxiv. 1. xxvii. 30. xxx. 14. & 18. xlii. Atque horum ubique magnus est proventus: Etenim τὰ φυόμενα π κὴ ἀπεφέμενα, ὁκόταν ἐς τὴν γὴν ἔλθῃ, ἔλκει ἔνφσον τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ἑωυτῷ ξυνὸν ἐν τῇ γῇ· ἔνι δὲ κὴ ὀξὺ, κὴ πικρὸν κὴ γλυκὺ κὴ ἁλμυ-ρὸν, κὴ παντοῖον· uti loquitur Hippocrates, Lib. de Nat. Humana x. Id est, juxta vulgarem Interpretem, Ex terra nascentia & in ipsam plantata & seminata, ubi in terram pervenerint, unumquodque trahit id, quod natura sua familiare in terra existit. Inest autem in terra & acidum, & amarum, & dulce, & salsum, & omnigenum; & uti docet lib. iv. de Morb. v. 8. μυρίαι ἐν αὐτῇ δυνάμεις εἰσί. innumerae sunt in ipsa terra facultates. Idem de aëre, aqua & igne non sine ratione quis dixerit: omnia igitur, quæ ex illis constant, illorum omnium aut quorundam saltem magis minusque participia esse res ipsa loquitur, & ratione atque infinitis experimentis comprobatur. Non igitur sine evidenti ratione. Hippocrates illorum maximam vult haberi rationem sive alimentis sive medicamentis insint, sive existant in homine, sive extrà hominem, sive edantur, sive bibantur, sive extrinsecus illinantur, aut quomodocunque formata adhibeantur, lib. de Vet. Med. xxvii. 22. 23. 24. &c. etenim eodem docente Text. xxv. 5. ciborum quicunque nobis incommodi sunt & ingesti hominem laedunt, quidam aut amarus est & meracus ac intemperatus, aut salsus aut acidus, aut alius quis intemperatus & fortis. Tanti porrò facit salsum, acidum, amarum, aliaque similli acrimoniâ praedita, ut ea statuat omnium, (videlicet quae non fiunt à quadam violentiâ, ut loquitur lib. iv. de Morb.) morborum causas esse. lib. de Vet. Med. Text. xxv. Hinc raucedines, anginam, erysipelata, peripneumoniam & febrem deducit, ubi vero fluxiones crassiores & maturiores factae fuerint, & ab omni acrimonia liberatae, tunc, inquit, jam & febres & alia hominem laedentia solvuntur loco citato Text. xxxiii. 8, 9, 10. &c. Illa autem, ait, cujusque effecti causas esse, quae illis praesentibus excitantur, iis vero temperatis cessant, omnino necesse est. Unde ibidem Text. xxxiv. amplius, inquit, porro etiam alia quaecunque homo patitur, omnia a potentiis proficiscuntur. itaque cum amaritudo quaedam diffusa fuerit, quam bilem flavam appellare solemus, quales statim anxietates & aestus & impotentia occupant! frigiditatem vero, uti loquitur ibid. Text. xxvii. 30. & caliditatem ego omnium facultatum minime potentes esse in corpore existimo, quandoquidem uti Text. xxviii. xxix. & xxxiii. demonstrat corpus simpliciter refrigeratum vel etiam calefactum, id est solo calore aut frigore male malè affectum, nullaque alia facultate infectum uti monet Text. xxxiii. 15. &c. facili negotio, simplici videlicet calore & frigore ad naturalem temperiem reducitur. quod fiet, ὅταν μεταβάλλῃ ἐκ τῆς ψυχρῆς ἐς τὸ θερμόν. καὶ ἐκ τῆς θερμῆς ἐς τὸ ψυχρόν. si ex frigido in calidum permutatum: fuerit, aut ex calido in frigidum: si homo videlicet frigidus ad ignem accedat, aut stragulis opertus fuerit, uti loquitur Text. xxix. 19. calidus verò sub Jove frigido commorabitur, &c. Unde lib. cit. Text. i. 38. concludit, cui igitur brevi adeò contrarium accedit, cuique vis adimitur sua sponte, quidnam ab hoc magnum aut grave fiat, aut quid opus est multo ad hoc auxilio.
units.tr: and strength. Hence he everywhere calls these, par excellence, facultates and potentiae [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]: Book iv On Diseases, ch. 8; On Ancient Medicine, Text. xxiv. 28; ibid. Text. xxx. 14; and xxxiii. 17, xxxiv. 1, xxvii. 30, xxx. 14 and 18, xlii. And of these there is everywhere a great abundance. For, as Hippocrates says in On the Nature of Man, x: Plants sprouting from the earth, when planted and sown in it, and coming into the earth, each draws to itself from the earth what is naturally kin to it. There is in the earth both acid and bitter and sweet and salt, and every kind; and, as Book iv On Diseases, ch. 8 teaches, countless powers are in it [μυρίαι ἐν αὐτῇ δυνάμεις εἰσί], that is, innumerable faculties are in the earth itself. One may say the same with reason of air, water and fire. Therefore everything that consists of them is, in its own nature, a sharer in all of them, or at least some of them, more or less; and the thing itself speaks to this, and it is confirmed by reason and by countless experiments. Not without evident reason, then, Hippocrates wants the greatest account taken of them, whether they are in foods or in medicines, whether they exist in the man or outside the man, whether they are eaten or drunk, or applied externally by anointing, or used in whatever form, On Ancient Medicine xxvii. 22, 23, 24, etc. For, as he teaches in Text. xxv. 5: of the foods that are unsuitable for us, whatever is taken in harms the man: some are bitter and undiluted and intemperate, or salt or sour, or some other intemperate and strong. He values salt, sour, bitter and other things endowed with similar sharpness so highly that he holds them to be the causes of all diseases (namely those which do not arise from some violence, as he says in Book iv On Diseases). On Ancient Medicine, Text. xxv. From these he derives hoarseness, quinsy, erysipelas, peripneumonia and fever: but when the thicker and riper discharges have been formed and freed from all sharpness, then, he says, fevers and other things harming man are resolved, in the passage cited, Text. xxxiii. 8, 9, 10, etc. Now those, he says, which are excited while these are present, and cease when these are tempered, must of necessity be the causes of each effect. Whence in the same place, Text. xxxiv: Further, he says, whatever else a man suffers, all proceed from the faculties. Thus when some diffused bitterness has come, which we are accustomed to call yellow bile, what anxieties and heats and helplessness immediately seize him! But cold and heat, as Text. xxvii. 30 puts it, I consider to be the least powerful of all the faculties in the body, since, as Text. xxviii, xxix and xxxiii show, a body simply cooled or even heated, that is badly affected by heat or cold alone, and not infected by any other faculty, as Text. xxxiii. 15 warns, is brought back to its natural temperament with easy effort, namely by simple heat and cold. This happens [ὅταν μεταβάλλῃ ἐκ τῆς ψυχρῆς ἐς τὸ θερμόν. καὶ ἐκ τῆς θερμῆς ἐς τὸ ψυχρόν.] when it is changed from the cold to the hot, or from the hot to the cold; namely if a chilled man approaches the fire, or is covered with blankets, as Text. xxix. 19 says; whereas a hot man will remain under a cold sky, and so on. Whence, in the book cited, Text. i. 38, he concludes: For what great or grave thing can come of this, when that which is briefly brought to its opposite has its power taken away of its own accord? Or what need is there of much help for this?

units.la: Ab acido verò, salso & amaro excedentibus non restituimur, nisi postquam depravati illi humores fuerint temperati, aut ab iis fuimus repurgati, aut sponte aut per medicamentum, ut loquitur Venerandus Senex ibid. Text.
units.tr: But we are not restored from acid, salty and bitter excesses unless those depraved humours have first been tempered, or we have been purged of them, either spontaneously or by medicine, as the Venerable Old Man says in the same text.

units.la: XXXIV. 7. Ὅσον δὲ ἂν χρόνον τοῦτο μετέω- σι, &c. Quamdiu autem eadem nimium effervescunt & cruda & meraca ac intemperata, nulla arte neque dolores neque febres sedare possis, & quos quidem acuta acrisque ac æruginosa bilis affligit, quales mox rabies & morsus viscerum & desperatio? Ibid. n°. 13. Ne autem sine remedio Lectores suos dimittat, triplicia illis tradit remedia, inquiens l.c.n°.21. Non sedatur autem hæc priusquam eadem expurgetur, καταστρέψαι prosternatur, id est, præcipitetur, & aliis permisceatur, id est, temperetur. Unde facta comparatione inter calidum & frigidum affectum, atque temperiem acidam, salsam & amaram, ita loquitur Text. xxxi. 19. ibid. Omnibus autem liberatio hæc est, ut frigore videlicet solo affecti percalefiant, ex ardore vero perfrigerentur. atque hæc brevi accedunt & concoctione nulla opus habent. Reliquæ autem omnes fluxiones, quas propter humorum acrimonias & intem- peranerantias ego fieri sentio. Restituuntur & curantur ubi temperatæ fuerint & concoctæ. Sic paulò antè, Inflamma-
units.tr: XXXIV. 7. As long as these things ferment [Ὅσον δὲ ἂν χρόνον τοῦτο μετέωσι], etc.: As long as the same humours effervesce too much, raw, unmixed and intemperate, you can calm neither pains nor fevers by any art, and what of those whom sharp, acrid and corrosive bile afflicts, such as presently rage, gnawing of the bowels and despair? Ibid. n. 13. Lest he dismiss his readers without a remedy, he gives them three remedies, saying in the same place, n. 21: This is not calmed until the same is purged, [καταστρέψαι] overturned, that is, cast down, and mixed with others, that is, tempered. Hence, having compared the hot and cold affection with the acid, salty and bitter temperament, he speaks thus in text xxxi. 19 of the same work: For all people this is the release: those affected only by cold grow warm, and those from heat grow cold. These come on quickly and need no concoction. But all the other fluxions, which I judge to arise from the acrimony and intemperance of the humours, are restored and cured when they have been tempered and concocted. So a little earlier he teaches that inflammation of the nostrils is not cured unless the flux has become thicker, less acrid, concocted and more mixed with the former; then indeed the burning also ceases.

units.la: ionem narium non curari docet, nisi postquam fluxus crassior & minus acris concoctusque & magis permixtus priore fuerit, tunc sanè ardor quoque cessat. Idem docet Inflammationi & exulce-
units.tr: He teaches the same thing about inflammation and ulceration of the eyelids, and about what happens to the cheeks.

units.la: rationi palpebrarum, illique, quæ genis accidit, contingere. Et quò dubium omne discutiat Text.xxx.objeƈtioni satisfaciens ait: verùm dixerit aliquis. qui ardente febre febricitant, itemque peripneumoniis & aliis fortibus morbis, non citò ex calore liberantur, neque adest hîc frigidum adversùs calidum. adeoque non videtur iste calor ex effervescentia acrium illorum humorum ortus. Cui Respondens, atqui ego, inquit, hoc maximum signum esse puto, quòd non propter calidum simpliciter homines febricitent, neque hoc fit simpliciter afflictionis caussa: sed est & amarum ac calidum idem, & calidum & acidum, & salsum ac calidum, & alia infinita ; & rursus frigidum cum aliis facultatibus conjunctum. Haec itaque sunt quae ledunt, si simul adest autem & calidum robore participans, nimirum ducens & exacerbans & augens simul cum illis, verùm nullam potentiam majorem quàm convenit videlicet, habens. Atque haec quidem sic se habent. Quod aliquanto manifestius apparet in iis, qui solo victu actu frigido vitam sustentare solent, & nihilo minus non temperato modo calore gaudent naturaliter dispositi, sed & quandoque in caulum incidentes sanguinis incendio pereunt. Calor igitur naturalis sive mediocris sufficit, ut excitentur primariae illae potentiae toties repetitae, ut earum vi ingens calor in humano corpore excitetur. Qui certè calor, utpote temperatus, in humido, à quo obtunditur, ad tantum excessum semetipsum promovere non potest: ut necessariò concedendum sit, calorem illum lum excedentem, qui & illos quandoque infestat, vi exorbitantis effervescentiæ ab humoribus contrariâ crimoniâ præditis esse productum, deoque calorem naturalem vi naturalis effervescentiæ in humano corpore exoriri,& propterea Medico calorem, & eadem est frigoris ratio, in corpore humano non considerandum ut qualitatem primam, ut vulgò putatur; sed ut secundam, utpote ab effervescentia crium in corpore existentium dependentem. Hinc seriò monet unus omnium Medicorum præstantissimus; l. c. Text. XLII. Oportere Medicum potentias humorum, & quid singguli ipsorum in homine facere possunt, perspectum habere: uti & quam affinitatem humores inter sese habeant, an videlicet dulcis humor in aliam speciem mutetur, non à contemperamento, sed ipse desciscens & immutatus ab eo qualis primùm fuerat. amarus aut salsus aut acerbus aut acidus ( sit sanè acidus ) ergo acidus humor reliquos præcellens maximè incommodus fuerit; si utique dulcis, omnium commodissimus existit: id quod si quis forinsecus quærens consequi possit, is semper quod melius est consequi queat. Optimum autem est quod longissimè ab incommodo abest. Idem supra Text. xxxix. sedulò inculcat, nempè Facultatem esse, humorum summas vires ac robur nosse. quod quidem, ibidem docet, ex manifestis forinsecus condiscere oportere.
units.tr: And so that he may remove every doubt, answering an objection in text xxx, he says: But someone may say: those who are feverish with burning fever, and likewise those with pneumonia and other severe diseases, are not quickly freed from the heat, and cold is not present against the heat here. So this heat does not seem to arise from the effervescence of those acrid humours. Answering this, he says: But I think this is the greatest sign that people do not become feverish simply because of heat, nor does this happen simply as the cause of the affliction. Rather, the bitter is also hot, the hot is also sour, the salty is also hot, and there are countless other combinations; and again, cold is joined with other qualities. These, then, are the things that harm; but if heat is present, sharing in their strength, namely leading, exacerbating and increasing along with them, it has no greater power than what is proper to it. And these things stand thus. This appears somewhat more clearly in those who usually sustain life by a diet of purely cold food, and yet, naturally disposed, enjoy a heat that is not tempered, and sometimes, falling into a fever of the blood, perish. Natural or moderate heat is therefore enough to excite those primary powers, so often repeated, that by their force a great heat is aroused in the human body. Surely this heat, being tempered, cannot, since it is blunted by the moisture, advance itself to such an excess; so it must necessarily be conceded that that excessive heat, which at times also troubles those people, is produced by the force of an exorbitant effervescence from humours endowed with a contrary acrimony. Thus natural heat arises in the human body by the force of natural effervescence, and for that reason the physician must consider heat, and the same reasoning holds for cold, in the human body not as a first quality, as is commonly thought, but as a second, dependent on the effervescence of the acrid humours present in the body. Hence one of the most outstanding of all physicians seriously warns us, l.c. text XLII: The physician ought to have a clear grasp of the powers of the humours and what each of them can do in the human being; and also what affinity the humours have among themselves, whether a sweet humour is changed into another kind, not by a change of temperament, but when it itself deserts and is altered from what it was at first. A bitter, salty, harsh or sour humour (let it be sour) will then be especially harmful, above all others; if indeed it is sweet, it is the most suitable of all. If anyone seeking from outside can attain this, he can always attain what is better. The best is what lies furthest from harm. The same author, in text xxxix above, insistently urges: that it is the skill to know the greatest powers and strength of the humours; which, he teaches in the same place, one must learn from manifest things outside.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem eos laudat, qui acidum, salsum & amarum apprimè norunt, sic etiam eos vehementer perstringit ibid. Text. xxiii. quicunque hæc non considerantes non norunt. quomodo enim, inquit, illi affectiones in homine cognoscere possunt, ab unoquoque enim afficitur & alteratur homo, vel hoc vel alio modo, & ex his omnis vita, & sano, & ex morbo convalescenti & ægroto. Sunt enim istæ potentiæ Sanitatis & Morborum non caussæ modò, sed & ipsa Sanitas & Morbus. Non igitur fine ratione Vir Incomparabilis ibid. Text. xxxvi. 18. judicat neces-sarium esse, ut omnis Medicus naturam intelligat, & omni studio annitatur ut cognoscat, si modò aliquid eorum, quæ fieri debent, rectè præstare velit. Neque enim sufficere illi debet in genere novisse ↄaseum Ex. gr. pravum esse alimentum doloris caussam, si quis eum avidiùs devoraverit; sed novisse oportet, quem dolorem & propter quid, & cui parti noceat. Nam & alius multiplex cibus & totus naturâ pravus est, hominemque af-ficit, sed non eodem modo. Quorum omnium diversitatem à salso, spirituoso, acido, acerbo, austero, amaro & similibus dependere toto libro de Veteri Medicina docet.
units.tr: Just as he praises those who thoroughly know the acid, salty and bitter, so in the same text, xxiii, he vehemently censures those who, not considering these things, do not know them: For how can they know the affections in a human being? Each person is affected and altered in this or that way, and from these come all life, both in health and in convalescence from disease and in sickness. For these powers are not only the causes of health and disease, but health and disease themselves. Therefore, not without reason, that incomparable man, in the same place, text xxxvi. 18, judges it necessary that every physician understand nature and strive with all zeal to know it, if he wishes to perform rightly what ought to be done. For it should not be enough for him to know in general that bad food is a cause of pain if someone devours it too greedily; he must know what pain it causes, and why, and in which part it harms. For other manifold food is also wholly bad by nature and affects a human being, but not in the same way. Their whole book On Ancient Medicine teaches that the diversity of all these depends on the salty, spirituous, sour, harsh, austere, bitter and similar qualities.

units.la: Aristoteles verò, ut de Galeno nil dicam, cujus singula folia idem protestantur, Hippocratis doctrinâ utcumque imbutus Sect. v. Probl. 17. quantam præservandæ sanitatis regulam, (quâ Hippocrates lib.vi.Epid.Sect.v. art. 34. monet, ne impuro corpore validius exerceamur, quandoquidem ulcera per cutem nostram proru mperent) explicans ait, ulcerum caussas esse χυμῶς μεχθηρῶς, ὀξεῖς καὶ πικρῶς καὶ ἁλμυρῶς, humores pravos, id est, acidos, amaros, salsos.
units.tr: Aristotle, not to speak of Galen, whose individual pages all attest the same, having been somewhat imbued with the teaching of Hippocrates, in Sect. v, Probl. 17, explains the rule for preserving health (by which Hippocrates in Book vi of the Epidemics, Sect. v, art. 34, warns us not to exercise ourselves too vigorously with an impure body, since ulcers would break out through our skin), and says that the causes of ulcers are bad humours [χυμοὺς μοχθηροὺς], that is, sour, bitter, salty [ὀξεῖς καὶ πικρὰς καὶ ἁλμυρούς].

units.la: Hinc acrium horum humorum excretioni natura varios duċtus fabricavit, per quos illi secernerentur & inutiles excernerentur, ut docet Hipp. lib. iv. de Morbis xv. quibus annumeramus, Bilarium & pancreaticum, ex quorum obstructionibus quanta exoriantur mala, infrà, verbo notabo, unde illorum frequentem in medicina mentionem esse faciendam sponte sequitur.
units.tr: Hence nature has fashioned various ducts for the excretion of these acrid humours, through which they are separated and the useless ones are expelled, as Hippocrates teaches in Book iv, On Diseases, text xv. We count among these the biliary and pancreatic ducts; what great evils arise from their obstructions I shall note below, under the proper heading, whence it follows of its own accord that their frequent mention must be made in medicine.

units.la: Quod Sylvio quoque vitio vertit, quasi nimis liberalem Spirituum mentionem faciat, suâ se tollit absurditate. Nec cuiquam, uti opinor, latet omnimoda spirituum naturalium, vitalium & ani[illegible, ~3 letters]x animalium utilitas & necessitas. [?]
units.tr: What he also finds fault with in Sylvius, as though he makes too generous a mention of spirits, refutes itself by its own absurdity. Nor, I think, is the complete usefulness and necessity of natural, vital and animal spirits hidden from anyone.

units.la: rra fiunt, quique vitæ & morborum causæ sunt. Verba illius l. c. num. 8, 10, 11, 24. sic sonant: π' ̓γ̓ ἀνὸ τςπέϛ ϒἠοιτο ἂν. &c. i. e. Quid autem sine hoc fit tandem? aut cui rei non adest? Omne enim quod inter cælum & terram est, spiritu repletum est. & 18: ὡς π γὴ τ ̓γ ἡλὶϛ δρό-μῳ ἀέννααν ἐόντα ὁ ἀὴς, ἀέννα ̓ ἡ λεπτὸς ἐὼν, εἶναι παρέχοντα. i. e. Et solis perpetuum cursum aër perpetuus & tenuis conservat: quem & paulò post vocat ὀχημα τ γῆς i. e. vehiculum terræ. & 24: neque quicquam usquam spiritu est vacuum. & Text. vi. Mortalibus, inquit, vitæ, & morborum ægrotis, solus is est auctor.
units.tr: earth, and which are the causes of life and disease. His words, in the passage cited, sections 8, 10, 11 and 24, run thus: "But what is done without this at all? Or to what thing is it not present? For everything that lies between heaven and earth is filled with spirit." And at section 18: the air, being perpetual and thin, preserves the perpetual course of the sun. He also soon calls it the vehicle of the earth [ὀχημα τῆς γῆς]. And at section 24: "Nothing anywhere is empty of spirit." And in text 6: "For mortals," he says, "the sole author of life and of sickness in the sick is this."

units.la: Quod si igitur Salsum, fixum & volatile, acidum, amarum, spiritus cum aliis corpus humanum constituunt, iisque omnis aut saltim primaria efficacia eorum, quæ in corpore contingunt, debetur; quæque adeò Hippocrati omnibusque Veteribus dicuntur primariæ potentiæ, in quibus, quatenus naturaliter aut præternaturaliter sese habent, Sanitas aut Morbus [illegible, ~6 letters]bus consistit, quæque insuper principes sunt Sanitatis & morborum causæ, à quibus homo semper atque in omni vitæ statu omnique ætate afficitur, ex quibus præterea omnia componuntur alimenta & medicamenta, quorum itidem præcipuæ facultates, sunt salsum, acidum, amarum & spiritus, uti præter Hippocratem omnesque Heroas, qui cum ipso veritatis vestigia presso pede sequuntur, Ratio & Experientia proteguantur; omninò sequitur D. Le Vasseur toti Antiquitati, rationi, & sensui communi contradicere, dum primen vocat, Sylvium, Practicum, cujus est Sanitatem protegere, morbosque propellere, in sua Praxi identidem eorum facere mentionem, sine quibus nec Sanitas conservari aut præservari, nec morbi profligari, neque symptomata mitigari possunt. Certè primen est, & capitale, non semper illa attendere, agyrtarum more solis generalibus, purgatione, phlebotomiâ & similibus, quibus isti sæpius nocent, quàm prosunt, contentum esse, atque primariis istis Medicinæ præsidiis turpiter neglectis, forte fortunâ sanare, adeoque & forte fortunâ interimere, ipsamque vitam humanam pariter atque divinam Artem prostituere. quasi, scilicet, jus vitæ & necis Doctoribus Medicinæ in quosvis competeret, illisque velut privilegio liceret humanas animas negotiari atque, Eumenidum furiarum more, hominibus vitam eripere, quibus eam diviti accepta mercede fraudulenter promittunt. Vide Hipp. de Vet. Med. Text. I. & II. de Lege Text. I. de Locis in homine Text. LVII. qui & alibi postquam Medicinam omnium Artium præclarissimam vocasset, ferio queritur, eam ineptorum istorum Pragmaticorum, quos vulgus pro veris Medicis veneratur, ignorantiâ prostitui: quos personatos Medicos graphicè describens, eos os personis Scenicis simillimos facit, uae habitu mentiuntur, quod reapse on sunt. & sane Medicinae titulo inignos esse, qui praecipuas sanitatis & morborum causas cum Le Vasseur gnorant, vel ipsorum injuria caesi protestantur.
units.tr: If, then, spirits constitute the human body together with salt, the fixed and the volatile, the acid and the bitter, and if all, or at least the chief efficacy, of what happens in the body is owed to them; and if these are the primary powers which Hippocrates and all the Ancients call such, and in which health or disease consists, insofar as they are disposed naturally or unnaturally; and if they are moreover the principal causes of health and disease, by which man is affected always, in every state of life and at every age; and if from them all foods and medicines are compounded, whose chief faculties likewise are salt, acid, bitter and spirits, as reason and experience confirm, besides Hippocrates and all the great men who followed the footsteps of truth with him; then it follows entirely that Dr. Le Vasseur contradicts all antiquity, reason and common sense, when he calls Sylvius, a practitioner whose office is to protect health and drive out disease, a man who in his own practice repeatedly mentions these things, without which neither health can be preserved or guarded, nor diseases overcome, nor symptoms relieved. Certainly it is a foolish and chief error not to attend to these things, to be content, in the manner of charlatans, with general remedies such as purging, bloodletting and the like, which these men harm more often than help; and, shamefully neglecting these primary safeguards of medicine, to cure by chance and so by chance to kill, thereby prostituting human life and the divine art alike, as if the right of life and death belonged to the doctors of medicine, and by some privilege it were lawful for them to traffic in human souls and, in the manner of the Furies, to snatch life from men whom, for a fraudulent reward, they promise to restore it. See Hippocrates, On Ancient Medicine, texts 1 and 2; On the Law, text 1; On Places in Man, text 57, who also elsewhere, after calling medicine the most distinguished of all arts, complains bitterly that it is debased by the ignorance of those quack pragmatists whom the crowd venerates as true physicians; describing these masked doctors vividly, he makes them very like stage actors, who pretend by their dress to be what in fact they are not. And indeed, those who are ignorant of the chief causes of health and disease, as Le Vasseur is, are proved to be unworthy of the title of medicine, or to be the injured victims of their own ignorance.

units.la: Judicet igitur oculatus Lector quid e Doctore Le Vasseur judicandum t. qui ignorans acidum, salsum, amaum & Spiritus, praecipuas Sanitatis z Morborum causas, Sylvio exporat, quod Salia fixa, volatilia, acida, piritus ad ravim usque ingeminet; uorum, uti visum, omnes apud Hipocratem paginae sunt plenissimae. ui Sylvium Novatorem & Veterum ibilatorem vocat, quia eam Mediciam docet, quae ipsi Hippocrati Veteum Medicina vocatur, quaeque, ut sa veritas, est vetustissima. Prodiiosae profecto memoriae nec dissimis judicii sit oportet, cui haec nova: ui velut venenatum monstrum traducit Praxin Medicam Sylvii, quia inter alia Spiritibus regendis, inque acido, salso, amaro, pro re nata excitandis, temperandis, digerendis, concoquendis, secernendis, concentrandis praecipitandis, vel etiam, si aut copia aut loco peccent, aut subigi nequeant, secernendis & excernendis est occupata. Cùm tamen Hippocrates Veterum Medicinam à plebejorum impostu-ris hoc praecipuè argumento distinguat, quòd plebeji circà calidum, frigidum, humidum & siccum sint occupati, Veterum autem Medicina in istorum causis saepius enumeratis conservandis, corrigendis aut tollendis primariò consistat, docens quid sit curare ex Arte, quid verò forte fortunâ: adeò ut Hippocrates de Vet. Med. Text. xxxix. Totam Medicinam revocet ad haec duo, videlicet; ad cognoscendas humorum facultates summas & figuras partium solidiorum: quarum constitutio, ut plurimùm, ab humorum norum temperie aut intemperie sive ictis potestatibus dependet : quam Veterum Artem tàm certo fundamento & methodo confirmatam statuit, ut eam Deorum donum, cælitùs humano generi concessum, dicitet, atque jure meritoque statuat præter hanc Veterum Artem nullam prorsùs aliam inveniri posse, atque errones & impostores esse, qui aliâ viâ aliaque forma Artem sese invenisse gloriantur. Verba illius, ita latinè sonant de Veterum Med. Text. III.15. Quicunque vero rejectis ac omnibus reprobatis, aliâ aliaque formâ inquirere conatur, & quid invenisse gloriatur, falsus est & salsitur.
units.tr: Let the attentive Reader therefore judge what is to be judged of Doctor Le Vasseur, who, ignorant of the acid, the salt, the bitter and the spirits, the principal causes of health and disease, reproaches Sylvius because he repeats the salts, fixed, volatile and acid, and the spirits, to the point of tedium; yet, as is plain, all the pages of Hippocrates are full of them. He calls Sylvius a Novator and a Destroyer of the Ancients, because he teaches that Medicine which is called by Hippocrates himself Ancient Medicine, and which, as the truth is, is most ancient. He must surely have a memory of prodigious quality and a judgment not unlike it, who brings forward these new things, and who, like a venomous monster, traduces the medical practice of Sylvius, because among other things it is occupied with governing the spirits, and with rousing, tempering, digesting, concocting, separating, concentrating and precipitating the acid, the salt and the bitter as the occasion demands, or even with separating and excreting them if they err in quantity or place, or cannot be subdued. Yet Hippocrates distinguishes Ancient Medicine from the trickery of the common people chiefly by this argument: that the common people are occupied with the hot, the cold, the moist and the dry, whereas Ancient Medicine consists chiefly in preserving, correcting or removing those causes of theirs which are so often enumerated, teaching what it is to cure by art and what to cure by chance. Accordingly, in On Ancient Medicine, Text 39, Hippocrates reduces the whole of Medicine to these two things, namely, to knowing the chief faculties of the humours and the figures of the solid parts: the constitution of which, for the most part, depends on the temperament or intemperament of the humours, or on their active powers. He establishes this Ancient Art on so certain a foundation and method that he calls it a gift of the gods, granted from heaven to the human race, and rightly and justly declares that no other art whatever can be found besides this Ancient Art, and that those who boast that they have found the Art by another way and in another form are wanderers and impostors. His words, in Latin, in On Ancient Medicine, Text 3.15, run: Whoever, however, rejecting and condemning all things, tries to search by one form or another, and boasts that he has found something, is mistaken and is deceived.

units.la: Si Doctori Le Vasseur, uti præ se fert, animus fuisset Praxin Sylvii refutare, probandum illi fuisset, Sylvium acida, salsa, volatilia & fixa, amara & spiritus aliaque sua simplicia & composita medicamenta, aut nunquam aut nunquam ex Arte præscripsisse, aut singulis lis curandi intentionibus distincte non satisfecisse.
units.tr: If Doctor Le Vasseur had truly intended, as he professes, to refute the practice of Sylvius, he would have had to prove that Sylvius either never prescribed, or prescribed contrary to the Art, the acid, salt, volatile and fixed, the bitter and the spirits, and his other simple and compound remedies, or that he did not satisfy each of the intentions of cure distinctly.

units.la: Pergit eodem quo cepit pede Sylvio officium Medici exprobrare, quia scilicet frequens illi de effervescentia & præcipitatione sermo est. At vero iteratò loqui audet de re, quæ captum suum superat, quapropter grave, quod hîc committit, vitium, multorum & propè dixerim, omnium, quos commisit, errorum causam penitùs expungi necesse est.
units.tr: He goes on with the same foot with which he began, upbraiding Sylvius for failing in the duty of a physician, because, of course, Sylvius often speaks of effervescence and precipitation. But he dares again to speak of a matter that exceeds his grasp; wherefore the serious fault he commits here must be wholly rooted out, as the cause of many, and I might almost say of all, the errors he has committed.

units.la: Quod ut ordine fiat, totum illius libellum, confusum chaos, ad methodum quandam reduci, necesse est, secundum quam examinabimus, 1. An tres illi humores, de quibus quæstio, in intestino tenui reperiantur. 2. An illorum dispositio sit subcontraria. 3. An inde exoriatur effervescentia in tenui intestino. 4. An cor vi effervescentiæ illius afficiatur, atque febris à quodam istius effervescentiæ vitio excitari possit.
units.tr: So that this may be done in order, his whole little book, a confused chaos, must be reduced to some method, according to which we shall examine: (1) whether those three humours in question are found in the small intestine; (2) whether their disposition is subcontrary; (3) whether effervescence arises from this in the small intestine; (4) whether the heart is affected by the force of that effervescence, and whether a fever can be excited by some fault of this effervescence.

units.la: Tres priores quæstiones determiat Sylvius hisce verbis, lib. 1. prareos suæ, cap. xi. 1. Non tantum, uandò è ventriculo ad intestina propeluntur alimenta fermentata, confluunt uoque in tenue Intestinum Bilis & Succus Pancreaticus; verum continuò, deoque illo etiam tempore, quo nullum ssumptum, vel ad Intestina deductum st alimentum, eò feruntur, ac necessaiò ibidem propter partium suarum dispotionem subcontrariam in Concursu suo Effervescentiam excitant, in Sanitatis uidem statu, hoc est,quandiu bene dispoitus, temperatusque est uterque, blaniam & Naturæ amicam; ubi verò aleruter, aut uterque intemperatus est, & acrior, vitiosam & noxiam. Quious sese opponens Le Vasseur, non quidem negat humores illos ibi repeiri: sed primùm carpit Sylvii phrain ,paginâ suâ 7. Mirabèris, inquit, ndefessum & inexplebile novandi stulium Sylvii, quia scilicet dixerat bilem & succum pancreaticum confluere in intestinum, quasi, inquit, unicum sit, nec distet a jejuno ἔκφυσις. Nae hic subtilis est Anatomicus! Quis non credat ipsum cum Herophilo sexcenta cadavera dissecuisse? Non animadvertit severus noster Censor Sylvium uti phrasibus Hippocratis, Galeni, Celsi. Adesdum Hippocrates, & manum tuam huic Orbilio subde; dixisti enim Lib. de affectionibus Text. XXIV. φοτέρ δὲ καὶ τὸ ἔντερον καὶ ἕυστην καὶ ἐλκοῦται, aegrotat autem & intestinum & raditur & exulceratur; similiter τῆς σύτερα mentionem facere non erubuisti, ibid. Text. XXII. 11. 14. 15. & infinitis aliis locis: quasi sex, quae recenseri solent, intestina, unicum esset, uti profecto unica duntaxat est fistula intestinalis. Eidem scilicet culpae assinis est Galenus, qui cap. 3. lib. v. de usu partium eundem bilis effluxum explicans de quo quaestio, eadem phrasi, qua Sylvius, mentionem facit it τῆς χολώδες ἀποπώμασι εἰς τὸ ἔντερον. ἐκπλώσεως. effluxus excrementi biliosi in intestinum. qui loquendi modi illis vitio erti non debent, cum alibi intestina, um opus est, satis accuratè distinguant. Nec minorem, scilicet, solœssimum committit Celsus, cap. 16. lib. iv. quod inscribit De tenuioris intestini morbis, & cap. sequenti, cujus summa emma fecit, De morbis intestini plenioribus. Usus igitur fuit Sylvius phrasi veterandi Triumviratûs, Hippocratis, Galeni atque Celsi, omnium, quotquot latinè de re Medica commentati sunt, Scriptorum accuratissimi, qui ducentum circiter & quinquaginta annos ante Galeni tempora floruit, atque rerum pondere, & singulari verborum proprietate omnium calculo Hippocrates Romanus appellatur, cui vir summæ auctoritatis, & illius æqualis, Columella lib. i. cap. i. summam in politiori literatura laudem tribuit, & cujus styli cultum & nitorem literatorum difertissimus Quintilianus meritis extollit laudibus, lib. 10. cap. 1. in hoc, inquam, concinnæ locutionis specimen, imo in sacro-sanctum illum Medicinæ Triumviratum injurius esse debuit, antequam Triumviratum Sylvii contumeliis posset lacessere. Lepidum est, Sylvium ut novatorem traduci, cum phrasibus utitur ipsius antiquitatis. Appositè sanè Hippocrates, inscitiæ prolem vocat audaciam. Neque enim, uti opinor, Le Vasseur unquam ausus fuisset Sylvio novandi studium objicere, quia intestinum tenue dixerat, numero singulari, si scivisset Veteres ita passim fuisse locutos.
units.tr: Sylvius determines the first three questions in these words, in Book 1 of his Praxis, chapter 11: Not only when the fermented foods are driven from the stomach into the intestines do the bile and the pancreatic juice flow together into the small intestine; but continually, and also at that time when no food has been taken or led down into the intestines, they are carried there, and necessarily there, on account of the subcontrary disposition of their parts, they excite effervescence in their meeting; in the state of health, that is, as long as each is well disposed and tempered, it is a pleasant thing and friendly to Nature; but when either or both is intemperate and sharper, it is harmful and noxious. Opposing this, Le Vasseur does not indeed deny that those humours are found there; but first he carps at Sylvius's phrase, on his page 7: You will be amazed, he says, at the tireless and insatiable itch of Sylvius for innovating, because he had said that bile and pancreatic juice flow together into the intestine, as if, he says, there were only one, and it did not differ from the jejunum, an ekphysis. Oh, what a subtle Anatomist here! Who would not believe that he had dissected six hundred corpses with Herophilus? Our stern Censor has not noticed that Sylvius uses the phrases of Hippocrates, Galen and Celsus. Come forward, Hippocrates, and submit your hand to this schoolmaster; for you said, in the book On Affections, Text 24: [ἀμφότερα δὲ τό τε ἔντερον καὶ ἐξυέται καὶ ἑλκοῦται] that is, the intestine also suffers, both is scraped and is ulcerated; and similarly you did not blush to make mention of the intestines [τὰ ἔντερα] in the same book, Text 22, sections 11, 14, 15, and in countless other places: as if the six intestines, which are commonly enumerated, were one, just as indeed there is only one intestinal tube. The same fault is charged against Galen, who, in Book 5, chapter 3, On the Use of the Parts, explaining the same flow of bile that is the subject of our question, speaks in the same phrase as Sylvius of [τῆς χολώδους ἀποπλύσεως εἰς τὸ ἔντερον], that is, the outflow of bilious excrement into the intestine. Such modes of speaking ought not to be counted as faults in them, since elsewhere they distinguish the intestines, when it is needed, quite accurately. Likewise, Celsus commits no lesser solecism, chapter 16 of Book 4, which he entitles On the Diseases of the Thinner Intestine, and in the following chapter, whose summary he made On the Diseases of the Fuller Intestine. Sylvius therefore used the phrase of that venerable triumvirate, Hippocrates, Galen and Celsus, the most accurate of all the writers who have treated of medicine in Latin; Hippocrates, who flourished about two hundred and fifty years before the time of Galen, is by the consensus of all, on account of the weight of his matter and the singular propriety of his words, called the Roman Hippocrates. To him Columella, a man of the highest authority and his contemporary, gives the highest praise in polished literature (Book 1, chapter 1), and the most eloquent Quintilian deservedly extols the cultivation and brilliance of his style with praise (Book 10, chapter 1). Upon this, I say, as a specimen of elegant expression, or rather upon that most sacred Triumvirate of Medicine, he ought to have been wronged before he could assail the Triumvirate of Sylvius with insults. It is a charming thing that Sylvius should be called an innovator when he uses the phrases of antiquity itself. Aptly indeed Hippocrates calls audacity the offspring of ignorance. For I think Le Vasseur would never have dared to charge Sylvius with the zeal for innovation because he said the small intestine in the singular, if he had known that the Ancients so commonly spoke in that way.

units.la: Præterea Bilem & succum pancreaticum semper in duodenum confluere negat, pag. 7. quia nihil in corpore, ut in universa natura frustra fit, ut est in omnium Philosophorum ore. At verò istud, quo axiomatis loco utitur, quodque ut omnium Philosophorum effatum ostentat, Galenus, qui illi Doctor irrefragabilis, atque Ariftoteles reprobant. Galenus quidem lib. 5. de usu partium, cap. 3. inquiens "Ἐνίοις ἐδέμιλαν χρείαν γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπέρχεσ ἐξ ἀνάγ-κης ἕπεσθαι, ἃ δὲ μέρεα εἶναι, ἀλλὰ τινὰ σύμ-πλοκα, quædam fieri nullius usus gratia, sed sequi quædam alia, quæ fiunt necessariò, non ut partes, sed ut quædam simul concincidentia. Et paulò post ait, hinc intelligitur, hanc quidem primorum involucrorum inanitionem nullius usus causa exstitisse, quod & alibi dixerat. Aristoteles verò 8. Metaph. cap. 4. ubi inquirens in causam Eclipseos nullam illius agnoscit materiam præter lunam quæ patitur: causa autem agens & corrumpens lumen lunæ illi est terra, τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἕνεκα ἵνας οὐκ ἐστι[?], at causa finalis hîc nulla est. Et certè vana & fallax est sententia Doctoris Le Vasseur, si putet nihil frustra fieri, significare, omnia intendere finem, uti sunt quàm plurimi, eodem lacte, quo Le Vasseur, enutri-ti, ti, qui hujus commenti gratiâ, multiplicem appetitum & intentionem etiam ex ficto quodam instinctu sine ulla rei appetentis cognitione comminiscuntur. Etenim cum finis nihil aliud sit quàm propositum, quod mediis acquirere studemus, constat, finem non nisi à ratione utentibus intendi. Quicquid sit, quamvis, ut de rebus majoris momenti nihil dicam, singulæ omnium fluctuum maris agitationes, omnium graminum, cæterarumque herbarum, foliorum & ramusculorum omnium arborum, omniumque miasmatum, cæterorumque insensibilium totius mundi motus non sint frustra, cum opus naturæ sit opus intelligentiæ, non tamen illi dicendum fuisset, hoc verum esse ex omnium Philosophorum mente, utpote qui Galenum appellat omniscium atque jurat in verba Aristotelis, qui ambo è diametro Doctori Le Vasseur contradicunt, uti visum est. Sed quid inde? [?]nde? In corpore, inquit, ut in universa natura nihil frustra fit; Ergò Bilis & Succus pancreaticus non fluunt in Intestinum duodenum, etiam illo tempore ...
units.tr: Furthermore, he denies (p. 7) that bile and pancreatic juice always flow together into the duodenum, because nothing in the body is done in vain, as in the whole of nature, as is on the lips of all philosophers. But that maxim, which he uses as an axiom and presents as the saying of all philosophers, is in fact rejected by Galen, whom he calls his irrefragable doctor, and by Aristotle. Galen, in book 5 of On the Use of the Parts, chapter 3, says: "Some things come about for no use, but follow of necessity; these are not parts but certain concomitants [Ἐνίοις ἐδέμιλαν χρείαν γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπέρχεσ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἕπεσθαι, ἃ δὲ μέρεα εἶναι, ἀλλὰ τινὰ σύμπλοκα]: some things are made for no use, but certain other things follow them, which come about of necessity, not as parts but as things happening together. And a little later he says: hence it is understood that this emptiness of the first envelopes existed for no use, which he had also said elsewhere. Aristotle, in book 8 of the Metaphysics, chapter 4, where he inquires into the cause of an eclipse, recognises no matter for it except the moon, which suffers the eclipse; the agent and cause that obstructs the light of the moon is the earth, but the final cause [τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἕνεκα ἵνας οὐκ ἐστι[?]] is none here. Certainly the opinion of Doctor Le Vasseur is empty and false, if he thinks that nothing is done in vain means that all things aim at an end, as many do who were nursed on the same milk as Le Vasseur, and who, to support this fiction, invent a manifold appetite and intention even from some imaginary instinct without any knowledge in the thing that desires. For since an end is nothing other than the purpose which we strive to attain by means, it is clear that an end is aimed at only by those who use reason. Be that as it may: although I say nothing of matters of greater moment, the single movements of all the waves of the sea, of all the grasses and other herbs, of the leaves and twigs of all trees, and of all vapours and other insensible motions of the whole world are not in vain, since the work of nature is the work of intelligence. Yet he should not have said that this is true by the mind of all philosophers, since they call Galen all-knowing and swear by the words of Aristotle, and both of them, as has been seen, contradict Doctor Le Vasseur directly. But what follows from this? In the body, he says, as in the whole of nature, nothing is done in vain; therefore the bile and pancreatic juice do not flow into the duodenum, even at that time…

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] tilia pondera ventris commodè excernantur, uti de Bile loquitur Galenus lib. v. de usu part. cap. 3. Nec hoc tantum, sed & affluentes illi humores incidunt pituitam viscidam, qua intestinorum parietes si non purgarentur nimium conspurcarentur & incrustarentur, utpote quæ etiam naturaliter disposita sunt loca τελμαπώδεα, paludosa, cænosa, putredinibus apta, uti loquitur Galenus lib. de gland. ad Hipp. quâ pituitâ sensus intestinorum nimium obtunderetur, atque venarum lactearum pori, aliiqué per quos segregatus chylus ad reliquum corpus affluit, occluderentur & obstruerentur, qualem fere usum, quia Galeni tempore pancreas, hoc demum seculo à Wirzungio inventum, nondum innotuerat, soli quoque bili adscripsit, quod utrique humori, videlicet bili & succo pancreatico competit; postquam enim demonstrasset pituitæ copiam in intestino gigni, niniam miam illius copiam tolli docet, L.v. de usu part. c. inquiens, necessarium igitur esse, tum in Ventriculo, tum in intestinis ejusmodi excrementi, videlicet pituitosi, proventum, alibi ut dixi demonstravimus. Caeterum, quod generetur, declarat tum anatome, tum etiam morbi, quibus quotidie homines prehenduntur, ab hujusmodi superfluorum abundantia. Quorum curatio est simplex, eorum scilicet, quae crassa ac viscosa dividere, incidere, atque abstergere possunt, exhibitio. Ob eam igitur causam mox a principio natura praesidium ipsis comparavit, acrem atque abstersorium hunc succum, quem omnino oportebat e corpore secerni, non in intestinum aliquod ano propinquum, sed in primam ecphysin, nec aliquod inferiorum intestinorum externo aliquando indigeret auxilio. Porro, quamdiu recte animalis corpus gubernatur, pituitosum excrementum quotidie ipsi detergetur.
units.tr: [illegible, ~40 letters] that the heavy burdens of the belly may be conveniently discharged, as Galen speaks of bile in book 5 of On the Use of the Parts, chapter 3. And not only this, but those humours flowing in also fall upon the viscous phlegm, which, if the walls of the intestines were not cleansed, would be too much fouled and encrusted, since these places are naturally disposed to be τελμαπώδεα, paludosa, cænosa, putredinibus apta [marshy, swampy, muddy, apt for putrefaction], as Galen speaks in his book On the Glands, to Hippocrates. By this phlegm the sense of the intestines would be too much dulled, and the pores of the lacteal veins, and the others through which the separated chyle flows to the rest of the body, would be closed and blocked up. Galen, because in his time the pancreas, discovered only in this century by Wirsung, was not yet known, ascribed almost this same use to bile alone, which belongs to both humours, namely bile and pancreatic juice. For after demonstrating that phlegm is generated in the intestine, he teaches that its excessive quantity is removed; in book 5 of On the Use of the Parts, chapter [?], he says: it is therefore necessary that there be a supply of such excrement, that is, of phlegmatic matter, both in the stomach and in the intestines, as I have shown elsewhere. Moreover, that it is generated is declared both by anatomy and by the diseases, which men daily suffer from an abundance of such superfluities. Their cure is simple, namely the administration of things which can divide, cut and wipe away what is thick and viscous. For this reason, therefore, from the very beginning nature provided for them a remedy, this sharp and cleansing juice, which had to be secreted from the body altogether, not into some intestine near the anus, but into the first passage; nor would any of the lower intestines ever need external help. Furthermore, as long as the animal body is rightly governed, the phlegmatic excrement is cleansed away from it every day.

units.la: At, cum ex pravo quopiam corporis affectu copiosius est collectum, nihil addubitant Medicorum præstantissimi, quin ilei, lienteriæ, ac tenesmi, omnium, qui ventri contingunt, morborum gravissimi sint secuturi. Non contemnendum itaque, neque translatitium quiddam natura ad sanitatem animalibus ex opportuna meatus biliosi (& pancreatici) immissione prospexit. Taceo hoscce humores naturaliter constitutos intestina à putredine præservare, & denique ne hoc quidem sequitur quod in intestinis nihil operatur, frustra in illa effunditur; poslet enim in ea effundi ut excernatur. uti pars magna & comprimis Crassior Bilis & Succi pancreatici. quos omnes usus qui ignorat, næ ille in Medicina hospes est! Quia igitur præter primum illum usum, quo diximus bilem & succum pancreaticum chylo permisceri, ut purior illius pars ab eo segregetur, multiplices alios assignavimus, sequitur etiam seposito primo illo usu bilem & succum pancreaticum non frustra ad intestina propelli, etiam tum temporis, quando è ventriculo ad intestina alimenta fermentata non propelluntur: adeoque hîc nihil otiosum esse præter rudem censuram Doctoris Le Vasseur; Imò quia hoc loco negat bilem & Succum pancreaticum in duodenum profluere, cum nullum ad intestina deducitur alimentum; atque pag. 16. negat quoque bilem ad intestina profluere cum alimentum sive cibus in stomacho fermentatus eò deducitur, sequitur ex absona hac Doctoris Le Vasseur sententia omninò frustra esse duƈtum bilarium intestinalem tam manifestum, & per quem bilem effundi, præter auƈtoritatem Galeni modò citatam, manifestissimâ probatur experientiâ, adeò ut ex frustra proposita illius argumentatione sequatur aliquid in humano corpore frustra esse, quod, velut prorsus absonum, totius illius disputationis basim posuerat. At v. horum trium humorum in intestinis existentiam & affluxum infrà ratione, experientia & αὐτοψία manifestissimè constabit.
units.tr: But when a larger quantity has been gathered from some bad condition of the body, the most outstanding physicians do not doubt that the ileus, lientery and tenesmus, the most grievous of all the diseases which befall the belly, will follow. Therefore nature provided for the health of animals, by the timely admission of the biliary (and pancreatic) duct, something not to be despised and not foreign to them. I say nothing of how these humours, as naturally constituted, preserve the intestines from putrefaction; and finally, it does not follow that what is poured into the intestines does nothing there and is poured in in vain, for it could be poured in so that it is expelled, as a large part of the thicker bile and pancreatic juice is. Whoever does not know all these uses, indeed, is a stranger to medicine! Therefore, since besides that first use, by which we said the bile and pancreatic juice are mixed with the chyle so that the purer part of it is separated from it, we have assigned many other uses, it follows that, even setting aside that first use, the bile and pancreatic juice are not driven into the intestines in vain, even at that time when fermented food is not being driven from the stomach into the intestines. Thus nothing here is idle, except by the crude judgement of Doctor Le Vasseur. Indeed, because here he denies that bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum when no food is conveyed to the intestines, and at p. 16 he likewise denies that bile flows into the intestines when food or fermented matter is carried there from the stomach, it follows from this absurd opinion of Doctor Le Vasseur that the intestinal biliary duct, so manifest and through which bile is poured out, is quite in vain. This is proved not only by the authority of Galen just cited but by the plainest experience, so that from the argument he has put forward in vain it would follow that something in the human body is in vain, which, as utterly absurd, he had laid down as the basis of his whole disquisition. But the existence and inflow of these three humours into the intestines will be most plainly established below by reason, by experience and by autopsy [αὐτοψία].

units.la: Non minori argutiâ Sylvium taxat pag.8. quòd Succo pancreatico & bili partium dispositionem adscripserit, quam Sylvii phrasiologiam sub finem ejusdem paginæ Idiotismum & Acurologiam vocat, postquam supra dixisset hunc, vel si mavis, hanc, scilicet humorum dispositionem, non capio. Nec mirum quandoquidem nihil capit nisi sensibus, nisi quod videt, pag. 11. & 12.Sed addere conatur rationem,nam, inquit, si diathesin cum Philosophis intellexit, res est ab hoc loco abhorrens, ubi de potentiis naturalibus agitur, diversa videlicet qualitatum classe., ubi certè nihil dicendo, multa dixisse videtur: sed quid istud monstri? si diathesin cum Philosophis intellexit, Anne Medicus eandem rem aliter intelligere, id est, verè percipere potest, quam veri Philosophi, id est, veritatis assertores? Toto coelo errant, qui Medicinam à Philosophia tanto intervallo sejunctam putant, utpote quæ nihil quicquam est præter applicationem philosophicorum dogmatum ad praxin. Cum igitur Medicus nil rectè agere possit, nisi intellecta rei, circa quam versatur, essentiâ, atque mutationibus quæ illi accidere possunt, accuratè penficulatis, cujus ideas generaliores Philosophia tradit: Sequitur veram Philosophiam cum vera Medicina convenire, & vice versa: adeò ut Medicus φιλόσοφος, sit Asinus ad Lyram: contra verò ἀντὶς φιλόσοφος ἰσόξεος, hinc toties philosophiam Medicis enixè commendat Hipp.: ut liquet vel ex dictis p. 23. sed quid opus est Virum tantum testem adducere ubi res ipsa loquitur. Quia igitur Bilis falsa est & amara, Succus verò pancreaticus acidus, omnino sequitur humores illos tales esse per certam suarum particularum dispositionem: sive enim illarum particularum præcisè & velut in abstracto consideratarum constitutio consideretur, aliter esse dispositas particulas salsas, quàm acidas, effecta utrarumque manifestè diversa palàm indigitant. Hinc est quod salinæ particulæ pungant, acidæ, utpote minus rigidæ & flexiliores, scindant, uti accuratè docet des Cartes lib.de homine: sed & in se mutuò agunt, sese mutuò temperant & uti liquet post effervescentiam Spiritus salis, aut Vitrioli & tartari, aut salis volatilis; ergo diversæ sunt & contrariæ, aut, uti post clarius innotescet, subcontrariæ dispositionis: valdè erroneum est, corporibus diversa operantibus partium dispositionem negare, quia per se in oculos non incurrit, certè particulis acidis & salsis, quia corpora sunt, licet parva, non minus positura, id est, partium dispositio atque situs competit, quam corporibus majoribus: quod Le Vasseur, pag. 8. existimat plane ad rem non facere: quin etiam dispositio convenit hisce humoribus ratione craseos sive temperamenti, unde denominantur acidi, salsi & amari; temperamentum enim requirit certum situm & ordinem particularum sibi permixtarum, qualis in liquido servari potest & debet, sine quibus mixtio aut temperamentum ne concipi quidem potest: adeò ut violatâ illâ particularum positurâ atque ordine sive per præcipitationem, sublimationem, aliamve illarum à se mutuò separationem, unio illa partium dissolvatur, qua miscibilia illa suo modo jungebantur: mixtio enim definiente Aristotele, est miscibilium alteratorum unio, unde Temperies sine mutua habitudine, dispositione situ & respectu partium ne concipi quidem potest. Humoribus denique istis rectè tribuitur dispositio, quatenus à qualitatibus, quibus præditæ sunt, illis est facilitas sua peragendi. Sed quandoquidem rationes minus capit, capiat authoritatem. Galenus certè sanitatem definit, quod sit, Διάθεσις κατὰ φύσιν ἐνεργείας ποιητικὴ, Dispositio secundum naturam actiones edens. Ubi nota Dispositionem per potentiam activam explicari. Similiter Galenus morbum vocat Διάθεσιν παρὰ φύσιν. quia igitur sanitas & morbus sunt Diathefes, definiente Galeno, sequitur si humoribus competat sanitas & morbus, iis omninò dispositionem quandam competere. Hùc facit Hippocrates libro de affectionibus Textu XXIV.10. νοσεῖ τὸ αἷμα, ἢ ἀλλοχρεῖ ἐφθαρμένον, ægrotat sanguis & corruptus secedit. si ægrotat malè dispositus, procul dubio sanus erit bene dispositus, adeoque & utraque diathesis, εὐδιάθετος nempe & κακοδιάθετος humoribus competit. Hinc etiam sanguini εὐξία accidit, sive bonus, & nimis bonus habitus, Aph. 3. Secti. 1. & morbus ratione humorum nondum prorsus vitiatorum, quique adeò nondum acquisiverunt habitum, dicuntur ἀτελεῖς[?], in dispositione, ut ab ἕξεως, jam in habitum conversis, distinguantur. Rectè igitur Clariss. Sylvius partium dispositionem humoribus illis attribuit. Sed objicit Le Vasseur p.8.dispositionem non posse esse potentiam naturalem, quandoquidem dispositio & potentia naturalis in diversa qualitatum classe videntur contineri. quamvis istud parum ad rem, nam Sylvius illud non asserit; Revereatur tamen primùm auctoritatem Hippocratis,quem ut Numen, quamvis sibi ignotum,adorat, qui libro de Vet. Med. humores acidos, salsos & amaros, quique eatenus ad tertiam qualitatis speciem spectant, non semel vocat δυνάμεις sive potentias, quibus insuper dispositionem propriè competere suprà abundè demonstravimus. Præterea potentiam, etiam consistere in temperie, quam ex miscibilium mixtione
units.tr: Sylvius is criticised with no less subtlety at p. 8 for having ascribed to the pancreatic juice and the bile a disposition of their parts. Sylvius's phrasing, which at the end of the same page he calls idiotism and barbarous usage, comes after he had said that he does not understand this (or, if you prefer, this), namely disposition of the humours. That is no surprise, since he understands nothing except through the senses, nothing except what he sees (pp. 11 and 12). But he tries to give a reason: if he understood "diathesis" as the Philosophers do, it is a thing out of place here, where we are dealing with natural powers, that is, in a different class of qualities. Here he seems to say a great deal while saying nothing. But what monstrous thing is this? If he understood "diathesis" as the Philosophers do, can the Physician not understand the same thing differently, that is, truly perceive it, than the true Philosophers, that is, the advocates of truth, do? Those are wholly mistaken who think that Medicine is separated from Philosophy by so great a distance, as if it were nothing more than the application of philosophical doctrines to practice.
