Since therefore the Physician can do nothing rightly unless he has understood the essence of the thing with which he deals, and has carefully examined the changes that can befall it, whose more general ideas Philosophy teaches, it follows that true Philosophy agrees with true Medicine, and conversely, so that the Physician who is a philosopher is no ass at the lyre; on the contrary, the philosopher who is not a physician is an ass at the lyre. Hence Hippocrates so often earnestly commends philosophy to physicians, as is clear even from what was said at p. 23. But why bring in a man as witness when the thing itself speaks? Since therefore bile is bitter and false, and pancreatic juice is acid, it certainly follows that these humours are such through a certain disposition of their particles. For whether one considers the constitution of those particles precisely and as if taken in the abstract, the salty particles are disposed differently from the acid ones, and the clearly different effects of each plainly point this out. Hence salty particles prick, while acid particles, being less rigid and more flexible, cut, as Descartes teaches accurately in his book On Man. Moreover they act upon one another and temper one another, as is clear after the effervescence of spirit of salt, or of vitriol and tartar, or of volatile salt. Therefore they are of different and contrary dispositions, or, as will become clearer afterwards, of a somewhat contrary disposition. It is quite wrong to deny a disposition of parts to bodies that produce different effects merely because it does not fall directly under the eyes. Certainly to acid and salty particles, since they are bodies, though small, position, that is, arrangement and situation, belongs no less than to larger bodies. Le Vasseur, at p. 8, thinks this plainly has nothing to do with the matter. Indeed, disposition also belongs to these humours by reason of their crasis or temperament, from which they are called acid, salty and bitter. For temperament requires a definite situation and order of the particles mixed together, such as can and must be kept in a liquid, and without which mixture or temperament cannot even be conceived. So when that position and order of the particles is violated, whether by precipitation, sublimation, or some other separation of them from one another, that union of parts is dissolved by which those miscible things were joined in their own way. For mixture, as Aristotle defines it, is the union of altered miscibles; hence temperament cannot even be conceived without mutual relation, disposition, situation and respect of the parts. Finally, disposition is rightly ascribed to these humours in so far as their ease of acting comes from the qualities with which they are endowed. But since he understands the reasons less, let him grasp the authority. Galen certainly defines health as being a disposition according to nature producing actions [Διάθεσις κατὰ φύσιν ἐνεργείας ποιητικὴ], a disposition according to nature producing actions. Note here that disposition is explained through an active power. Similarly Galen calls disease a disposition contrary to nature [Διάθεσιν παρὰ φύσιν]. Therefore, since health and disease are dispositions, as Galen defines them, it follows that if health and disease belong to humours, some disposition belongs to them entirely. Hippocrates in his book On Affections, text 24.10, bears on this: the blood falls sick, or, corrupted, it secedes from the mixture [νοσεῖ τὸ αἷμα, ἢ ἀλλοχρεῖ ἐφθαρμένον]. If blood falls sick when ill disposed, it will undoubtedly be healthy when well disposed, and so both dispositions, the good disposition [εὐδιάθετος] and the bad disposition [κακοδιάθετος], belong to humours. Hence also blood acquires plethora [εὐξία], that is, a good and overly good state, Aphorisms 3, section 1. And a disease with respect to humours not yet wholly vitiated, which have therefore not yet acquired a state, are called imperfect [ἀτελεῖς] in disposition, so that they are distinguished from those already converted into a state [ἕξις]. Rightly therefore the most distinguished Sylvius attributes a disposition of parts to those humours. But Le Vasseur objects at p. 8 that disposition cannot be a natural power, since disposition and natural power seem to be contained in a different class of qualities. Yet this has little to do with the matter, for Sylvius does not assert that. Nevertheless let him first show reverence to the authority of Hippocrates, whom he adores as a divinity, though unknown to him. In his book On Ancient Medicine Hippocrates more than once calls the acid, salty and bitter humours, which so far belong to the third species of quality, powers [δυνάμεις], to which, moreover, we have above amply shown that disposition properly belongs. Further, that power also consists in temperament, which arises from the mixture of miscibles,

units.la: Hippocratis: Hippocrates. Hippocratis atque adeò certa quadam dispositione constare modò probavimus, docet illud Galenus totidem verbis Lib. de præcognitione ex pulsu, inquiens ἡ ἐσία τὴν δυναμέως ἐνάσχ τ μ̓ελίων ἐν τῇ καθ' ἕκαστον αὐτῶν διαφορίᾳ τέπαντεν, facultatis essentia singularum partium ( dicamus potiùs humorum ) in singularum illarum bono temperamento consistit. Si igitur Galeno εὐκρασία est εὐδιάθεσις, sive bona dispositio ( nam esse morbos intemperiei, quos δυσκρασίας vocat, modò fuit probatum ) sequitur omnino dispositionem eam quâ acidum est acidum, & eadem est falsi & amari & reliquorum ratio, revera esse potentiam naturalem. Quod non minùs manifestum est ex vulgaribus principiis logicis, cum quibus putabat sententiam Sylvii è diametro pugnare: etenim amaritudo bilis, & eadem est ratio aciditatis succi pancreatici, ex illa vulgari, quam sequitur, sententia, est patibilis qualitas, adeoque ad tertiam qualitatis speciem refertur, utpote quæ efficit passionem in sensu: & quia efficit, sive facit, est potentia, vis, Virtus, & efficacia sive facultas, eoque sensu etiam est potentia naturalis adeoque ad secundam qualitatis speciem pertinet, & quatenus eadem illa qualitas est humoribus adventitia ad operandum cum facilitate, χελικὴ ἢ ἐχελικὴ, ad quod efficiendum sunt idonei, ad primam qualitatis speciem revocari possunt; idem ergò non modò ad duas, sed & ad tres qualitatis species revocari potest. Quin etiam citatis verbis Arist.lib.iv. Metaphys. cap.12. Artem οἱ δυναμικὴ καὶ ἰατρικὴ vocat δυνάμεις.phrasi ab Hippocrate mutuatâ, quâ uti alibi utitur, ita & lib. de Vet. Med. xxxix. 5. ubi novisse summas vires & robur potentiarum Δυνάμων vocat. Cum tamen ars sit in prima qualitatis specie,potentia verò in secunda. Discat igitur Le Vasseur rerum, veritatem ad vulgarem illam Logicam, regulam Lesbiam, non esse examinandam: sed vitiosam Logicam secundum rerum veritatem, quod unicum solidi judici fundamentum est, prudenter reformare. Hoc ni fallor voluit Hippocrates, docens, Philosophos à Medicis hæc & similia discere oportere. Quamvis & vulgaris illius Logicæ Commentatores putent res in Categoriis dispositas omnes non differre κατ' ἐσίαν, sed sufficere si Distinguan-tur κατὰ τόπον τῆς χρήμας τῆς κατηγορίας.
units.tr: Hippocrates: Hippocrates. Hippocrates, and therefore consists in a certain definite disposition, as we have just proved. Galen teaches this in the same words in his book On Prognosis from the Pulse, saying: the essence of the faculty of each part (let us rather say of the humours) consists in the good temperament of each of those parts [ἡ οὐσία τῆς δυνάμεως ἑκάστου τῶν μορίων ἐν τῇ καθ' ἕκαστον αὐτῶν εὐκρασίᾳ]. If therefore for Galen good crasis is good disposition [εὐδιάθεσις], that is, a good disposition (for that diseases of bad temperament, which he calls dyscrasias [δυσκρασίαι], are diseases of intemperance has just been proved), it follows entirely that the disposition by which the acid is acid, and the same reasoning for the bitter and the salty and the rest, is in truth a natural power. This is no less clear from the common principles of logic, with which he thought Sylvius's opinion was in flat contradiction. For the bitterness of bile, and the same reasoning applies to the acidity of pancreatic juice, according to the common doctrine which he follows, is a passible quality, and so is referred to the third species of quality, as what produces a passion in the sense. And because it produces, or makes, it is a power, strength, virtue, and efficacy or faculty; and in that sense it is also a natural power, and so belongs to the second species of quality. And in so far as that same quality is adventitious to the humours, for acting with facility, capable [δεικτικὴ ἢ ἐνεργητικὴ] of bringing about this effect, it can be referred to the first species of quality. The same thing therefore can be referred not only to two but to three species of quality. Indeed, in the passage of Aristotle cited, Metaphysics Book IV, chapter 12, he calls the art of medicine powers [δυνάμεις], using a phrase borrowed from Hippocrates, which he uses elsewhere, and also in the book On Ancient Medicine, chapter 39, section 5, where he calls the knowledge of the greatest powers and strength of potencies powers. Yet art belongs to the first species of quality, while power belongs to the second. Let Le Vasseur therefore learn that the truth of things is not to be tested by that common logic, the Lesbian rule, but that a faulty logic must be prudently reformed according to the truth of things, which is the only solid foundation of sound judgement. This, if I am not mistaken, is what Hippocrates meant, teaching that Philosophers ought to learn these and similar things from Physicians. Although even the commentators on that common logic think that all things arranged in the Categories do not differ in substance, but that it is enough if they are distinguished by the place of the question of the category.

units.la: Rectè igitur & Hippocraticè huc usque Sylvius tribuit humoribus dispositionem. Neque repugnat dispositionem esse potentiam naturalem, uti miserrimus putabat Philosophus.
units.tr: Rightly and in Hippocrates' manner, Sylvius has so far attributed a disposition to the humours. Nor does it conflict with this that disposition is a natural power, as that most wretched philosopher thought.

units.la: Sed offendit porrò Doctorem Le Vasseur dispositionem Succi pancreatici & Bilis à Sylvio statui sibi mutuò subcontrariam. Adeò nihil à Sylvio prosectum est quod illi placet: Subcontrarietas tamen utriusque Succi ad sese mutuò probatur, quia & Sylvius Praxeos eos suæ, cap. 10. paragr. 7. & 10. statuit, & Le Vasseur palam agnoscit Succum pancreatis subacidum esse, bilem vero naturaliter amaram, non quidem semper, uti opinor, summo excessu, qualis est æruginosa & acerrima, sed subamaram & subsalsam, quòd nemo, uti opinor, ibit inficias: qua propter, quia sub-acida & sub-amara & subsalsa sunt subcontrariæ dispositionis, omninò sequitur bilem & Succum pancreaticum esse dispositionis subcontrariæ.
units.tr: But further, Doctor Le Vasseur takes offence that Sylvius has set the disposition of the pancreatic juice and of the bile as mutually subcontrary. So little has Sylvius done anything that pleases him. Yet the subcontrariety of each of these juices to the other is proved, because Sylvius, in his Praxis, chapter 10, paragraphs 7 and 10, establishes them as such, and Le Vasseur openly acknowledges that the pancreatic juice is subacid, while bile is naturally bitter, though not always, I think, to the highest degree, as is the verdigris-like and most acrid kind, but subbitter and subsalt. No one, I think, will deny this. Therefore, since the subacid, the subbitter and the subsalt are of subcontrary disposition, it follows entirely that bile and the pancreatic juice are of subcontrary disposition.

units.la: Doctorem autem Le Vasseur fateri Succum pancreaticum esse subacidum, liquet ex illius pag. 19. ubi inquit, Succum pancreaticum aliquando duntaxat acrem, sæpe sæpius lanquidè acescentem, id est, uti illud interpretor, ordinariò subacidum esse, quotidiana, inquit, & antiqua Veslingii observatione constat. Quapropter quia acida & amara mutuâ actione effervescunt magis minusve pro ratione majoris aut minoris acrimoniæ utriusque; magis etiam vel minus in sese mutuo agunt, sese mutuò infringunt & temperant. Acerrima quidem, utpote contraria, majori vi & ebullitione; minus autem acria minori; fermè verò temperata, utpote subcontraria, acida & amara blandâ effervescentiâ concitari docet Sylvius praxeos suae cap. II. I & ratione & experientiâ infra probabitur. Sufficiat hoc loco Hippocratis authoritas qui libro de victu acutorum textu XXIX. 8. 9. docet amara dissolvi & in phlegma transfire, frigidiora & insipida reddi, μετα-πεξόμενα ὑπὸ ὀξέος, effervescentiam passa cum acido: effervescit igitur bilis cum Succo subacido pancreatico. Quin etiam ipse Le Vasseur pag. 18. expressis verbis dicit, acida bilem frangere, compescere, mitigare, (sed vocem μεταπεξόμενα qua usus fuerat Hippocrates, ne sibi palam contradiceret, ibi oblitus esset latinè vertere) quod & authoritate omniscii, uti ibi loqui amat, Galeni probat. Certè quæ talia sunt, esse subcontraria nec prorsus similia & ratio docet, simile enim non agit in simile, & authoritas tùm Aristotelis dicentis contraria esse, quæ adversis qualitatibus se mutuò destruunt; tum Hippocratis Aph. 22. S. 11. docentis subcontraria esse subcontrariorum remedia: postquam enim dixisset morbos qui ex repletione fiunt, curat evacuatio, eos verò, qui ex evacuatione, repletio, subjicit ἡ δὲ ἀλλων ἡ ὑπενανϊίωσις, & in cæteris subcontrarietas remedio est. Nota ibi ὑπεναντίωσις subcontrarietatis nomen, quo Sylvius cum Hippocrate usus fuerat; quod quidem in Libro Aphorismorum minus accuratè verti solet per contrarietatem, sed libro de Vet. Med. xxvii. 8. ὑπεναντίωσις per subcontraria diserte explicantur. quod addo, quia subcontrarietatis nomen novum videtur, aut durum nostro Doctori. ὑπεναντίωσις autem Aristoteli dicuntur ὑπεναντία μεταξύ, quod interpres recte
units.tr: That Doctor Le Vasseur admits the pancreatic juice is subacid is clear from his page 19, where he says: the pancreatic juice is only sometimes sharp, but very often feebly turning sour. That is, as I interpret it, it is ordinarily subacid. This is established, he says, by daily observation and by the old observation of Vesling. Therefore, since acid and bitter substances effervesce with one another, more or less according to the degree of greater or lesser sharpness of each, they also act upon one another more or less, they mutually break and temper one another. Sylvius, in chapter 11 of his Praxis, teaches that the most acrid, being contrary, fight with greater force and effervescence, while the less acrid do so with less; and that the nearly temperate, being subcontrary, are stirred up by a gentle effervescence. This will also be proved below by reason and experience. For the present, let the authority of Hippocrates suffice, who, in the book On the Diet of Acute Diseases, text 29 (8, 9), teaches that bitter things are dissolved and pass into phlegm, and are made colder and tasteless, being affected by an acid [μεταπεξόμενα ὑπὸ ὀξέος], having undergone effervescence with the acid. Therefore bile effervesces with the subacid pancreatic juice. Indeed, Le Vasseur himself, on page 18, says in so many words that acids break, check and soften bile (but he forgot to translate into Latin the word μεταπεξόμενα that Hippocrates had used, lest he should openly contradict himself there), and he proves this by the authority of Galen, the all-knowing, as he likes to call him. Certainly things of this kind are subcontrary and not wholly alike, and reason teaches this too, for like does not act upon like. The authority of Aristotle also agrees, who says that contraries are those which destroy each other by opposing qualities; and that of Hippocrates in Aphorism 22, section 11, who teaches that subcontraries are the remedies of subcontraries. For after saying diseases that arise from repletion are cured by evacuation, and those from evacuation by repletion, he adds [ἡ δὲ ἀλλων ἡ ὑπεναντίωσις], and in other cases subcontrariety is the remedy. Note here that ὑπεναντίωσις is the name of subcontrariety, which Sylvius used together with Hippocrates. In the Aphorisms this is usually translated rather carelessly as contrariety, but in the book On Ancient Medicine, chapter 27, section 8, ὑπεναντίωσις is clearly explained as subcontraries. I add this because the word subcontrariety seems new or harsh to our Doctor. Aristotle calls ὑπεναντία [ὑπεναντία μεταξύ] which the translator rightly

units.la: Verba Hippocratis in Aphorismis, sectione 2, aphorismo 11, in Latino corrupta vertuntur. recte vocavit contraria media. Et quemadmodum modo ex Hippocrat adduximus ἐναντιότης ... μέσα. Sic etiam Hippocr. lib. de flatibus inquit, τὰ ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων ἐστὶν ἡ μέσα, contraria contrariorum sunt remedia.
units.tr: The words of Hippocrates in the Aphorisms, section 2, aphorism 11, are rendered corruptly in the Latin. He rightly called them intermediate contraries. And just as we have just adduced from Hippocrates [ἐναντιότης] ... [μέσα], so too Hippocrates, in the book On Flatulence, says [τὰ ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων ἐστὶν ἡ μέσα], that is, contraries are the remedies of contraries.

units.la: Contraria enim atque subcontraria vires sibi mutuò frangunt, alterumque alterius actione remittitur. Discat illud praeter mille experimenta, nam princeps curandi ratio in eo consistit, ex Aristot. de Gen. & Corr. Lib. I. cap. 7. docente φανερὸν ὅτι πο-
units.tr: For contraries and subcontraries break each other's force, and the one is checked by the action of the other. Let him learn this, apart from a thousand experiments, for the chief method of healing rests on it, as Aristotle teaches in On Generation and Corruption, book 1, chapter 7, where he says [φανερὸν ὅτι ποιητικὸν]

units.la: ιητικὸν καὶ ποιητικὸν ἀλλήλων ἐστὶ τὰ, τὰ ἐναντία καὶ τὰ μεταξύ, id est, tùm contraria, tùm, quae inter ea media sunt, id est, subcontraria, inter se mutuo activa & passiva esse constat. Quibus subdit, Etenim omnino generatio & corruptio in hisce consistunt. Quam ob rem & ignem calefacere, & frigidum frigefacere & omnino activum id quod patitur sibi simile reddere iam rationi consentaneum est. Unde infert necesse esse ut patiens in id mutetur quod agendi vim habet. hoc enim pacto in contrarium erit generatio. Quia igitur uti ratione & experientiâ constat, quam ipse admittit, contraria non modò in summo gradu, sed etiam minùs excedentia pugnare,atqueHippocratis authoritate subacidum temperare bilem, adeoque illi esse subcontrarium: sequitur Succum pancreaticum, quem Le Vasseur agnoscit naturaliter subacidum, itidem bili esse subcontrarium. Sed quid multis? Si calidum & frigidum utrumque non in summo gradu procul omni dubio subcontraria sunt dicenda, nunquam Doctor Le Vasseur bilem & Succum Pancreaticum negasset subcontraria constare dispositione, si non oblitus fuisset sese aliud agentem pag. 18. ex sua & Hippocratis sententia asserere, acida bilem frangere, compescere, mitigare, atque ψυχτικὴν καὶ πῄγωνικὴν, frigidum & adstringens pariter esse ὄξος sive acetum; & pag. 33. acidum esse frigidum, quâ de re infrà prolixiùs: bilem autem esse calidam, pag. 18. ubi inquit, ὀξῶ habet luculenter in se quo bilis ardori frenum injiciat. Optandum sanè fuisset ipsum in seipsum tàm duram non tulisse sententiam, quâ, ingenuâne dicam confessione, an dissolutâ assertione pag. 57. dicit esse hominis non sanæ mentis, qui calida componat frigidis. Pueriles igitur næuias, quibus mirè sibi placet pag. 8. nescio an excutere deceat, quibus porrò suum errorem, ne quid durius dicam, Lectoribus suis persuadere conatur non esse bilem & succum Pancreaticum contraria, quia, ut ait, συμπαθείας potius agunt, ita ut concitati motus amoris potius quàm odii argumenta sint; eventus, inquit, indicio est, unio nempe alicujus partis quæ per obstantes alias quærenda fuit. Jejunè admodum oculatum hoc seculum amandat ad Sympathiam jàm dudum dirutum ignorantiæ asylum: quasi res nec sentientes nec intelligentes amore aut odio tangerentur; effetque ignoti quædam vel cupido, vel aversatio; aut acidis atque amaris quædam ineslet cognitio. Cætera verò quàm belle quadrant cum iis quæ habet pag. 18. ubi horum oblitus ex Hippocrate & Galeno docet acida bilem frangere, compescere, mitigare, illius ardori frænum injicere, &c. idem fere ingeminat p. 63. acidi vim, occurrente bile, quodammodo fractam ac prostratam languere. Quæ sanè si sint amoris effecta, si Doctor Le Vasseur ita eos, quos amat, excipit, amicitiam cum illo contrahant alii, non ego. Minùs impostcrum mirandum publicas Veneres decoloratas quandoque prodire, quandoquidem malè excipi & frangi amoris effecta sunt huic novo Doctori: neque etiam, si naturæ placet, impostcrum frigida pugnabunt calidis, humentia siccis: mutuis enim osculis sese excipient. Sed ne videatur sine ratione lusisse subdit, eventus tus indicio est, Unio nempe alicujus partis, quæ per obstantes alias quærenda fuit. Hinc Veneri Medicus noster supremum altare sacrat, cui unicè litandum palàm profitetur facetus cavillator sacro hoc Lucretii hymno, Rerum naturam sola gubernas Nec sine te quidquam dias in luminis oras, Exoritur; Neque fit lætum nec amabile quicquam.
units.tr: [ιητικὸν καὶ ποιητικὸν ἀλλήλων ἐστὶ τὰ, τὰ ἐναντία καὶ τὰ μεταξύ]: that is, it is established that contraries and the things that lie between them, that is, subcontraries, are mutually active and passive towards one another. He adds: For generation and corruption consist entirely in these. Hence it is now consistent with reason that fire heats, the cold chills, and in general what acts makes what is acted upon like itself. From this he infers that it is necessary for the patient to be changed into that which has the power of acting; for in this way generation will be into the contrary. Since, therefore, it is established both by reason and by experience, which he himself admits, that contraries fight not only at the highest degree but even when they exceed less, and since by the authority of Hippocrates the subacid tempers bile, and so is subcontrary to it, it follows that the pancreatic juice, which Le Vasseur acknowledges is naturally subacid, is likewise subcontrary to bile. But why say more? If hot and cold, not at the highest degree, are undoubtedly to be called subcontraries, the Doctor Le Vasseur would never have denied that bile and the pancreatic juice agree in being subcontrary in disposition, had he not forgotten, while arguing otherwise on page 18, that by his own and Hippocrates' opinion acids break, check and soften bile, and that acid is [ψυχτικὴν καὶ πῄγωνικὴν], cold and astringent alike, the [ὄξος] or vinegar; and on page 33 that acid is cold, about which more at length below. But bile is hot, as he says on page 18, where he says that acid [ὀξῶ] has in itself a bridle to check the heat of bile. Indeed it would have been well for him not to have pronounced against himself so harsh a judgement, which, to speak frankly, or rather in a loosened assertion, he gives on page 57: it is the mark of a man not of sound mind who puts hot things together with cold. I do not know whether it becomes me to shake off the childish trifles in which he takes such odd pleasure on page 8, by which, to say nothing harsher, he tries to persuade his readers that bile and the pancreatic juice are not contraries, because, as he says, they act by sympathy, so that their excited motions are signs of love rather than hatred; the outcome, he says, is the indication, namely the union of some part which had to be sought through other obstacles. This very dull age sends the blind to Sympathy, long since demolished as a refuge of ignorance, as if things that neither feel nor understand were touched by love or hatred, and as if there were some desire or aversion of the unknown, or as if some knowledge were inherent in acids and bitters. How prettily the rest fits with what he has on page 18, where, forgetting this, he teaches from Hippocrates and Galen that acids break, check and soften bile, and put a bridle on its heat, and so on. He repeats much the same on page 63: the force of the acid, when bile meets it, languishes as if somehow broken and prostrated. If these are the effects of love, and if Doctor Le Vasseur so receives those whom he loves, let others make friends with him, not I. It is no wonder if in future the public Venuses should sometimes come forth faded, since to this new Doctor the effects of love are being badly received and broken. Nor, if nature pleases, will cold things in future fight hot, or wet things dry; for they will receive each other with mutual kisses. But lest he seem to have jested without reason, he adds: the outcome is the indication, namely the union of some part, which had to be sought through other obstacles. Hence our Doctor consecrates the highest altar to Venus, to which, as the witty mocker openly professes, one must sacrifice alone, with this sacred hymn of Lucretius: You alone govern the nature of things, nor without you does anything arise into the bright shores of light, nor is anything made joyful or lovable.

units.la: Risum teneatis Amici, & mirari desinatis stylum, & argumenta hujus Medici fœminina. Certè finitâ pugnâ miscentur, coacervantur & uniuntur contraria corpora, uti post cruentum prælium cadavera, neque unquam contraria nisi viribus fractis coëunt, uti & pax & concordia, discordiæ & belli finis est. ut ex Arist. quoque probatum p.56. Non videt Le Vasseur, pugnam, litem, uti & amicitiam, &c. cùm animâ destitutis adscribitur, non nisi metaphoricè sumi, quia cum obsoletis Philosophis appetitum quoque naturalem, ignotum idolon, adorat. Sed quid multis? Ipse pag. 32. alii negotio intentus prolixè probare annititur hominem ex mutuo discrepantium & dissidentium connubio constare, quæ discrepantia & dissidentia ut commonstret ex Hippocrate libro de Vet. Med. refert locum suprà citatum, in homine est amarum, salsum, dulce & acidum, acerbum, humidum & infinita alia, omnigenas facultates habentia, copiamque & robur; quæ igitur Doctori Le Vasseur pag. 8. sunt amica, eadem illa pag. 32. sunt discrepantia & dissidentia, pro libitu videlicet. Notandum & aliud exemplum cohærentiæ idearum, quibus cerebrum Doctoris Le Vasseur instructum est: pag. enim 8. asserit & vel Poëtarum flosculis probare annititur effervescentiam fieri unionis gratiâ, adeoque esse amoris actum, uti ex verbis illius statim relatis videre licet: pag. vero sequenti, quia Sylvius dixerat confictu eo, sive effervescentiâ acidi & bilis aliquam fieri concretionem, indigna inquit Viro Philosopho ἡυθάχενος abusio & offucias imperitis factura; cum hic de πνευματικός subtilisatione, potius quàm συμπήξει concretione, agatur: & quasi re bene gestâ; possunt, inquit, id audere Rhetores, sed
units.tr: Friends, hold back your laughter and stop wondering at this physician's style and his womanish arguments. Once the fight is over, bodies are mixed, heaped together and joined, as corpses are after a bloody battle. Opposites never come together unless their strength is broken, just as peace and concord come only when discord and war end. This is also proved from Aristotle, p. 56. Le Vasseur does not see that strife, dispute, and likewise friendship, etc., are ascribed to things deprived of soul only in a metaphorical sense. He adores, with the outdated philosophers, a natural appetite, an unknown idol. But why say more? On p. 32, busy with another matter, he labours at length to prove that man is made up of a mutual marriage of things that disagree and dissent. To show these "disagreements and dissents," he cites from Hippocrates' book On Ancient Medicine the passage quoted above: in man there is bitter, salt, sweet and sour, astringent, moist and infinitely many other things, having every kind of faculty, quantity and strength. So the things that are friendly to Doctor Le Vasseur on p. 8 are, on p. 32, disagreeing and dissenting, at his pleasure, of course. Notice also another example of the incoherence of ideas with which Doctor Le Vasseur's brain is furnished. On p. 8 he asserts, and tries to prove even from the flowers of the poets, that effervescence happens for the sake of union, and so is an act of love, as can be seen from his words quoted immediately afterwards. But on the following page, because Sylvius had said that from that mixing, or effervescence, of acid and bile some concretion arises, he says: an abuse [ἡυθάχενος] unworthy of a philosophical man, and one that will deceive the inexperienced, since here we are dealing with a subtilisation of a pneumatic [πνευματικός] kind, rather than a concretion [συμπήξει]. And as if he had done a fine thing: Rhetoricians may dare that, he says, but

units.la: Nobis non licet esse tam disertis,
units.tr: We are not allowed to be so eloquent,

units.la: Qui musas colimus severiores.
units.tr: We who cultivate the Muses more austerely.

units.la: Masculè me hercule ! sed quomodo secum conveniat Le Vasseur,& quantâ rerum gravitate venerandus sit, judicet æquus Lector. Etenim ex nullo alio argumento, quàm quod ex συμπήξει, sive concretione & unione defumpserat, præcedenti paginâ probare contendit effervescentiam esse amoris actum; hîc verò sibi non minùs quàm Sylvio contradicens, cùm de efferves-centia agitur συμπήξει ne mentionem quidem faciendam esse putat.
units.tr: Manfully, by Hercules! But let the fair reader judge how Le Vasseur agrees with himself, and with what weight of matter he is to be venerated. For on the previous page he argues, from no other argument than what he had drawn from συμπήξει, that is from concretion and union, that effervescence is an act of love; but here, contradicting himself no less than Sylvius, he thinks that when effervescence is under discussion, συμπήξει should not even be mentioned.

units.la: Hactenus, nisi vehementer fallor, evievicimus humores illos, videlicet bidem & succum pancreaticum, rectè dictos fuisse dispositione subcontraria affectos. An vero subcontrariorum illorum humorum permixtione in illis oriatur effervescentia discutiendum suscipit Le Vasseur pag. 10. ubi chartam diris & puerilibus implens execrationibus exclamat Dii Vostram fi-dem! & quæ præterea sunt maniæ illius symptomata quæ illi ignoscenda, supra monitum; sed ante omnia examinandum, an Le Vasseur intelligat quid sit effervescentia, quam tanto molimine negat. Doctor igitur noster nominalis derivat effervescentiam [?] ab igne, eam vocans [?] pag. 6. [?] pag. 10. unde effervescentiam frigori non modo opponit, pag. 25. his verbis frigore nequaquam densari hoc phlegma; quod tamen necesse est si effervescentiâ liquetur: Quâ de re latius suo loco: Sed etiam vi nominis, uti solent rerum ignari, à veritate abductus, qualis omnis effervescentia non calida modo esset, sed & incendium, pag. 35. 41. &c. & conflagratio, pag. 44. in Sylvium pag. 35. his verbis debacchatur, primo inquit displicet, quod non à putredine, sed à pugna solummodo fervorem incendiumque febrile deducat. Unde etiam humores effervescentiam passos igneum flumen vocat p. 30. Cùm tamen Sylvius non modo istud nusquam dixerit, sed & prorsus contrarium sæpius inculcaverit, dari videlicet effervescentiam febremque frigidam: quin etiam ipse Le Vasseur, pag. 9. & 70. agnoscit, Sylvium docere in sanitatis statu temperatam, blandam, & naturæ amicam effervescentiam excitari; & certè neque nominis Etymologia, aut illius usus, aut res ipsa Sylvii sententiæ repugnat: etenim teste Perotto à fero fit ferveo verbum, quod est bullio, feror, agitor: atque latius longè sumitur, quam de iis, quæ vi ignis fervent teste este Nonio Marcello peripatetico, cap. 6. ubi inquit fervere non solùm est ex incendio calere, sed ex quibuscunque molestiis perturbari, unde & æstus marini & exæstuatio animi sub hac significatione recte posita sentiuntur, hinc Virgilius Georg. l. I.
units.tr: Thus far, unless I am greatly mistaken, we have shown that those humours, namely the bile and the pancreatic juice, were rightly said to be affected by a subcontrary disposition. Whether effervescence arises from the mixing of these subcontrary humours is taken up for discussion by Le Vasseur on p. 10, where, filling the paper with dire and childish curses, he cries out Gods, your faith! and whatever other symptoms of that madness there are, which must be pardoned him, as noted above. But before all things it must be examined whether Le Vasseur understands what effervescence is, which he denies with such great effort. Our nominal doctor therefore derives effervescence [?] from fire, calling it [?] on p. 6 and [?] on p. 10. Whence he not only opposes effervescence to cold, on p. 25, in these words: this phlegm is by no means thickened by cold; yet it must be so if it is liquefied by effervescence, a matter to be treated more fully in its place. But also, by the force of the word, as those ignorant of things commonly do, drawn away from the truth, as if every effervescence were not only hot but also an incendium (pp. 35, 41, etc.) and a conflagration (p. 44). Against Sylvius, on p. 35, he rages in these words: first, he says, it displeases me that he derives the heat and febrile fire not from putrefaction but from conflict alone. Hence he also calls the humours that have undergone effervescence a fiery river, p. 30. Yet Sylvius not only never said this, but has often insisted on the very opposite, namely that there is an effervescence that is cold, and a cold fever. Indeed Le Vasseur himself, on pp. 9 and 70, acknowledges that Sylvius teaches that in a state of health an effervescence tempered, mild, and friendly to nature is stirred up; and surely neither the etymology of the word, nor its usage, nor the thing itself, contradicts Sylvius's opinion. For, according to Perottus, from fero comes the verb ferveo, which means to boil, to be carried along, to be stirred; and it is taken far more widely than of those things that boil by the force of fire, according to Nonius Marcellus the Peripatetic, ch. 6, where he says: to be hot is not only to glow from a fire, but to be disturbed by any troubles whatever; whence the surges of the sea and the agitation of the mind are rightly perceived under this meaning. Hence Virgil, Georgics, book I:

units.la: Omnia tunc pariter vento nymbis-
units.tr: All things then seem to be alike with wind and storms

units.la: que videntur
units.tr: and

units.la: Fervere.
units.tr: To Seethe.

units.la: Nec dispari sensu Plinius, lib. 17. cap. 2. Tellus, inquit, nive fermentescit: & Galenus, terram fermentari atra bile quae acore suo eam solvit, docet lib. de atra bile: nam & fermentum dici à ferveo, neminem, uti opinor, fugit. Sed quid multis? res ipsa loquatur, Sal Tartari & Spiritus Vitrioli, aut spiritus salis, acetum & creta, cerevisia pocularis, & infinita alia frigidâ effervescentiâ ebulliunt; frigida, inquam, respectu aëris in quo illa ctio exercetur, uti si vitreo tubulo, in cum finem excogitato à Doctore Swammerdam, acres isti humores excipiantur, cuivis innotescet, quo sanè, gradibus illi applicatis, uti in fig. A. frigus in aëre, illo tubulo contento, vi effervescentiæ productum, non minus accuratè quisque percipiet, quàm mutationem aëris frigefacti beneficio thermometræ. Et sanè ζέσις, ebullitio, cui apud Græcos & Germanos nomen à sono, quem humores, cum effervescunt, edunt, quam per πνεύμα-τον, ὀγκωσιν καὶ αὔξησιν utcunque explicant boni authores, non minus locum habet in effervescentia frigida, quàm calida. Datur ergò effervescentia frigida, si visui & tactui credendum, cujus oppositum tamen facit præcipuum opusculi sui fundamentum, uti postconstabit. Quod si fermentum cognitionis Medicæ diligentius sectatus fuisset, quàm contortas & intricatas multi loquentiæ bracteas, non impugnasset, quod nescit.
units.tr: Pliny, book 17, chapter 2, means nothing different: "The earth, he says, ferments with snow." Galen, in his book on black bile, teaches that "the earth is fermented by black bile, which dissolves it by its sharpness." Nor, I think, is anyone unaware that fermentum is derived from ferveo. But why say more? The thing itself speaks for itself. Salt of tartar and spirit of vitriol, or spirit of salt, vinegar and chalk, drinking beer, and countless other things bubble up with a cold effervescence. I say cold with respect to the air in which the action takes place. If these sharp humours are received in a glass tube devised for this purpose by Doctor Swammerdam, and the vessel is applied to the degrees as in fig. A, the cold produced in the air inside the tube by the force of effervescence will be perceived no less accurately by anyone than a change in air made cold is perceived with the help of a thermometer. Indeed, zesis, boiling, to which the Greeks and Germans give a name from the sound that humours make when they effervesce, and which good authors explain in some way by pneuma, swelling and increase, applies no less to cold effervescence than to hot. Cold effervescence therefore exists, if we trust sight and touch. Yet the opposite is the chief foundation of his little work, as will be shown later. But if he had pursued the fermentation of medical knowledge more diligently, instead of the twisted and tangled gilding of much verbiage, he would not have attacked what he does not know.

units.la: Gloriam inventionis effervescentiæ tiæ in humano corpore, quamvis ea ne de nomine quidem illi innotescat, invidens Sylvio, qui eam sibi nunquam arrogavit, & vivos & mortuos in ipsum excitare conatur. Provocat Clariss. D. Willisium, evocat manes Sennerti, effervescentiæ scilicet in humano corpore inventores; ignorans Hippocratem hujus inventionem Veteribus adscripsisse. Unus atque alter locus ex multis nostro scopo suffecerit. Libro igitur de Vet. Med. Text. xxxiv. docet humores in visceribus ab acriori bile μεπεωφίζεως, id est, effervescere : Idem de victu acutorum, Text. xxix. 8. 9. acredines, inquit, sive aciditates ex aceto amara bile abundantibus magis conferunt quam atrabilariis, amara enim dissolvuntur & in pituitam transeunt μελεωφιζώμενα ὑπ' αὐτῆς dum ab ipso attolluntur, ut inquit interpres, id est, effervescunt; nigra vero, inquit ζυμῶνται καὶ μπεωφιζονται ἡ πολλα- πλασιῶνται, fermentantur & attolluntur, id est, effervescunt, ac multiplicantur. Hinc Arist. lib. 20. & 21. de respirat. ζέσιν καὶ σφύξιν explicat per ἔγχεσιν τῇ αὔξησιν ἕ θερμῷ, cum calidum, inquit Hofmannus, attollit sanguinem in majorem molem, itaque auget, aut certè augere videtur, ut majus spacium occupet. Neque aliter explicandum esse locum Hippocratis, ubi docet æstuosa biliosa in ventre tormina excitantia μετεωρισμάτα, id est, cum effervescunt, inferne subducere ex illis locis, docet Foësius, inquiens μετεωρισμάτα vocantur humores sursum elevati exæstuantes & ebullientes, adeò ut μετεωρισμὸς sit causa & ὀγκᾶν, turgere, quatenus hoc humoribus adscribitur, quorum ὀγκάσμως frequens apud bonos Authores est mentio, sufficiat Aph. 22. Sect. 1. & Sect. iv. 10. & 19. Et certè in sublime attolluntur humores contrariâ acredine præditi, sibi permixti intestino velut bello: acrium enim particularum contrariarum in sese mutuò incurrentium agiagitatione humor, illorum receptaculum, non potest non distendi, acres enim illæ particulæ vehementius circumactæ, majorem locum exigunt, quàm si essent magis quietæ. Etenim subtilis materia arctiora interstitia, quæ inter humorum particulas acidas & salsas sibi permixtas reperiuntur, facilius transiens particulas illas acres heterogeneas, & diverso situ sese mutuò respicientes, tumultuario quodam motu intestino diversimodè agitat: particulæ verò illein orbem actemajorem locum occupantes, quàm cum quiescerent, humores distendunt imò vehementius actæ flatuum bullarumve in ebulliente illo humore contentarum, atque præternaturalis humorum illorum distensionis, sæpius memoratæ, causæ sunt: humor itaque ille ex humoribus diversâ acredine constantibus & vehementer actis compositus effervescit, attollitur, turget, id est, μετεωρίζεται[?] [illegible, ~4 letters], uti ex fundamentis à Cartesio diligenligentiùs excultis, quæ Hippocratici dogmatibus prorsus respondent, lucê clariùs innotescit. Unde sequitur Sylvium, cum de effervescentia loquitur sequi Hippocratis vestigia: & quia effervescentia causa est plurimorum naturalium, etiam præternaturalium atque pravorum effectorum in humano corpore, quatenus naturaliter sese habet, vel præternaturaliter est auáta, imminuta, abolita aut depravata, hinc diarrhœæ, choleræ & febres, quæque præterea Hippocrates recenset, de Vet. Med. Text. xxxiv. rectè igitur Sylvius præeunte Hippocrate de effervescentia sæpenumerò loquitur, de qua præstitisset D.Le Vasseur tacuisse.
units.tr: He begrudges Sylvius the glory of discovering effervescence in the human body, though the man does not even know it by name, and Sylvius never claimed it for himself. Our author tries to stir up both living and dead against him. He challenges the most distinguished Dr Willis and calls up the shade of Sennert, the discoverers of effervescence in the human body. He is ignorant that Hippocrates ascribed this discovery to the ancients. One or two passages out of many will suffice for our purpose. So, in the book On Ancient Medicine, text 34, he teaches that the humours in the viscera are [μετεωρίζεως], that is, they effervesce. The same author, in On Acute Diseases, text 29, sections 8 and 9, says: "Sharpnesses or acidities from vinegar are more favourable to those abounding in bitter bile than to those with black bile; for the bitter are dissolved and turn into phlegm [μετεωριζόμενα ὑπ' αὐτῆς] while they are lifted up by it," as the translator says, that is, they effervesce; "but the black, he says, [ζυμοῦνται καὶ μετεωρίζονται ἢ πολλαπλασιάζονται], are fermented and lifted up," that is, they effervesce, "and multiplied." Hence Aristotle, in books 20 and 21 On Respiration, explains [ζέσιν καὶ σφυγμόν] by the infusion of heat into increase, "when the heat, as Hofmann says, lifts the blood into a larger mass, and so increases it, or at least seems to increase it, so that it occupies a larger space." Nor is the passage of Hippocrates to be explained otherwise, where he teaches that the painful bilious and hot colics in the belly, the [μετεωρισμάτα], that is, when they effervesce, draw downward from those places. Foesius teaches this, saying that the [μετεωρισμάτα] are called "humours raised upward, seething and boiling," so that [μετεωρισμός] is the cause, and [ὀγκᾶν], "to swell," in so far as this is ascribed to the humours, whose [ὀγκασμός] is frequently mentioned by good authors. Aphorism 22, section 1, and sections 4, 10 and 19, will be enough. And certainly humours endowed with contrary sharpness are lifted up on high when mixed with each other, as in an intestine war. For the humour, which is their receptacle, cannot but be distended by the agitation of the contrary sharp particles colliding with each other. Those sharp particles, driven about more vehemently, require a larger place than if they were more at rest. Indeed, the subtle matter, passing more easily through the narrower interstices found between the acid and salty particles mixed together, agitates those heterogeneous sharp particles, which face each other in diverse positions, in a diverse way with a tumultuous intestine motion. The particles, when driven in a circle, occupy a larger place than when they were at rest, and distend the humours. Indeed, the gases and bubbles contained in that boiling humour, when more violently driven, are the causes of that unnatural distension of the humours mentioned so often. Thus that humour, composed of humours of diverse sharpness and violently agitated, effervesces, is lifted up, swells, that is, [μετεωρίζεται], as is made clearer than light from the foundations more carefully worked out by Descartes, which correspond entirely to the Hippocratic doctrines. From this it follows that Sylvius, when he speaks of effervescence, follows in the footsteps of Hippocrates. And because effervescence is the cause of very many natural effects, and also of unnatural and bad effects in the human body, insofar as it is naturally constituted, or is unnaturally increased, diminished, abolished or corrupted, hence come diarrhoeas, cholera and fevers, and whatever else Hippocrates lists in On Ancient Medicine, text 34. Rightly, therefore, Sylvius, following Hippocrates, often speaks of effervescence, about which Le Vasseur would have done better to keep silent.

units.la: Pag. verò 11. paulò dilucidiori intervallo, saltim aliquid dicere conatur: legitur, inquit, apud Hipp. naturam refingere invisibilem, non possibile: habitat namque mens cauta recessus, sacraque ejus non minus quam θεῖα mysteriis abundant ac exornantur. Non una res est, quam sacro tegat involucro natura; ed oculatior quam quisque fuit Sylvius, em nec visam, nec ut fatetur, ejus indo- is ut oculis usurpari posit, stylo ita deingit, ac si in Æsculapii templo dormiissiet. Nec repugnans αὐτοψίας hominem intrepidum movet, aut a sententia, ut ar est, usque deterret. Novit Philosohorum vulgus, nihil esse in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu. Florum quàm fructuum avidior Le Vasseur, praeter opinionem Hippocratis sententiam in Sylvio iterùm carpens extra oleas vagatur: non enim hîc est quæstio de natura reformanda, cui leges sunt præscriptæ, quæ violari nequeunt, cui limites sunt positi, quos ultra citraque nequit consistere. Sed quæstio est, an bilis & succus pancreaticus, quia subcontraria dispositione sunt prædita in tenue intestinum concurrentia effervescentiam excitent, quod statuit Sylvius, negat verò Le Vasseur; primùm, quia naturæ opera sunt occulta sive mysteria, velut ὄργια Libe sacra, quæ ut occulta naturæ miracul quoque crepat pag.74. In quem quæso concinnius quadrat illud Hippo cratis, lib. de Lege, Text. iii. 18
units.tr: But on page 11, after a rather clearer interval, he tries at least to say something: "It is read, he says, in Hippocrates that it is not possible to remodel nature, which is invisible; for the cautious mind dwells in recesses, and its sacred rites, no less than divine mysteries, abound and are adorned. It is not one thing that nature covers with a sacred veil. But Sylvius, more keen-sighted than anyone, describes in his style things that were neither seen nor, as he confesses, could be used by the eyes, as if he had slept in the temple of Aesculapius." Nor does this move the fearless man who is opposed to [αὐτοψία], or deter him from the view as it stands. The crowd of philosophers knows that there is nothing in the intellect which was not first in the senses. Le Vasseur, more eager for flowers than for fruit, again carps at Sylvius contrary to the opinion of Hippocrates and wanders outside the olive groves. For the question here is not about reforming nature, for which laws have been prescribed that cannot be violated, and for which limits have been set that it cannot pass beyond or fall short of. The question is whether bile and pancreatic juice, because they meet in the small intestine with a contrary disposition, excite effervescence. Sylvius holds this, but Le Vasseur denies it. First, he says, because the works of nature are "occult" or "mysteries," like the orgies of Liber's sacred rites, which he also rattles on about as "occult miracles of nature" at p. 74. To whom, I ask, does that saying of Hippocrates fit more aptly, from the book On the Law, text 3, 18:

units.la: Τὰ δὲ ἱερὰ ἐόντα πηγμάτα ἱερῶσιν ἀνθρώποις δεικνυται· βεβήλοισι δὲ, ὁ ἥμις, πρὶν ἢ τελεσθῆναι σιν ὀργίοισιν ἐπισήμης. Res sacræ sacris hominibus demonstrantur: profanis id fa non est, priusquam scientiæ orgiis initientur. At vero crudior est hæc caro quàm ut ad scientiarum sacrarium ad mittatur, quamdiu putat hominibu datum non esse supra sensus sapere aut quicquam admittere, quod oculi non percipitur. &, uti pag. 74. ultrò fatetur, naturæ vim sensibus non percipi: Est enim, inquit, varia diversaque adeo in parandis operibus secreta hæc, unde manant omnia, vis atque potestas, ut latentia ejus miracula, manifestis illius moliminibus mancipare,perdelirum sit. Quapropter quia citata pag. II. naturam vocat invisibilem: non modo palàm fatetur sese naturam ignorare, sine cujus tamen cognitione Medicus titulo suo indignus est, vel Hippocrate adstipulante Lib. de Vet. Medic. xxxvi. 18. sed & totum genus humanum suo pede metiens, negat quemquam ullius rei claram &evientem cognitionem habere posse: bla igitur vulgari, plebeja, & rustica cognitione suffultus, nil prorsus nisi quod videt, & quidem crassa duntaxat Minervâ, sese percipere aut quemquam cognoscere fatetur. O miseras hominum mentes! O pectora cæca! nihil sciunt mortales præterquam quod oculis percipitur. Enim verò, non tantum id, quod putarent sese videre, ignorarent; sed & sese videre scirent. Neque enim rerum essentiæ videntur, neque etiam nos vide-re, oculis percipitur, sed mente. Multo minus, an visus non erret, visu percipitur, sed mente dijudicatur; quod vel ex Aristotele discere potuisset, docente, nos certiores esse non posse de sensuum nostrorum opera, nisi constet organa esse legitimè disposita, objectum esse in debita distantia & medium requisitum: hæc enim omnia examinare, conferre & recognoscere, non sensuum esse, sed intellectûs, qui non videt, sensu rationis destituitur.
units.tr: Sacred things are shown to sacred men, but to the profane they are not shown before they are initiated into the rites of knowledge [Τὰ δὲ ἱερὰ ἐόντα πράγματα ἱεροῖσιν ἀνθρώποισι δεικνυται· βεβήλοισι δὲ οὐ θέμις, πρὶν ἢ τελεσθῆναι σφιν ὀργίοισιν ἐπιστήμης]. But this flesh is too crude to be admitted to the sanctuary of the sciences, so long as it thinks that men have not been given the power to know beyond the senses, or to admit anything that the eyes do not perceive. And, as he freely confesses at p. 74, the power of nature is not perceived by the senses: "For there is, he says, such a varied and diverse secret power in producing works, from which all things flow, that it is mad to subject its hidden miracles to its manifest efforts." Therefore, since at the cited p. 11 he calls nature "invisible," he not only openly confesses that he does not know nature, without whose knowledge the physician is unworthy of his title, Hippocrates agreeing in On Ancient Medicine, xxxvi. 18. He also, measuring the whole human race by his own foot, denies that anyone can have a clear and evident knowledge of anything. So, propped up by vulgar, plebeian and rustic knowledge, he confesses that he perceives nothing except what he sees, and that only with mere crude wit, and that he recognises no one. O wretched minds of men! O blind hearts! Mortals know nothing except what is perceived by the eyes. Indeed, they would not only be ignorant of what they thought they saw, but would not even know that they saw it. For the essences of things are not seen, nor do we see with the eyes but with the mind. Much less is it perceived by sight whether sight errs; it is judged by the mind. He could have learned this even from Aristotle, who teaches that we cannot be more certain of the workings of our senses unless it is established that the organs are rightly disposed, the object at the due distance, and the required medium present. For to examine, compare and recognise all these things belongs not to the senses but to the intellect, which does not see; it is deprived of the sense of reason.

units.la: Longè aliter Hippocrates, qui quamvis lib. 1. de flatibus, Text. v. 3. spiritus & aëris efficaciam philosophico stylo ad vivum delineet, quâ, ut ait, non fluctus modò maris concitantur, arbores evelluntur, naves in altum disjiciuntur, hyems & æstas generantur,& quomodo λεπτὸς ἀὴρ, tenuis aër, vel ut alii loquuntur, subtilis materia sit motus solis & lunæ causa, atque terræ vehiculum, τῆς γῆς ὄχημα nihilominus tamen disertè docet 1. c. Text. v. 5. τοιαύτην μὲν ἓν ἐν τυπέοιιν ἔχει δυνάμιν· ἀ ἀλλ' μὲν ἐσί γε τῇ μὲν ὀψὶ ἀφανὴς, τῇ δὲ λογισμῷ φανερὸς. Talem itaque vim in in ista exercet, etiamsi oculis minime sit conspicuus, & tantum ratiocinio cognoscatur, & effectu suo fiat manifestus. Ubi certe agnoscit Hippocrates τῇ ὄψει ἀφανὲς, oculis inconspicuum, τῷ λογισμῷ φανερὸν, ratione conspicuum esse: etenim ὅσα γὰρ τῶν τῆς ὁμματῶν ὄψιν ἐκφεύγει, τούτα τῇ τῆς γνώμης ὄψει κεκρύπτηται; Quaecunque enim oculorum conspectum effugiunt, ea mentis oculis obtinentur & superantur. Hipp. de Arte xix. 9. Planè eodem modo, imò à priori Sylvius Praxeos suae p. 109. probat effervescentiam fieri in intestino duodeno, his verbis talē, hoc est, quovis modo vel gradu acidum pancreatis succum impossibile est commisceri cum Bile amara & sale volatili abundante, quin mox excitetur inde effervescentia infinitis ex Chymia & aliunde petitis exemplis confirmanda. Argumentatur igitur Sylvius à causis necessariis ad effectum, uti modo Hippocrates ab effectu ad causam, quorum tamen connexio non nisi mentis oculis conspicua est. Non ergò Sylvius hac in re quàm quisque oculatior ; sed qui ita coecutit ut Le Vasseur , quovis Medico caecior est. Hic iterum constat quantus LeVasseur fitHippocraticus, qui more solito Sylvio non magis quàm Hippocrati praeter intentionem contradicit. Unde porrò sequitur Doctorem le Vasseur in densissimis Peripateticorum tenebris stertentem, ineptissimum esse qui de aliis quàm de rebus vulgaribus rustico more judicet. Nec mirum , quandoquidem fatetur nil cognosci nisi quod oculos ferit, ipsum nescire quid dicat. Certè illi ipsi, quibus arridet futilissimum illud , & omni cognitioni è diametro repugnans axioma , nihil esse in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu, non paucis distinctiunculis essatum suum stabilire contendunt, adeò ut illa quoque dicantur sensibus excipi , quorum necessariae causae & effecta in sensus incurrunt , quamvis ipsa sensibus lateant. Quamvis ne illo quidem sensu axioma generaliter verum sit, cum mens nostra suâ ipsius cognitione, etiam omni prorsus sensuum percep-tione post habita, sibi clarè & distinctè innotescat: atque Deus Opt.Max. sua ideâ nobis innata sese intimis nostris cogitationibus clarissimè & distinctissimè offerat: tùm etiam quia qui nescit rerum essentias nullas incurrere in sensus, nihil novit, cùm hæc sint rectæ cognitionis elementa: Sed hoc persequi nimiæ molis esset. Orationem de scientiarum veritate à me habitam huic libello subjunxi, ut sit quædam manuductio ad Philosophiam, quam conterraneus illius, incomparabilis Des Cartes, juxta D. Augustini monita, sedulò excoluit, ut, sieri si possit, expergefiat atque discat, quid sit sentire, quid intelligere: quomodo ex sensuum monitis mens occasionem capiat de rebus judicandi, atque puræ cogitationis claritatem, evidentiam, certitudinem, & sese insensibilem, & Deum infinitum indubitatò cognoscat, sensuum præjudiciis non modò non consideratis, sed & iisdem pro tempore abnegatis.Imò & sensus iis, qui mentem nondum à præjudiciis repurgatam habent,rerum veris ideis concipiendis maximoperè obesse. Quia tamen mente à falsis præjudiciis & obscuris atque minùs accuratis ideis repurgata, atque sensibus illi subditis ut fidis satellitibus, homo illis uti potest & debet tanquam literis; occasione effectuum rerum corporearum, aut iis, quæ circa illa accidunt, oculis aliisve sensibus observatis, in rerum illarum cognitionem, earumque essentiam & existentiam deducimur. Quod non minus Augustinianum esse quàm Cartesianum probat, ni fallor, Oratio huic opusculo in hunc finem affixa. Graviter igitur errat Le Vasseur, qui loco ex Aristotele importunè citato probare
units.tr: Quite differently Hippocrates, who, although in the first book of On Flatulence (text 3) he portrays in a philosophical style the power of spirit and air to the life, by which, as he says, not only the waves of the sea are stirred up, trees uprooted, and ships flung on high, and winter and summer produced, and by which the thin air [λεπτὸς ἀὴρ], or as others say subtle matter, is the cause of the motion of the sun and moon and the vehicle of the earth [τῆς γῆς ὄχημα], nevertheless teaches plainly in the same work (text 5): [τοιαύτην μὲν ἐν τυπέοιιν ἔχει δυνάμιν· ἀφανὴς μὲν ἐστι τῇ ὄψει, φανερὸς δὲ τῷ λογισμῷ]. Such a power it exercises, even though it is not at all conspicuous to the eyes, but is known only by reasoning, and becomes manifest through its effect. There Hippocrates certainly recognises what is invisible to the sight [τῇ ὄψει ἀφανές], inconspicuous to the eyes, and what is manifest to reason [τῷ λογισμῷ φανερόν], conspicuous to the reason. For whatever escapes the sight of the eyes [ὅσα γὰρ τῶν τῆς ὄψιος ἐκφεύγει, ταῦτα τῇ τῆς γνώμης ὄψει κεκράτηται] is grasped by the eye of the mind: whatever escapes the sight of the eyes is held and mastered by the eyes of the mind. Hipp. de Arte xix. 9. In exactly the same way, and even more a priori, Sylvius in his Praxis (p. 109) proves that effervescence occurs in the duodenum, in these words: "that is, in whatever manner or degree, it is impossible for the acid juice of the pancreas to be mixed with the bitter bile and abundant volatile salt without an effervescence being immediately excited thereby," to be confirmed by countless examples drawn from chemistry and elsewhere. Sylvius therefore argues from necessary causes to their effect, just as Hippocrates now argues from the effect to the cause; and the connection between them is perceptible only to the eyes of the mind. Sylvius, then, in this matter is not more sharp-sighted than anyone else; but whoever has gone so blind as Le Vasseur is blinder than any physician. Here again it is clear how much of a Hippocratist Le Vasseur is, who, as usual, contradicts Sylvius no more than he contradicts Hippocrates, beside the point. From this it further follows that Doctor Le Vasseur, snoring in the very thick darkness of the Peripatetics, is most inept in judging matters other than common things in a rustic manner. Nor is it surprising that, since he admits nothing is known except what strikes the eyes, he himself does not know what he is saying. Certainly those very men who are charmed by that most trifling axiom, utterly opposed to all knowledge, there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, strive to establish their saying by not a few little distinctions, so that even those things are said to be received by the senses whose necessary causes and effects fall upon the senses, although they themselves lie hidden from the senses. Yet not even in that sense is the axiom true in general, since our mind, even when all perception by the senses has been set aside, becomes clearly and distinctly known to itself by its own knowledge; and God, the Best and Greatest, offers himself to our innermost thoughts most clearly and most distinctly through his idea innate in us. Moreover, whoever does not know that no essences of things fall upon the senses knows nothing, since these are the elements of right knowledge. But to pursue this would be too great a labour. I have appended to this little book the Oration on the Truth of the Sciences which I delivered, so that it may serve as a certain introduction to philosophy, which that fellow countryman of his, the incomparable Descartes, following the admonitions of St Augustine, cultivated diligently, so that, if it can be done, the mind may awake and learn what it is to sense and what to understand, how from the warnings of the senses the mind takes occasion to judge of things, and how it knows the clarity, evidence and certainty of pure thought, and itself as unbodily, and God as infinite, beyond doubt, the prejudices of the senses not only being disregarded but even for the time being renounced. Indeed the senses are also greatly harmful to those who have not yet cleansed their minds of prejudices, in conceiving true ideas of things. Yet since the mind, cleansed of false prejudices and obscure and less accurate ideas, and with the senses subjected to it as faithful attendants, man can and must use them as letters: by means of the effects of bodily things, or of what happens around those things, observed by the eyes or other senses, we are led to knowledge of those things, of their essence and existence. The Oration appended to this little work for this purpose proves, unless I am mistaken, that this is as much Augustinian as Cartesian. Le Vasseur therefore errs grievously, who strives in vain to prove from a passage of Aristotle, inopportunely cited, as if Sylvius taught that the senses are to be dismissed; he, in a style wholly Hippocratic, hunts from necessary visible causes for necessary effects, though invisible, and from visible effects for a hidden cause. Therefore his inference is shameless: "what is not seen is not." And his next remark is elegant: "nor, he says, does a thing opposed to autopsia move the fearless man," as if there were another thing opposed to autopsia than not seeing, which he had said before. For although he sees as sharply as either an eagle or the Epidaurian serpent, yet he could not assert that he had grasped by autopsia what he denies can be grasped. That autopsia of Doctor Le Vasseur is therefore nothing at all, so it is no wonder that Sylvius is not moved by it, since the affections of what does not exist are nothing. But, like a comic player on the stage, the Doctor performs a comedy: Famished hunger for fame, to what do you not drive hearts that are not made of flesh! He cites a comic poet so that by his authority he may establish the truth: "Our hands," he says, "have eyes, and they believe what they see." But here we complain of the blindness of the mind of those who believe nothing except what they see with external eyes. Yet, once the little objections of Doctor Le Vasseur are dissolved, by which he denies that effervescence of bile and pancreatic juice really occurs in the small intestine, I shall make it so conspicuous, not only to the mind but to the bodily eyes, that from now on no one can doubt it.

units.la: Note: the leading words are printed in the source as "evidentiam" with the preceding "ex" fragment absent; no further footnotes. bare frustrà annititur, quasi Sylvius sensus dimittendos esse doceat; qui Stylo prorsus hippocratico ex necessariis causis visibilibus, necessaria essecta, licet invisibilia; atque ex effectis visibilibus, causam reconditam venatur. Impudens igitur illatio est, quod non videtur, non est. Et elegans est alterum quod subdit, nec, inquit, repugnans αὐτοψία hominem intrepidum movet, quasi aliud esset, repugnans αὐτοψία, quàm non videre, quod antea dixerat. Licet enim tàm cernat acutum, quàm aut àquila aut serpens Epidaurius, non tamen asserere posset autopsiâ sese apprehendisse, quod negat dari. Nulla igitur est illa Doctoris Le Vasseur autopsia, ut mirum non sit, quia non entis nullæ sunt affectiones, Sylvium eâ non commoveri. Sed quasi in Theatro Scenicus Doctor comœdiam ageret, quo non carnalia pectora cogis Famæ sacra fames! Comicum citat ut illius authoritate veritatem adstruat, Manus, inquit, nostræ oculatæ sunt, credunt quod vident: sed hic querimur de cæcitate mentis illorum, qui nil credunt, nisi quod oculis externis vident: at verò solutis objectiunculis Doctoris Le Vasseur, quibus effervescentiam Bilis & Succi pancreatici in intestino tenui revera dari negat, eam non mentis modò, sed corporeis oculis tàm conspicuam reddam, ut impostterum de eâ nemo dubitare possit.
units.tr: ...in vain, as if Sylvius taught that the senses should be dismissed. He, in a thoroughly Hippocratic style, infers necessary effects, though invisible, from necessary visible causes, and hunts out a hidden cause from visible effects. It is therefore an impudent inference that what is not seen does not exist. Also elegant is what he adds: "Nor," he says, "does it move a fearless man that this is contrary to autopsy [αὐτοψία]," as if being contrary to autopsy were something other than not seeing, which he had said before. For although he sees as sharply as either an eagle or the Epidaurian serpent, he could not claim to have grasped by autopsy what he denies can be grasped. That autopsy of Doctor Le Vasseur is therefore nothing, and it is no wonder that Sylvius is not moved by it, since non-entities have no affections. But as if the Doctor were performing a comedy on the stage: "To what do you not compel mortal hearts, accursed hunger for fame!" He cites a comic poet so that his authority may establish the truth: "Our hands are eyed, he says, they believe what they see." But here we lament the blindness of the mind of those who believe nothing unless they see it with external eyes. Yet, with the little objections of Doctor Le Vasseur dissolved, by which he denies that the effervescence of bile and pancreatic juice truly occurs in the small intestine, I shall make it so conspicuous, not only to the mind but to the bodily eyes, that no one can doubt it hereafter.

units.la: Interea ausu plusquàm herculeo Doctissimum quoque D. De Graef, cujus ingeniosa opuscula singularem ejus doctrinam & dexteritatem abundè probant, sinistrè aggreditur. Eminus quàm cominus depugnare mavult, toties Parisiis à D. De Graef provocatus, cùm in ædibus Nobiliss. & accuratæ Philosophiæ Studiosissimi D. Bourdeloti libellum suum per duos circiter menses publicè ventilandum proponeret, ne hiscere quidem ausus fuit: jàm verò è longinquo atque ex insidiis in eum invehitur, & ut ipsum videatur superasse, illi affingit, quod nunquam cogitavit: ait enim pag. 12. illum dixisse intemeratis manibus, nec effuso cum sanguine & spiritibus calore, quo ea fovetur, haud quaquam perveniri queat, cum solummodò ad sibi objecta respond erit D. De Graef haud difficile videri illis qui manum operi non admovent aperire intestina, atque humores in iis contentos examinare, quandoquidem ea quae intestinis insunt, videri nequeunt nisi illis apertis, & cum aperiuntur, multa vasa necessariò dissecantur ex quibus tanta copia sanguinis profluit, ut impossibile sit, (uti sæpe experti sumus) optatam effervescentiam videre, uti loquitur Doctor De Graef, p. 63. At verò necesse non est ut liti inter D. Le Vasseur & D. De Graef ulterius memet immisceam, etenim paulò post effervescentiam illam succi pancreatici bilis & pituitæ, de qua quæstio, etiam in intestinis oculis
units.tr: Meanwhile, with more than Herculean daring, he also attacks, and not kindly, the most learned Mr. De Graef, whose ingenious little works abundantly show his singular learning and skill. He prefers to fight at a distance rather than hand to hand. Although he was often challenged in Paris by De Graef, when De Graef proposed to have his little book publicly debated for about two months in the house of the most noble and diligent student of philosophy, Mr. Bourdelot, he did not even dare to open his mouth. Now he attacks from afar and from ambush, and in order to seem to have won, he ascribes to him what he never thought. For he says on page 12 that De Graef said "that one cannot by any means arrive at it with undefiled hands, and without the blood spilled and the warmth of the spirits with which it is cherished," whereas De Graef, answering only the objections put to him, said: "It seems not difficult to those who do not put a hand to the work to open the intestines and examine the humours contained in them, since what lies within the intestines cannot be seen unless they are opened; and when they are opened, many vessels are necessarily cut, from which so much blood flows that it is impossible (as we have often experienced) to see the desired effervescence," as Doctor De Graef says, p. 63. But I need not involve myself further in the quarrel between Le Vasseur and De Graef, for a little later I shall display that effervescence of pancreatic juice, bile and phlegm, which is the question, even in the intestines, to the eyes of each, clearer than light.

units.la: { } oculis cujusque luce clariùs exhibebo. Certè verissimum est, Spiritum volatilem excalefactum & ebullientem in thermometra contentum dicto citius subsidere cum thermometra, qui ante hermeticè fuerat clausus, subitò aperitur. Sic etiam apertis intestinis diffundi Spiritus, causas effervescentiæ primarias, ideoque effervescentiam in primis blandam imminui, aut saltem vehementiorem minùs apparere non videtur inconveniens. Imò verò quotiescunque effervescentia humoris minus vifcidi in intestino excitatur, beneficio ex. gr. limaturæ ferri & aquæ fortis, turgens intestinum facto foramine derepentè detumescit flaccefcitque, flatibus subitò sese in auram recipientibus. Deinde nescit effervefcentiam non semper oculis percipi, licet humor effervescens à nobis conspiciatur: agnoscit enim ipse fanguinem in corde effervescere nunquam tamen, uti opinor, aperto corde vidit sanguinis in corde ebullitionem. Idem accidit cerevisiae poculari, cujus effervescentia demum apparet aperto poculo. Sed quid istud est absurditatis! quis faストus! quae arrogantia! Audivit, inquit pag. 13. ut puto, ignorare enim foedum foret & illiberale; scit, inquam, ni, quod deperit ardenter ἐπιφλόγισμα, ut alia Circe, totum apud se eum detinuerit; quo fiat pacto partus, ut vulgo fertur, Caesareus. Matre tantum non spirante, vulnus infligitur vulvae, incolumis infans educitur: vixit ab obitu matris illud audacis naturae miraculum, immuni vita extincta superfuit; & aestuans ille succus, ejusque fervor, in fervido adhuc corpore tamen, eo arbitrante, extingueretur. Et quid exemplum partus caesarei hîc facit ad rem? foetus enim mortua matre, non amplius veluti illius viscera, matri unitus vivit: sed sanguis in illius corde aliquandiu propria sua effervescit constitutione, ut pullus in ovo, nō matris, sed insita vi. Deinde uti ex dictis manifestum, etiamsi foetus iste aperiretur, effervescentia, quam ille in sola manifesta ebullitione consistere existimat, ne tum quidem oculis perciperetur; quia tanta effervescentia quâ sanguis ad oculum ebulliat, humano cordi, cui, uti toti corpori, omne nimium inimicum est, non nisi in certo quodam statu valdè praeternaturali contingit. Sed omnem absurditatem superat, cum inquit pag. 12. fimum tempore fermentationis cieri: ergo & tepor ille qui in intestino tenui reperitur, eo aperto sufficeret, ut effervescentia ibidem continuaretur: Sed quid inde? nullus unquam negavit, aperto abdomine, effervescentiam aliquam in intestinis dari, quamdiu dantur effervescentiae causae: sed duntaxat negavit De Graef eam oculis esse obviam, neque enim illa vel in fimo equino percipitur cum mitis aut suavis tepor illius fermentationem excitat. Et quaenam est ea Hyperbole, à calore fimi, inquit p. 4. quantum recedat expirantis hominis calor, difficile dictu foret, nisi potiorem hunc illo quis esse judicaret, præsertim cum
units.tr: {} I shall make it plainer than daylight to anyone's eyes. It is certainly true that volatile spirit, heated and boiling inside a thermometer, sinks down more quickly than said, as soon as the thermometer, which had been sealed hermetically, is suddenly opened. So too, when the intestines are opened, the spirits diffuse, which are the primary causes of effervescence; it is therefore no absurd suggestion that the mild effervescence is diminished, or at least that a more violent one appears less. Indeed, whenever an effervescence of a less viscous humour is excited in the intestine, for example by filings of iron and aqua fortis, the swollen intestine, once a hole is made, suddenly subsides and grows flaccid, the winds at once escaping into the air. Next, he does not know that effervescence is not always perceived by the eyes, even when the effervescing humour is seen by us. For he himself acknowledges that blood effervesces in the heart, yet I suppose he has never seen the boiling of blood in the heart with the heart laid open. The same happens with a cup of beer, whose effervescence appears only when the cup is opened. But what absurdity is this! What arrogance! What pride! He has heard, he says on p. 13, as I suppose, for it would be foul and ungentlemanly to be ignorant; he knows, I say, whether the ardently desired epiphlogism, like another Circe, has held him entirely in its power; by what means the birth occurs, as is commonly reported, by Caesarean section. With the mother scarcely breathing, a wound is made in the womb, and the child is drawn out unharmed. That miracle of audacious nature has survived the mother's death, living on in an unharmed state; and that seething juice, and its ferment, would be extinguished, he thinks, in a body still warm. And what does the example of a Caesarean birth do here? For when the mother is dead, the foetus no longer lives as if joined to her viscera; rather, the blood in its heart effervesces for some time by its own constitution, like a chick in the egg, by an inborn force and not the mother's. Next, as is clear from what has been said, even if that foetus were opened, the effervescence, which he thinks consists solely in manifest boiling, would not even then be perceived by the eyes; for such an effervescence by which the blood boils up to the eye is not compatible with the human heart, to which everything excessive is hostile, as it is to the whole body, except in a certain highly unnatural state. But he surpasses all absurdity when he says on p. 12 that dung is stirred up by the time of fermentation: so then that warmth which is found in the small intestine, once it is opened, would suffice for effervescence to continue there. But what follows from that? No one has ever denied that, with the abdomen opened, some effervescence exists in the intestines as long as the causes of effervescence exist; but De Graef merely denied that it is open to the eyes, for it is not perceived even in horse dung, when a mild or gentle warmth excites its fermentation. And what is that hyperbole, from the heat of dung, he says on p. 4, how far the heat of an expiring man falls short would be hard to say, unless someone judged this to be the stronger, especially since

units.la: Clara (dederunt) incendia lucem, antequam itum sit Illuc, unde negant redire quemquam.
units.tr: Bright fires gave light before anyone went thither, whence they say no one returns.

units.la: Anne mentem ut incendium, flammam, lucem, ut corpus, Lectori Christiano obtrudit? In hoc solo huc usque videtur Hippocraticus, cujus sententiam videsis Sect. VIII. Aph. 18. Hinc constat quare minus movetur iis quæ supra sensus sunt, imò verò mirum est eum, cujus mens flamma est quicquam nisi quod flammâ fortius est oculis percipere. At verò corpus nil quicquam intelligere posse ex oratione de Veritate Scientiarum & Artium huic libello affixa luce clariùs constat. Verum enimverò non est quod, sive propter difficultatem, sive propter celerem caloris & spirituum fugam, aut sanguinis profusionem diffidamus de probationibus omni exceptione majoribus, quibus demonstretur, humores istos tres bilem, succum pancreaticum atque pituitam in intestino tenui effervescere, enimvero bilem humori acido permixtam cum eo effervescere docet Hippocrates de victu acutorum xxix. 8. 9. his expressis verbis etiam supra data occasione citatis, ubi inquit πὰ μὲν γαρ ἀπεφ' ἀλύεται ἢ ἐπιφλεγμαίνεται, μετεωρ-ζόμενα ἐπ' αὐτὲς videlicet ὀξεῖα ὀξύτητες: amara enim dissolvuntur & in pituitam transeunt, dum ab acido attolluntur, id est, effervescunt, quapropter quia Doctor Le Vasseur pag. 19. agnoscit succum pancreaticum acidum, uti & probatum supra p. 53. atque ipsa αὐτοψία constat succum pancreaticum in intestino duodeno bili permisceri, in homine enim utrumque ductum, tum pancreaticum tum bilarium intestinalem, lem, per unum orificium suos humores exonerare, ex Anatomia manifestum est, adeò ut humores illi in humano corpore, in humano inquam corpore, eo non profluant, quin sibi permisceantur (in canibus enim paulò inferior est exitus duētus pancreatici quàm bilarii) omninò sequitur succum pancreaticum & bilem in intestino duodeno sibi permixta effervescere. Unde certè elucescit adoranda Dei providentia, qui, ut utriusque humoris acidi & amari acredo temperaretur, lege sancivit, ut in ipso affluxu ad intestina sibi mutuò permiscerentur, atque, præmissa effervescentiâ, velut prælio, alter alterius acrimoniâ frangeretur & temperaretur: hinc ab humano stercore non abhorrent canes, quamvis aliàs fastidiant amara bile infecta. Manifesto experimento amaritudinem bilis quo tinctæ sunt fæces humanæ à pituita & succo pancreatico fractam esse.
units.tr: Does he foist upon the Christian reader a mind like a fire, a flame, a light, like a body? In this alone so far he seems a Hippocratic; see his opinion in Sect. VIII, Aph. 18. Hence it is plain why he is less moved by things that are above the senses; indeed it is strange that he whose mind is a flame should perceive with his eyes nothing that is stronger than a flame. But that a body cannot understand anything is clear as daylight from the oration on the Truth of the Sciences and Arts appended to this little book. Truly, there is no reason, whether because of the difficulty, or the rapid flight of heat and spirits, or the loss of blood, to distrust the proofs, greater than any objection, by which it is shown that these three humours, bile, pancreatic juice and phlegm, effervesce in the small intestine. Indeed, Hippocrates, in On the Diet of Acute Diseases xxix. 8, 9, teaches that bile mixed with an acid humour effervesces with it, in the very words cited above on a suitable occasion, where he says: [τὰ μὲν γὰρ πικρὰ ἀπολύεται ἢ ἐπιφλεγμαίνεται, μετεωρίζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ὀξύτητος], that is, bitter things are dissolved and turn into phlegm, when they are lifted up by the acid, that is, they effervesce. Therefore, since Doctor Le Vasseur, p. 19, acknowledges that the pancreatic juice is acid, as also proved above on p. 53, and since anatomy itself shows that the pancreatic juice is mixed with bile in the duodenum, for in a human being both ducts, the pancreatic and the biliary, discharge their humours into the intestine through one opening, so that those humours in the human body, I say in the human body, do not flow out without being mixed together (for in dogs the exit of the pancreatic duct is a little lower than that of the bile duct), it certainly follows that the pancreatic juice and the bile, mixed together in the duodenum, effervesce. From this, surely, the adorable providence of God shines forth, who, so that the sharpness of each acid and bitter humour might be tempered, decreed by law that they should be mixed with each other at the very flow into the intestines, and that, once effervescence had taken place, as in battle, the one should be broken and tempered by the acrimony of the other. Hence dogs do not shrink from human excrement, although they otherwise disdain things tainted with bitter bile. By a manifest experiment, the bitterness of bile with which human faeces are tinged is broken by the phlegm and the pancreatic juice.

units.la: Quamvis talpâ cæcior sit, qui necessariam hanc consequentiam non videat, effervescentiam tamen, de qua quæstio, clariùs ob oculos ponemus, ut eam non modò à priori sive ex causis percipiat, quod nulli non Philosopho abundè sufficit, sed & ipsa experientia, quæ plebejorum magistra est, confirmetur. In hunc finem verbis & lineis referam experimenta, quæ multis præsentibus Studiosis exhibui; canis igitur vivi abdomine aperto duodenum haud procul à pylorO ligamento constrinxi, vinculo quoque injecto paulò infrà insertionem ductus pancreatici: canem deinde, confuto abdomine, sibi reliquimus; tribus horis elapsis, cane, uti videbatur adhuc vegeto, nam paucas duntaxat guttulas sanguinis amiserat, aperto abdomine invenimus spatium vinculis interceptum vehementer distentum, adeò ut illud digitorum compressioni omninò resisteret, atque rupturam mina-
