units.tr: However blinder than a mole is he who does not see this necessary consequence, we shall nevertheless set before the eyes more clearly the effervescence in question, so that it may be confirmed not only a priori, or from causes, which is enough for every philosopher, but also by experience itself, which is the teacher of the common people. To this end I shall relate in words and lines the experiments which I performed in the presence of many students. Accordingly, with the abdomen of a living dog opened, I tied the duodenum not far from the pylorus with a ligature, and also placed a second ligature a little below the insertion of the pancreatic duct. Then I left the dog with its abdomen closed. Three hours having passed, the dog, which still seemed lively, for it had lost only a few drops of blood, we found, with the abdomen opened, the space enclosed by the ligatures greatly distended, so much so that it resisted compression by the fingers altogether, and threatened rupture.

Nec eam duodeni [?]artem ita potuisse distendi, nec tanta [?]i dissipari humores, flatus, vapores [?]c exhalationes, nisi vi effervescentiæ sive agitatione particularum humorum horum contrariorum, qui cupit, capiet. Paucis interjectis diebus idem repetii experimentum præsentibus itidem multis studiosis: atque post duas præterpropter horas portio illa intestini quoque turgebat admodum, sed minus incalescebat: aperta vero intumescente illa intestini portione quam antea ligaveram, cum sonitu prorupere spumantes bullæ, quibus intestini illud spacium fuerat distentum, ut ne ipsa quidem impudentia de illius effervescentiæ veritate dubitare posset. Similem effervescentiam artis cum natura conjugio excitavimus, calidam quidem, miscendo oleum Therebinthinæ cum liquore Tartari: frigida vero confundendo spiritum Vitrioli cum oleo vel potius liquore Tartari, quę lagenulis contenta antea simili intestini portioni vinculis interceptę inclusueram, ut ex fig. B. constat, & paulo post effervescentia haud dissimili illa intestini partẽ distendi vidimus. Turgebat igitur intestinum in præmissis quibus experimentis propter materiæ ive humorum in eo contentorum, biis videlicet & succi pancreatici, præertim orgasmum: atque hinc constabat veritas comparationis Galeni, qua Comment. in I. Sect. Aphor. 22. & in IV. Aphor.10. ὀεγᾶν explicat. Quod it Metaphora ab animantibus conciatis in Venerem translata ad humoes: uti enim animalia libidine incena moventur ad feminis excretionem, imò & eorum genitalia turgent) sic & humores, dum motu feruntur concitatiore hominibus sunt molesti, & loca quæ occupant distendunt. Oculis insuper offerebatur quid esset μετεωρίζεσθαι effervescere, quod vulgò vertitur in sublime attolli, agitatis & distractis illis humorum particulis, acidis, salis & amaris, sive contrariis qualitatibus sive facultatibus in sese mutuò agentibus: Multò enim altior evadebat
units.tr: An instrument compressing the intestinal bile duct. The gall bladder. The cystic bile duct. D. The hepatic bile duct. E. The intestinal bile duct. F. The opening of the intestinal bile duct into the duodenum. G. The opening of the pancreatic duct into the intestine. HH. The intestine distended on account of the effervescence. II. The pancreas. KK. Ligatures constricting the intestinal duct above, and the duodenum within the opening of the pancreatic duct. L. The flaccid part of the duodenum. M. The pylorus. N. The stomach. O. Part of the gullet. [illegible] was tied, and the gall bladder of the dog I observed to be distended no less. A sensation of heat, as if burning, also occupied that part of the duodenum which had been enclosed. When I made a wound in it with a lancet, a certain liquid contained in it, together with wind, burst out with a noise and a crackling, and vapours and exhalations; from which a sharp stench struck the nostrils of all present, and which none of the students could bear when the intestine was opened more widely and it was received at close quarters. This was a clear proof not only that so great a quantity of bile and pancreatic juice had flowed into it, but also that an effervescence had been excited in them, not a mild or gentle one such as dogs normally undergo, but a violent one. For that part of the intestine was not merely full, but was distended by a certain force and ferment. Nor could that part of the duodenum have been so distended, nor such humours, winds, vapours and exhalations have been dissipated, unless by the force of effervescence, that is, by the agitation of the particles of these opposed humours. Let him who is able take this in. A few days later I repeated the same experiment, again in the presence of many students; and after about two hours that portion of the intestine was also very much swollen, but it grew less hot. But when that swollen portion of the intestine, which I had previously tied, was opened, foaming bubbles burst out with a sound, by which that space of the intestine had been distended, so that not even shameless impudence could doubt the truth of that effervescence. We excited a similar effervescence, warm by mixing oil of turpentine with a solution of tartar, and cold by mixing spirit of vitriol with oil, or rather with a solution of tartar; these liquids, kept in small flasks, I had previously enclosed in a similar portion of intestine held between ligatures, as is shown in Fig. B, and shortly afterwards we saw that portion of intestine distended by an effervescence not unlike that one. The intestine therefore swelled in these experiments on account of the matter or humours contained in it, namely the bile and the pancreatic juice, especially by their ferment. And from this the truth of Galen's comparison was established, which he explains in his Commentary on the first Section of the Aphorisms, Aphorism 22, and on Aphorism 10 of the fourth book, using the word ὀργᾶν [organ]. It is a metaphor transferred to humours from animals excited to lust; for just as animals, inflamed with desire, are moved towards the discharge of semen, and even their genitals swell, so also humours, when they are carried in a more violent motion, are troublesome to men and distend the places they occupy. Moreover, the eyes were shown what it means to be μετεωρίζεσθαι [metéōrízesthai], to effervesce, which is commonly rendered "to be raised up on high": the particles of the humours, acid, salt and bitter, or opposed qualities or faculties acting mutually upon one another, being agitated and pulled apart. For that portion of the duodenum became much higher, extended and distended.

units.la: Comment. in I. Sect. Aphor. 22. & in IV. Aphor. 10. bat extensa & distenta illa intestini duodeni portio. Quin etiam dubitare nemo poterat quid esset πομαυξησις sive mole augeri: uti & quid sit ζήσις, ὀγκωσις, πνεύματωσις καὶ αὔξησις, quibus σφύξιν definit Arist. lib. de resp. cap. 20. & 21. rarefacti enim illi humores, & flatibus bullisve effervescentiâ excitatis admodum distenti, non potuerunt non majorem locum occupare. Parvâ enim humorum copiâ effluente intestinū longè reddebatur flaccidius propter discessum subtilioris materiæ sive flatuum, vel si mavis halituosi spiritûs, interstitia distractorū humorum occupantium. Non ingratū erat intelligere quare subtilior illa materia, quæ per poros intestini illius ingressa fuerat, ex illo pari facilitate non effluat; sed ibidem permaneat: distractis videlicet humorum illorum partibus, intestino illo motu sive effervescentiâ, non possunt non illorum interstitia, quandoquidem omnia plena sunt, materiâ ria quadam impleri: quapropter quia illa nisi subtilior materia per intestini poros transfire poterit, ea ipsa in intestinum compellitur, ibique permanet, quamdiu humorum partes atque vapores agitantur aut distractæ sunt. Unde eadem constabat quare Hypochondriacus affectus sit flatuosus, murmuracus & borborygmos, ἀλγήματα καὶ ἐμφύσηματα immoderatosque cruciatus excitet, eaque ...
units.tr: Comment. in I. Sect. Aphor. 22. & in IV. Aphor. 10. was stretched and distended, that portion of the duodenum. Nor could anyone doubt what πομαυξησις [promauxēsis], or being increased in bulk, means, or what ζήσις [zēsis], ὀγκωσις [ogkōsis], πνεύματωσις [pneumatōsis] and αὔξησις [auxēsis] mean, by which Aristotle defines the σφύξιν [sphyxin, pulse] in the book On Respiration, chapters 20 and 21. For the humours, rarefied and greatly distended by puffs of wind and bubbles raised by effervescence, could not fail to occupy a larger space. When only a small amount of the humours flowed out, the intestine was made much flabbier, because the finer matter, or the wind, or if you prefer the vaporous spirit, which had filled the spaces between the separated humours, withdrew. It was not unwelcome to understand why that finer matter, which had entered through the pores of the intestine, does not escape by the same ease but remains there: since the parts of the humours are separated by that motion or effervescence, their interstices cannot but be filled with some material substance, for all things are full. Therefore, unless that finer matter can pass through the pores of the intestine, it is driven into the intestine itself and remains there as long as the parts and vapours of the humours are agitated or separated. Hence it was also clear why the hypochondriac patient is flatulent, has rumbling and borborygmi, and suffers ἀλγήματα καὶ ἐμφύσηματα [algēmata kai emphysēmata, pains and inflations] and excessive torments.

Adeoque mirum non videri acerbissimis doloribus corripi eos in quorum corpore spiritus flatulentus conclusus est.

units.la: Deinde alius canis itidem viventis abdomen eadem methodo aperui, atque ductu bilario intestinali, qui cystico & hepatico communis est, instrumento compresso, eo modo,quem figura exhibet, ut succus pancreaticus solus prodiret, trium propemodum horarum spatio collegimus succi acido-austeri præterpropter ʒij. cujus manifestus acor non gustus modò probabat, sed & illius cum calidiori lacte permixtione, lac ita coagulabatur, ut inde caseus fuerit efformatus: manifesto experimento omninò acidum in eo prævalere; nam licet sali communi non parum acidi insit, uti & alibi monuimus, vires tamen illius à sale puro ita infringuntur, ut sal com[illegible, ~8 letters]ommune lac coagulare nequeat, imò [illegible, ~3 letters] illud à coagulo confervet, quod ne [illegible, ~6 letters]isticos quidem aut coquos fugit. in-[illegible, ~3 letters]ubitato, uti opinor, argumento fuc[illegible, ~3 letters]um pancreaticum solum non turgere, [illegible, ~3 letters]ut effervescere, nec solam bilem, [illegible, ~3 letters]um sola in fellis folliculo continetur; [illegible, ~4 letters]hil enim agit in sese: sed utrumque [illegible, ~3 letters]umorem sibi permixtum blandè qui-[illegible, ~3 letters]em effervescere, in statu, videlicet, [illegible, ~3 letters]turali ob dispositionem illorum sub-[illegible, ~3 letters]ontrariam: vehementer verò ob eo-[illegible, ~3 letters]ndem dispositionem præternatura-[illegible, ~3 letters]m & magis contrariam:quod quam-[illegible, ~3 letters]s ex primo experimento fit manife[illegible, ~3 letters]issimum,remoto tamen instrumento [illegible, ~3 letters]bile liberè per ductū intestinalem in [illegible, ~3 letters]testinum profluente, flaccida paulò [illegible, ~3 letters]te intestina post duas horas enor[illegible, ~3 letters]iter intumuisse, totumque illud spa-[illegible, ~3 letters]um effervescentiâ distentum fuisse, [illegible, ~3 letters] bullis, quibus, cum aperiretur, sca-[illegible, ~3 letters]bat, palàm constitit. Quæ certè [illegible, ~3 letters]la totum libellum Doctoris LeVasseur prorsus refutant, eaque ob oculos ponunt quæ ratione capere non potuit.
units.tr: Then, in the same way, I opened the abdomen of another living dog, and, with the biliary intestinal duct, which is common to the cystic and hepatic ducts, compressed by an instrument in the manner the figure shows, so that only the pancreatic juice flowed out, I collected in about three hours roughly 3 j of pancreatic juice, acido-austere in character. Its clear sourness was shown not only by taste but also by its mixture with warmer milk: the milk was so coagulated that cheese was formed from it. This was a clear experiment that the acid predominates in it. For although common salt contains no little acidity, as we have also noted elsewhere, its strength is so broken by pure salt that common salt cannot coagulate milk, and indeed it [...] preserves it from curdling, which does not escape even the boiling-house workers or cooks. I think this is an argument not open to doubt: that the pancreatic juice alone does not swell or effervesce, nor is the bile alone, which is contained alone in the gall-bladder, for it does nothing against itself. But when each is mixed with the other, they effervesce gently in their natural state, owing to their oppositely disposed (sub-contrary) arrangement, and vehemently in the unnatural state, owing to the same disposition, but more contrary. This is most clear from the first experiment; yet with the instrument removed, the bile flowed freely through the intestinal duct into the intestine, and after two hours the flaccid intestines had swelled considerably, and that whole space was distended by effervescence, as was plain when it was opened, since it crackled with the bubbles. These things certainly refute utterly the whole little book of Doctor LeVasseur, and set before our eyes what he could not grasp by reason.

units.la: Si quis imprudentior dicat hanc esse præternaturalem animalis dispositionem, indeque non esse argumentandum : Responsum accipiat Sylvii praxin esse Therapeuticen, quæ primariò non nisi circa statum hominis præternaturalem est occupata. Concedimus quidem singula ista non esse naturali effervescentiæ attribuenda : negamus verò non licere argumentari ex vehementi illa ab intensis contrariis humoribus excitata effervescentia, quam canis patitur in statu illo præternaturali ad effervescentiam blandam, à subcontrariis humoribus ortam, quâ gaudet in naturali statu: etenim, quod & supra ex Aristotele probavimus, non modò contraria, sed & subcontraria in sese mutuò agunt. atque à majori istorum humorum copia, qui in statu præternaturali propter vim m corpori illatam per utrumque duum in intestinum tenue continuò roruit, ad minorem copiam illorum umorum, qui in statu naturali intestina blandè stillant: quanquidem eadem est materia, iidem nt humores, eædem & gradibus ntaxat diversæ acrimoniæ, iidem, iamvis magis aut minùs acti, spiris & calor excitantes & cooperantes; em denique est locus, in quo inteinum illud prælium committitur. t certè, perquàm ridiculum foret lle videre effervescentiam illorum umorum, & impedire media, quibus in conspectum prodeat; aut non mittere præternaturalem animalis nstitutionem, & velle scrutari intenorum contenta.
units.tr: If some rather imprudent person says that this is an unnatural disposition of the animal, and that no argument should be drawn from it, let him receive this answer: Sylvius's practice is therapeutics, which is chiefly concerned with the unnatural state of man. We grant indeed that these individual things are not to be attributed to natural effervescence; but we deny that it is not permitted to argue from that vehement effervescence, excited by intense contrary humours, which the dog suffers in that unnatural state, to the gentle effervescence, arising from the sub-contrary humours, which it enjoys in its natural state. For, as we also proved above from Aristotle, not only contraries but also sub-contraries act upon one another. And from the greater quantity of these humours, which in the unnatural state, owing to the force inflicted on the body, continually flowed down through both ducts into the small intestine, to the smaller quantity of those humours which in the natural state gently drip into the intestines: since the matter is the same, the humours are the same, and they differ only in degrees of acrimony; the same, although more or less driven, both excite and co-operate in producing heat and spirits; and the place is the same where that battle in the intestine is fought. Indeed it would be quite ridiculous to see the effervescence of those humours and to hinder the means by which it comes into view, or not to take account of the unnatural constitution of the animal and yet wish to examine the contents of the intestines.

units.la: Misella igitur est argumentatiunla, quâ triumphum ante victoriam nens pag. 14. ait D. Graefium suo se jugulare gladio, quia videlicet ille ncedit succum panci eaticum foris cum bile non effervescere, bilem tamen cum nitri spiritu solis ardoribus expositam ebullire: enim vero hujus diversitatis multiplex potest dari ratio. Primò, quia, uti visum, neutiquam sequitur: Humores illi extra corpus non effervescunt, ergo nec in corpore: disparitas exinde apparet, quia uti modò visum, vividi spiritus & calor effervescentiam in corpore vivo excitatam juvant. Sic memini me quondam in pulli generationis examine, triduo postquam ovis incubuisset gallina, observasse corculum illius saliisse cùm ovum primùm aperiretur; sed è vestigio ab aëre frigido correptû quievisse: pòst verò calidâ manu ex calefactum resumsisse vires. Idem contingebat aliquoties ex umbra, sub qua rigebat, solis radiis calidioribus exposito. Idem probat experientia, quâ calculus humanus lagenulâ contentus affuso Spiritu nitri vix aut ne vix quidem solvitur, nisi calore extraneo, [illegible, ~6 letters] minimum calidâ manu, efferveentiâ illâ excitatâ, aut saltem adjuâ, & quanta insuper est vis spirituum?
units.tr: It is therefore a wretched little argument, with which he sings of triumph before victory, at p. 14, and says that Mr. Graaf cuts his own throat with his own sword, because, of course, Graaf denies that pancreatic juice does not effervesce outside the body with bile, while bile exposed to the heat of the sun with spirit of nitre does boil up. But there can be many reasons for this difference. First, because, as has been seen, it by no means follows that: those humours do not effervesce outside the body, therefore neither do they within it. The difference is evident from this, that, as has just been seen, the lively spirits and the heat help the effervescence excited in a living body. So I remember that once, in an examination of the generation of a chick, three days after the hen had sat on the egg, I observed that its little heart leapt when the egg was first opened, but at once, seized by the cold air, it grew still; afterwards, when warmed by a warm hand, it recovered its strength. The same happened several times with a chick that lay chilled in the shade and was exposed to the warmer rays of the sun. The same is shown by experience, in which a human kidney-stone, held in a small flask, with spirit of nitre poured over it, is scarcely or hardly at all dissolved, unless by an external heat, [illegible, about six letters] at least by a warm hand, which excites that effervescence or at least helps it. And how great, moreover, is the power of the spirits!

units.la: 2. Ne ipse igitur stupor auderet objicere: Effervescit bilis cum Spiritu nitri extra corpus, radiis solis exposi-; ergo & bilis deberet etiam extra corpus effervescere cum succo pancreatico. Quis enim non videat multifariam differentiam? Deinde etiam experientiâ constat succum pancreaticum & bilem, cum calidè ex corpore canis seorsim collecta sibi permitentur, effervescere, uti ex vehementi exhalatione & fætore inde subitò certo manifestum est. Sed quæstio, an bilis extra corpus cum succo pancreatico effervescat, hîc nulla est: quandoquidem effervescentia eorum ad oculum in intestinis loco suo naturali observatur. Adstruximus igitur huusque, ni fallor, ad oculum effervescentiam in tenui intestino ortam ab humoribus acidis, biliosis & pituitofis adjuvante calore naturali atque spiritibus, nec non interfluente æthere, sive subtili materia, quæ Hippocrati dicitur, uti supra visum, ἀὴρ λεπτὸς, tenuis aër, qui est veluti calidum innatum macrocosmi, cujus imperio totus mundus subest, uti ex sapienti Hippocratis sententia lib. de Flatibus, Text. v. docet Philosophorum accuratissimus Des Cartes.
units.tr: 2. Let not that dullard then dare to object: bile effervesces with spirit of nitre outside the body when exposed to the rays of the sun; therefore bile too ought to effervesce outside the body with pancreatic juice. For who does not see the many-fold difference? Moreover, it is also established by experience that pancreatic juice and bile, when collected separately while still warm from the body of a dog, effervesce, as is clearly shown by the violent exhalation and stench that soon follows. But the question whether bile outside the body effervesces with pancreatic juice is no question here, since their effervescence is observed by the eye in the intestines, in its natural place. Thus, unless I am mistaken, we have so far established that, visibly, an effervescence arises in the thin intestine from acid, bilious and phlegmatic humours, with the natural heat and the spirits helping, and also the flowing ether, or subtle matter, which is called by Hippocrates, as seen above, ἀὴρ λεπτὸς [thin air], a fine air, which is as it were the innate heat of the macrocosm, by whose command the whole world is subject; as the most exact of philosophers, Descartes, teaches from the wise saying of Hippocrates in the book On Flatulence, text 5.

units.la: Porrò videamus qualis illa effervescentia statuatur à Clariss. D. Sylvio. In homine sano, quia neque bilis, neque succi pancreatici acrimonia valdè excedit, statuit fieri blandâ, quæ faciat ad maturationem & segregationem Chyli ab assumptis & in stomacho fermentatis, atque ad naturalem in corpore calorem & sanguinis consistentiam restituendam & conservandam. Adeò, ut inde neque excessus frigoris neque caloris oriatur, acidulo humore pancreatico calorem bilis temperante. In homine verò malè affecto, quia humoumores illi alia quam naturali proportione, cum excessu videlicet quantitatis & qualitatis sibi mutuò permittentur; mirum videri non debet effervescentiam tùm etiam non excitari naturalem; sed vel vehementiorem, sive calidam vel frigidam, vel tenuis blandam minusve sufficientem, vel magis vel minùs morbidâ illuvie, salinitibus & vaporibus noxiis nocitum.
units.tr: Next let us see what kind of effervescence is laid down by the most distinguished Mr. Sylvius. In a healthy man, because neither the bile nor the pancreatic juice is excessively sharp, he holds that it is gentle, and that it serves the ripening and separation of the chyle from what has been taken in and fermented in the stomach, and the restoration and preservation of the natural heat in the body and of the consistency of the blood. So that from it there arises neither an excess of cold nor of heat, the slightly acid pancreatic humour tempering the heat of the bile. But in a man who is ill, because those humours are mixed in a proportion other than the natural one, with an excess, that is, of quantity and quality, it ought not to seem strange that the natural effervescence is not then excited; but either it is more violent, whether hot or cold, or gentle and weaker than is sufficient, and it harms by a more or less morbid filth, by salts and noxious vapours.

units.la: Huic Sententiæ, ut ut rationi maximè convenienti, pergit sese oppugnare Doctor le Vasseur, asserens, acida, quæ postmodum ad acetum redigit, aut calida esse, aut dubium an ad calidorum ne an frigidorum tantum assem sint revocanda. Unde pag.61.
units.tr: Doctor Le Vasseur goes on to attack this opinion, although it is most agreeable to reason, asserting that the acids, which he afterwards reduces to vinegar, are either hot, or it is doubtful whether they must be counted only among the cold or the hot. Whence at p. 61:

units.la: Horum, inquit, acida, ut docet Sylvius, frigidorum tribu sint, adhuc sub judicis est: fuerunt tamen semper eorum, qui putredine aut empyreumati acida habere judicarunt, partes rationibus numeroque frequentes. Ita sui prorsus oblioblitus sibi ipsi pag. sua 18. plane contrarium statuenti e diametro contradicit. Sic diruit aedificat, ut mirum non sit, si conveniat nulli qui secum dissidet: etenim pag. 18. acidum atque acetum frigidum esse operose adstruxerat, etiam recitato Hippocratis loco, qui non extat, uti putat, in libro de Vet. Med. sed in libro de Victu Acutorum Text. xxix. 8. ubi, uti visum supra pag. 67. Hippocrates ait: aciditates picrocholis convenire, &c. Ita enim fatur Doctor Le Vasseur pag. sua citata 18. Ubi manifeste docet, videlicet Hippocrates, acida bilem frangere, compescere, mitigare: nigra vero duntaxat suscitare & accendere. Cum enim, ut alias habet ψυχλινδν, & πυρρολινδν pariter ἐξῶ audiat, habet luculenter in se, quo bilis ardori & ἀπληςίας frenum injiciat. Idem agnoscit omniscius noster Galenus, ut non pro rei veritate, sed pro libitu, & quatenus Scenae inservit, sententiam ferat
units.tr: Whether these acids, he says, as Sylvius teaches, belong to the tribe of cold things, is still under judgement; yet there have always been those who judged that acids are produced by putrefaction or by empyreuma, and their arguments and numbers are frequent. Thus, quite forgetful of himself, he contradicts himself flatly, at his own p. 18, asserting the opposite. So he tears down and builds up, so that it is no wonder if he agrees with no one who disagrees with him. For at p. 18 he had laboriously maintained that acid and vinegar are cold, even citing a passage of Hippocrates which, as he thinks, is found not in the book On Ancient Medicine but in the book On the Regimen in Acute Diseases, text 29, section 8, where, as was seen above at p. 67, Hippocrates says: acidities suit bitter-bile, etc. For thus Doctor Le Vasseur speaks at his cited p. 18: Where he manifestly teaches, namely Hippocrates, that acids break, check and mitigate bile; only black bile they arouse and inflame. For since, as he elsewhere has it, he hears ψυχλινδν and πυρρολινδν [cold and fiery] alike, he has in himself plainly a bridle to curb the heat of bile and its ἀπληςία [excess]. Our all-knowing Galen recognises the same thing, so that he pronounces his opinion not for the truth of the matter but as he pleases, and as suits the stage.

units.la: Chamæleon. Rectè Galenus lib. 1. de Naturali Facultate qui, inquit, ejusmodi Sectis sunt addicti, non solùm nihil morunt, sed ne discere quidem dignantur. Insanabilis quippe morbus Ignorantia cum Superbia. Et, uti sunt non cohærentia quæ obliviosi ignorantes effutiunt, pag.66. Scriptum, inquit, est ab Hippocrate, quòd τὸ ϑερμὸν ἀεὶ ἄνω φέρεται. Calidum semper sursum tendit. Nempe ut siccitas est lima caloris, sic calor levitatis parens; cujus est summa petere, ac semper niti, in flammantia mænia mundi.
units.tr: Chameleon. Galen rightly says in the first book On the Natural Faculties: those who are attached to such sects not only learn nothing, but do not even deign to learn. For ignorance together with pride is an incurable disease. And, as the forgetful ignorant pour out things that do not hang together, at p. 66: It is written, he says, by Hippocrates, that τὸ θερμὸν ἀεὶ ἄνω φέρεται [the hot always tends upward]. Hot always tends upward. Indeed, as dryness is the file of heat, so heat is the parent of lightness; whose nature is to seek the heights and always to strive toward the flaming walls of the world.

units.la: Hinc halitus, hinc vaporis, hinc flammæ, quæ fumus jure censetur accensus, ἀναφορὰ, ascensus, ac tàm constans εἰς τὸ μετέωρον versus superiora, propensio, ut, cùm nihil sit obici, minimè persuaderi possim, aliâ quàm ventriculo viâ emissos ab effervecentia vapores, perrupturos esse: paginâ verò 63. ait: cùm sint acida maximâ sui parte fixa, quod vapidum emittunt æstu, superasque effiant in oras, phlegma, (sic Chymici vocant) duntaxat insipidum esse, exploratore gustu liquet; ut in spiritu vitrioli rectificando, semper experiuntur Spagyrici, antequam nempe illum tantâ vi torqueant, quantâ nec ferri in corpore potest, nec reperiri. Fixa enim, ni ultimam ignis sævitiam sentiant, vix, ac ne vix quidem, à quoquam quiverunt uspiam, vel tantillo loco moveri. Quis unquam turpius suo se se jugulavit gladio? probavit pag. 18. authoritate Hippocratis & Galeni. atque ex essectis acetum esse frigidum, atque pag. 66. Omne calidum est volatile, & pag. 63. Nullum acidum esse volatile. Unde vel Tiro ex illius dictis necessariò inferat Ergo nullum acidum esse calidum. Sed videamus quibus machinis alibi diruat quod supra & infrà magno mo limine exstruxerat. Ante omnia verò notandum Succum Pancreaticum acidulum vel etiam acidiorem aliave acida Sylvio nunquam absolutè frigida fuisse denominata, sed ista illi ideò vocata fuisse frigida, quia Bilis ardorem spirituumque vitalium calorem refrænant, adeoque corpus humanum refrigerant. Nemo enim aceto nil calidi inesse nisi imprudenter asseruerit, uti ex mox sequentibus manifestum fiet.
units.tr: Hence breath, hence vapour, hence flame, which is rightly judged to be smoke set alight, ascent [ἀναφορὰ], and so constant a tendency towards the heights [εἰς τὸ μετέωρον], that, since nothing can be objected, I can by no means be persuaded that vapours released by effervescence will break through by any other way than the stomach. But at p. 63 he says: since acids are for the most part fixed, what they emit as vapid with heat, and what rises to the upper regions, the phlegm (as the chemists call it) is merely insipid, as taste shows on testing; as the Spagyrists always find when rectifying spirit of vitriol, namely before they twist it with such force as neither can be borne nor found in the body. For fixed things, unless they feel the last cruelty of fire, have scarcely, if at all, been able to be moved anywhere, even by the smallest space. Who ever cut his own throat with his own sword more shamefully? At p. 18 he proved, on the authority of Hippocrates and Galen, and from effects, that vinegar is cold; and at p. 66, Every hot thing is volatile; and at p. 63, No acid is volatile. Hence even a beginner could from his words necessarily infer: Therefore no acid is hot. But let us see with what engines he elsewhere tears down what above and below he had built with great effort. Above all, it must be noted that Sylvius never called pancreatic juice, slightly acid or even more acid, or other acids, absolutely cold; but these were called cold by him because they check the heat of bile and the warmth of the vital spirits, and so cool the human body. For no one would assert that vinegar has nothing hot in it, unless thoughtlessly, as will become clear from what follows.

units.la: Le Vasseur igitur, quò constet se ipsum in omnes transformare formas, hîc quoque dubitat de eo, quod antea diserte adstruxerat, atque alibi, uti visum, expressis verbis negaverat. Exoptat pag. 62. cum Galeno artem, quæ, inquit, nostrorum decore an dedecore temporum floret, ac sæpe sæpius nionio in pretio est, inveniendi, quà disjunctis acidorum partibus, quantum insit ejus, quod calidum est, liceret dilucidè cuspari. Primùm hîc opem Artis Chymicæ enixè implorat, quam odit, atque palàm agnoscit, sine hâc arte sciri non posse, quæ Medico sunt scitu necessaria. Dubitat tamen, illane ars nostro decore an dedecore temporum
units.tr: Le Vasseur therefore, so that it may be established that he transforms himself into every shape, here also doubts what he had earlier expressly maintained, and elsewhere, as was seen, had denied in plain words. He wishes, at p. 62, with Galen, for the art, which, he says, flourishes to the grace or disgrace of our times, and is more and more valued, of discovering, by which, the parts of acids being separated, one might be able to distinguish clearly how much of that which is hot is in them. First here he earnestly implores the aid of the chemical art, which he hates, and openly acknowledges that without this art what is necessary for a physician to know cannot be known. Yet he doubts whether that art flourishes to the grace or disgrace of our times,

units.la: floreat, quâ solâ rerum δυνάμεις potestates accuratè cognoscuntur. Sinè quarum cognitione, vel Hippocrate teste supra allegato, Medicus titulo suo indignus est. Sed misso aut suffiaminato dubio, Acetum calidum esse ait, quia acre est & subtilium partium. Quis enim, inquit pagina citatâ 61. tantam eorum acrimoniam & subtilitatem inertı ac supino prorsus frigori lubens adscribat. Ubi statum controversiae subdolè immutat: non enim lis est, an acetum, aut acidus Succus Pancreaticus, de quo solo quæstio est, omninò sive prorsus frigidus sit, sed an frigidus dici possit respectu humani corporis, circà quod Sylvius in suâ Praxi unicè est occupatus. Videamus igitur, an acida, & speciatim acetum, &, de quo solo quæstio est, an acidulus Succus Pancreaticus sit caloris in humano corpore auctor, an verò hujus calor ab acido infringatur? Pro calore acidorum & speciatim aceti militans, contrà semet ipsum, uti monitum, ita fatur : Antiqui laudante Galeno, acetum [Greek: οἶνον τεθνεῶτα νεκρούντε] dicebant, quod deposito, ut infit, vini calore, [Greek: σηπεδνώδη] alterum induere arbitrarentur pag. 61. Sed quid crepat Antiquos obsoletus Scriptor, cùm Hippocrates lib. 11. de Diæta xxiiii. 6. tàm diserte dicat [Greek: οἱ ὀξωπαῖοι οἶνοι ψύχεσθαι], uti statim visum. & paulò post N.º 9. [Greek: ὀξὺ ψυχρὸν] acetum frigefaciens vocitet. Sed Hippocrate hoc tempore res suas habere [illegible, ~6 letters]usso, in Galeno & Minjotio spem suam fragilem oppidò repositam habet. At quænam est illa oscitantia! Doctor Le Vasseur suprà pag. 18. inquit, Omniscium Galenum docere acidum bilem frangere, atque acetum esse [Greek: ψυχρὸν] frigidum; hîc verò nihil nō agit ut ejusdē Galeni authoritate probet, hoc jam verum esse, jam dubium, jam falsum. quę sanè crassa oblivio doli naturam redolet; ne stuporis majoris quàm qui in Doctorem cadere debet, ipsum accusem. Præterea minùs concinnè connectit hanc suam argumentationem, quâ ex acredine & subtilitate, quæ aceto inest, illius calorem elicere satagit, cum authoritate Galeni, qui lib. 1. de Simpl. Med. facult. cap. 18. huic illationi directè contradicens ait: Etiamsi quis & illud, uti dixi, concedat, quicquid mordax fuerit, esse tenuium partium, non statim tamen & illud calidum esse concesserit. Itaque nec acetum proinde, quòd mordax sit, calidum erit, sed tenuium partium, uti sër Borealis, non tamen calidum. Similiter loco citato lib. iv. cap. 7. Acida tenuitate pollent corporis, sed perinde ut adstringentia refrigerant. Cum quo consentiunt, quæ docet Galenus cap. 18. lib. 4. de Simpl. Med. facult. inquiens: haud perinde ut crustam facientia medicamenta, sed potius ut adstringentia & refrigerantia citrà crustam sanguinis fluorem sistunt. Eam tamen distinctionem adsert l. c. lib. iv. cap. 8. Quòd acidum in frigido subtilis consistat, uti austerum in frigido crasso. Et sanè Galenus 1. c. lib. iv. cap. 24. acetum vocat refrigerans & repellens; uti postea ibid. lib. iv. cap. 24. Acidum, inquit, omne quod tantum est acidum, quicquid id fuerit, plane frigidum est, sive pyrum, sive malum, sive acinus uvæ, sive rubi, Mora, sive mala Punica, sive quivis alius fructus, sive succus sive planta, ut oxylapathum sive oxalis; quippe si gustanti vehementem atque manifestam illi inesse aciditatem apparet, nec quicquam præ se ferat acrimonia, omninò hunc succum refrigerantem reperies, quin confidenter utitor, sive ad ardores, uti consultum est, hypochondriis impositò, sive ad Erysipelas, sive ad alium affectum calidum. Ab usu igitur Medico, à Juvantibus & Lædentibus probat Galenus mille locis acida esse frigida. Sed Galenum nihilominus suum vocat, pro sese citat levis armaturæ miles. Qui cùm hactenus sub Galeno delitescere diutius nequit, fugit ad Minjotium, ejus opem blanditiis demereri studens. Antiqui, inquit pag. 61. Acetum vocarunt οἶνον ἀλιέων, & Macrobius vini culpati nomine acetum insignivit, ut non dubito, legisti apud Heroëm nostrum, & omni prorsus encomio majorem, Minjotium, quem scio pariter ambo ferimus in oculis. Sed quid illud ad rem? quis nescit acetum non esse vinum inculpatum? quin inde postmodum probabimus prolixius spiritibus calidioribus vini consumtis, demum ex eo fieri acetum. Sed verò, nì vehementer fallor, ad rem facit, quod Doctissimus Doctor Minjotius pag. 36. Operis sui de Febribus malignis, alterantia praescribens, quibus praeter alia subsidia, quae ibi recenset, malignae febres debellentur, talia, inquit, eligantur, quae obstructas, forte, vias, una recludant, ut radices fragaria, graminis, dentis leonis, herba cichoracea, intybacea, endivia, cicerbita, bu-
units.tr: "...flourishes, by which alone the powers [δυνάμεις] of things are accurately known. Without knowledge of these, even by the testimony of Hippocrates cited above, the physician is unworthy of his title. But setting aside the doubt, he says vinegar is hot, because it is sharp and of subtle parts. For who, he says, at p. 61 cited, would gladly ascribe so much sharpness and subtlety to a wholly inert and sluggish cold? Here he quietly shifts the state of the controversy. For the dispute is not whether vinegar, or the acid pancreatic juice, which is the only thing in question, is utterly cold in itself, but whether it can be called cold with respect to the human body, which is what Sylvius in his Practice is solely concerned with. Let us see, then, whether acids, and vinegar in particular, and the acidulous pancreatic juice, which alone is in question, are the cause of heat in the human body, or whether their heat is rather broken by acid. Fighting for the heat of acids and of vinegar in particular, he speaks against himself, as the reader has been warned: The ancients, following Galen, used to call vinegar "killing dead wine" [οἶνον τεθνεῶτα νεκρούντε], because, when the warmth of the wine, as he puts it, was lost, they thought it took on another, putrid, character [σηπεδνώδη], p. 61. But why does this obsolete writer rattle on about the Ancients, when Hippocrates, Book 2 On Diet, section 24, sec. 6, says so plainly that vinegar-wines are cooled [οἱ ὀξωπαῖοι οἶνοι ψύχεσθαι], as is seen at once, and a little later, No. 9, calls it sharp cold [ὀξὺ ψυχρὸν], vinegar that cools? But as things stand, Hippocrates is in a sorry state, and he places his fragile hope firmly in Galen and Minjotius. And what a careless slip this is! Doctor Le Vasseur, above at p. 18, says that Galen, all-knowing, teaches that acid breaks bile and that vinegar is cold [ψυχρὸν]; yet here he does everything to prove by the same Galen's authority that this is now true, now doubtful, now false. This crude forgetfulness certainly smells of trickery; I will not accuse him of a greater stupidity than a Doctor ought to be liable to. Moreover, he links this argument of his less neatly: from the sharpness and subtlety that are in vinegar he strives to draw out its heat, though Galen's authority, Book 1 On the Powers of Simple Medicines, chapter 18, directly contradicts this inference, saying: Even if someone grants that, as I have said, whatever is biting is of subtle parts, he will not at once grant that it is hot. Therefore vinegar will not be hot merely because it is biting, but of subtle parts, like the north wind, yet not hot. Similarly, in the passage cited, Book 4, chapter 7: Acids are strong in the thinness of their body, but like astringents they cool. With this agree the things Galen teaches in chapter 18 of Book 4 On the Powers of Simple Medicines, saying: not in the way of medicines that form a crust, but rather, like astringents and coolers, they stop the flow of blood without a crust. He does, however, adduce this distinction in the same place, Book 4, chapter 8: that acid is subtle in a cold state, as the austere is in a cold and thick state. And indeed Galen, in the same place, Book 4, chapter 24, calls vinegar cooling and repelling; and afterwards in the same place, Book 4, chapter 24: Every acid, he says, which is merely acid, whatever it may be, is plainly cold, whether pear, or apple, or grape, or blackberry, or pomegranate, or any other fruit, or juice, or plant, such as sorrel or wood-sorrel; for if it appears to the taster to have a strong and manifest acidity and shows no sharpness, you will find this juice cooling, and you may use it confidently, whether it is placed on the hypochondria for burning heats, as is advised, or for erysipelas, or for another hot affection. Galen therefore proves by the Physician's practice, from the things that help and the things that harm, in a thousand places, that acids are cold. But, nonetheless, he calls Galen his own and, under his name, cites him as a light-armed soldier. When he can no longer lie hidden under Galen, he flees to Minjotius, eager to win his help by flattery. The ancients, he says at p. 61, called vinegar "wine of the fishermen" [οἶνον ἀλιέων], and Macrobius marked vinegar with the name of blamed wine, as I do not doubt you have read in our Heroës, and Minjotius, greater than any praise, whom, I know, we both hold in high esteem. But what has that to do with the matter? Who does not know that vinegar is not blameless wine? Indeed, we shall afterwards prove at greater length that vinegar is made from wine once its more fiery spirits are consumed. But truly, unless I am much mistaken, what bears on the matter is that the most learned Doctor Minjotius, at p. 36 of his work On Malignant Fevers, in prescribing alterants, by which, besides the other remedies he lists there, malignant fevers are overcome, says: Let such things be chosen as may open up obstructed passages, perhaps, all at once, such as the roots of strawberry, couch grass, dandelion, chicory, endive, endive-like and sow-thistle, bu-

units.la: glossum. lossum, borrago & oxytriphyllum praæteris convenientissimum propter aciditatem, sicut & oxalis præcipuè rotunda. Ut enim extrà corpus materia sulphurea & inflammabilitatem acida reprimunt, sic intrà corpus flammantem bilem frænant.
units.tr: bugloss. Borage and oxytriphyllon, especially suitable on account of their acidity, and likewise wood-sorrel, especially the round kind. For just as outside the body they check sulphurous matter and acid inflammability, so inside the body they restrain the inflaming bile.

units.la: Quod docet Hippocrates Sect. ʒ. de Dieta acutorum, ubi ait acetum picrocholis magis conferre quàm melancholicis, quoniam in his atrum humorem fermentat atque multiplicat: in illis verò ab aceto πὰ πικρῶν [illegible, ~6 letters] ὢ ἐκφλεγματίζοντα μιτιωεληζόμενα [illegible, ~4 letters] amara dissolvuntur ac pituitescunt, dum abipso in sublime attolluntur. Neque autem per ἐκφλεγματίζων intelligit Hippocrates in pituitam verti, sed pituitæ qualitatibus ut frigiditate & crassitie donari, quo sensu in senibus, bilis dicitur ἐκφλεγματίζων; ideoque reddi καλάρρονον. Itaque ex plantis dictis, maximè ex acidis parentur decocta ad amplas doses, quibus in gratiam ægrotantium, saccharum dissolvetur, sed in minima quantitate.
units.tr: This is what Hippocrates teaches in Section 3 On the Diet of Acute Diseases, where he says that vinegar is more useful in the bilious than in the melancholic, since in the latter it ferments and multiplies black humour, whereas in the former the bitter bile is dissolved by the vinegar and made phlegmatic [ἐκφλεγματίζοντα], and is lifted up into the upper parts. Nor does Hippocrates mean by ἐκφλεγματίζων that the bile is turned into phlegm, but that it is endowed with the qualities of phlegm, such as coldness and thickness; in this sense bile in old men is called phlegmatic, and therefore is rendered [καλάρρονον] mild. Accordingly, from the plants mentioned, and chiefly from the acids, decoctions are prepared in large doses, and to please the sick, sugar is dissolved in them, but only in a very small quantity.

units.la: Porrò si acetosa sunt calida atque calefacientia, perperàm Hippoc. toto libro de Victu in Morbis acutis, perperàm Galenus & quotquot posst eos praxin rectè exercuerunt præscripsêre Diætam medicamentosam ex acidis in febribus acutis ; quas omnes, si malignas excipias, à bile deducendas uno ore fatentur. Non aliâ de causâ Crisin in febribus à bile ortis fieri concipio, quàm vi effervescentiæ in humoribus excitatæ ab acido, quod in ægro oritur discessu quorundam spirituum atque Salis volatilis, vi febrilis effervescentiæ facto, unde Lymphæ major acor, quæ acore suo cum bile, primariâ mali caussâ, effervescens, eam temperat, atque eadem illâ actione materiam, quæ morbi causla est, secernit & excernit. Unde mirum non est, non modò in bona istiusmodi crisi, propter conflictum illum humorum inter sese ægrum multa pati, sed etiam antè crisin cunctis sese ad capitale prælium præparantibus : quâ de e videsis Hipp. Aphorism. 13. Sect.
units.tr: Moreover, if acid things are hot and heating, then Hippocrates, throughout the whole book On Regimen in Acute Diseases, and Galen, and all who have rightly practised medicine, wrongly prescribed a medicinal diet of acids in acute fevers; and all of them, unless you except the malignant, unanimously admit that these fevers arise from bile. For no other reason do I think that crisis occurs in fevers arising from bile than by the force of effervescence excited in the humours by the acid, which arises in the sick person when certain spirits and volatile salt withdraw, the force of the febrile effervescence having been produced. Hence comes the greater sourness of the lymph, which, effervescing with its sourness together with the bile, the primary cause of the disease, tempers it, and by that same action secretes and excretes the matter that is the cause of the disorder. Hence it is no wonder that the sick person suffers much, not only in a good crisis of this kind, because of that conflict of the humours among themselves, but also before the crisis, while all the parts prepare for the decisive battle; on this see Hippocrates, Aphorisms, section 1, aphorism 13.

units.la: 1. Hinc etiam in diuturnis lienteiis, sive intestinorum lævitatibus, bortis ὀξυρῤῆγμίαις ruētibus acidis, qui riùs non exstiterunt Hippocrates nos ene̅ ominari jubet, Aphorism. 1. ect. vi. acidum enim, fermentum omachi, optimum naturali effervescentiæ excitandæ remedium, in umano corpore tùm temporis augeri gnificat. Sed quid multis? ex aceti generatione manifestum est, acetum minùs calidiorum particularum concinere quàm vinum, quandoquidem propter spirituum calidorum, sive corpusculorum oleaginosorum discefsum proculdubio frigidioris fit temperamenti. In hunc finem vinum vase perto sudo cælo exponitur, ut, quidusdam spiritibus, quorum agitatione prohibebatur acidi & salsi conjunctio, dissolutis & separatis, atque aqueo humore quadantenus consumpto, acescentes particulæ facilius cum Sale & residuis spiritibus conjungantur & ut loquuntur, concentrentur. Unde acidi acrimonia. Sic ex acido & concentratis particulis quibusdam minimis Metallicis aut Lapideis Vitriolum acre, & Mercurius præcipitatus maximarum virium oritur, cùm aliàs Mercurius suopte ingenio flexilis sit, nec solus corpori bene disposito noceat, adeò ut author fide dignus referat rusticum Metallicis laboribus insudantem, haustum Mercurii in pocolo forte asservati distento gutture innoxium assumsisse. Sed quia Mercurii minimæ particulæ post quandam effervescentiam facilè adhærescunt acido, quæ, utut suâ naturâ flexiles, acido junctæ rigescunt & unitis viribus acrimoniam suam produnt, magna Mercurii copia in corpore acido acri abundante noxia esse posset. Hinc existimo eos, qui Lue Venereâ insecti sunt, Mercurio inungi, ut acidum, in quo præcipuè natura illius [illegible, ~6 letters]uis consistit, stimuletur, ut per dulicaturas & interstitia membranarum [illegible, ~3 letters]que vasa Lymphatica ad os unà cum Mercurio deferatur atque per salivam excernatur. Etenim Luem illam Veneream acidam esse liquet non tantum [illegible, ~3 letters]uia glandulas acido percolando determinatas maximè inficit, sed etiam [illegible, ~3 letters]uia ab ea consumuntur offa sale, uti [illegible, ~3 letters]otum, abundantia, & quidem præfertim in medio teretium ossium, atque universim eo loco, ubi offa minùs ifcido humore dulciore, quo acrimonia Luis illius obtunditur, irrigantur. Unde etiam quia in gingivis est ncidi copia, cum qua Mercurius eò elatus effervescit, infandos dolores in ibus patiuntur; dentes alveolis suis atque gingivis rarefactis vacillant; atque insuper utpote offa, eroduntur. Nec contagio nocet distantibus. Ex quibus manifestum est, Luem VenereAm esse Venenum minùs volatile, & acidum. Aliquos igitur, non tamen
units.tr: Hence also in long-lasting lientery, or in looseness of the bowels, and in the sour belchings [ὀξυρῤῆγμίαις] that rush up from acids, which Hippocrates bids us expect even when they have not arisen, Aphorism 1, section 6: for the acid, the ferment of the stomach, the best remedy for exciting natural effervescence, is shown to be increased in the human body at that time. But why say more? From the making of vinegar it is clear that vinegar agrees less with the warmer particles than wine does, since, through the departure of the warm spirits, or oily corpuscles, it certainly becomes of a colder temperament. To this end, wine is exposed in an open vessel to the sun, so that, certain spirits being dissolved and separated, by whose agitation the union of the acid and the salt was prevented, and the watery humour being in some measure consumed, the particles that turn sour more easily join with the salt and the remaining spirits, and, as they say, are concentrated. Hence comes the sharpness of the acid. So from acid and certain very small concentrated metallic or stony particles arises sharp vitriol and precipitated mercury of the greatest powers, whereas otherwise mercury, being pliant by its own nature, does not harm a well-disposed body alone; so much so that a trustworthy author relates that a rustic, toiling at metal works, swallowed with impunity a draught of mercury from a cup kept for the purpose, with his throat open. But since the smallest particles of mercury, after a certain effervescence, cling readily to acid, and these, though pliant by their own nature, when joined to acid grow stiff and reveal their sharpness with united strength, a large quantity of mercury could be harmful in a body abounding in sharp acid. Hence I think that those who are infected with venereal disease are anointed with mercury, so that the acid, in which the chief strength of that [mercury?] consists, may be stirred up, and that it may be carried by the folds and interstices of the membranes and the lymphatic vessels to the mouth, together with the mercury, and be excreted through the saliva. For it is clear that the venereal disease is acid, not only because it chiefly infects the glands, which are determined to filter acid, but also because the bones are consumed by its salt, as the whole of them, in abundance, and especially in the middle of the long bones, and generally in the places where the bones are watered by less acid, sweeter humour, by which the sourness of that disease is blunted. Hence also, because there is a plentiful supply of acid in the gums, into which the mercury, carried there, effervesces, they suffer unspeakable pains in the gums; the teeth, with their sockets and gums rarefied, wobble; and moreover, as the bones are eroded. Nor does the contagion harm those at a distance. From these things it is evident that the venereal disease is a poison less volatile and acid. Some, therefore, though not all, spirits must fly off so that vinegar may be made; which is shown by this, because otherwise the phlegm of rectified spirit of wine would become the best vinegar, which, however, nobody, as I think, doubts is not even acid. Hence, as the proverb has it, the sharpest vinegar comes from the best wine. Moreover…

units.la: omnes spiritus avolare debent, ut fiat acetum; quod vel hinc constat, quia aliàs phlegma spiritûs Vini rectificati optimum essiet acetum, quod tamen ne acidum quidem esse neminem, ut opinor, fugit. hinc, ut est in diverbio, optimi vini acerrimum acetum. Præterea non prorsus spiritibus destitutum esse acetum, manifestum, quia oleum amarum & spiritus inflammabilis dextrâ Chymicâ manu, sed parùm admodùm elicitur: quæ ratio est quare dixerimus acetum non quidem absolutè frigidum esse, sed frigidos in humano corpore effectus producere. En artem, quam modò cum Galeno optavit, ut rerum potentias scrutaretur! Neque acida pituitam incidunt suo calore, uti & modò ex Galeno probatū, sed suâ partium tenuitate, eâque illarum acrimoniæ dispositione, quâ cum sale, qui illi pituitæ inest, effervescunt, (non ergo effervescunt acida cum pituita insipida aut acescente) quâ effervescentiâ pituita
units.tr: all the spirits must fly off so that vinegar is made. This is clear from the fact that otherwise the phlegm of rectified spirit of wine would make the best vinegar, though I think no one doubts that it is not even sour. Hence, as the proverb has it, the best wine makes the sharpest vinegar. Moreover, that vinegar is not wholly without spirits is evident, since bitter oil and inflammable spirit are drawn out of it by the chemist's hand, though only in very small amounts. This is why we would say that vinegar is not absolutely cold, but produces cold effects in the human body. Behold the art which he has just wished, with Galen, for examining the powers of things! Acids do not cut phlegm by their heat, as has just been shown from Galen, but by the fineness of their parts and by the arrangement of their sharpness, by which they effervesce with the salt that is in that phlegm. (Acids, then, do not effervesce with insipid or sour phlegm.) By this effervescence the phlegm

units.tr: phlegm [?] is cut as if by so many little lances by the sharpness of the acid particles, and is thinned, and ὀρφνὸν φλέγμα (dark phlegm) becomes fluid phlegm, which before had been viscid. Or, if there is more of a tartarous and earthy phlegm, and it lies in a place from which it is not easily separated, it hardens, as it were after a battle, when the sharper salt and acid meet with the earthy parts that have been concentrated or coalesced, or even turns to stone. So too sometimes phlegm enclosed in some moist place hardens by the coagulation and drying of its contrary particles, once the watery vapours have been driven off by effervescence and heat. To this belongs Hippocrates, On the Affections, sections 14 and 15, where he shows that a dung in the hardened intestine has phlegm bound around it. Hence the round sputa of consumptives in the lungs, hard and sometimes stony. Meanwhile it must be noted in words that warm things

units.la: ropriè loquendo esse subtiliora, carem enim esse vehementiorem sublioris materiæ agitationem nemiem, uti opinor, fugit; crassiora verò orpora talia denominari, quia calida orpora in sese continent, aut illorum ccasione, calida corpora in illis aut rcà illa exoriuntur, aut exoriri posnt: quæ propterea dicuntur calida o loquendi modo, quo Magnes dicir trahere ferrum aut Magnetem: eoie sensu ferrum quamvis candens, ropriè non urit, sed hoc agere dicir denominatione ab igneo vortice r poros ferri & circum illud rapissimè acto: quæ utpote in vera Phisophia exercitatis manifesta, proli-xiùs xiùs explicare non est necesse. Qui igitur ad oculum tactumque demonstratum fuit, dari effervescentiam in Intestinis ab adversa acrimonia acidi & bilis ortam. Quia acidus Succus Pancreaticus frigore æstum bilis temperat, bilis verò caloris & æstûs caussa est, atque pituita pro ratione diversitatis temperamenti vel acrimoniæ utriusque temperat, vel etiam alterum alterumve adjuvat, facilè concipitur pro ratione copiæ aut acrimoniæ majoris vel minoris cujusque humoris illius Triumviratûs necessariò oriri debere effervescentiam vel naturalem moderatam, temperatam & blandam vel præternaturalem calidiorem, frigidiorem, vehementiorem, majorem diuturniorem vel contrà.
units.tr: are, properly speaking, finer. For heat is the more vehement agitation of a subtler matter, which I think no one fails to see. But grosser bodies are called warm because warm bodies are contained within them, or because warm bodies arise in them or from them, or can arise. They are therefore called warm in the same way that the magnet is said to draw iron, or that the magnet itself is said to draw. In this sense iron, though glowing, does not properly burn; but this is said to be done by a figure of speech, from the fiery vortex that is driven very swiftly through the pores of the iron and around it. Since this is plain to those practised in true philosophy, there is no need to explain it at greater length. Therefore, as has been shown to eye and touch, there arises in the intestines an effervescence caused by the opposed acrimony of acid and bile. Because the acid pancreatic juice tempers the heat and ferment of bile with its coldness, while bile is the cause of heat and ferment, and phlegm, according to the diversity of temperament or acrimony, either tempers both or helps one or the other, it is easily conceived that, according to the greater or lesser quantity or acrimony of each humour of that triumvirate, there must necessarily arise an effervescence, either natural, moderate, temperate and mild, or preternatural, hotter, colder, more vehement, greater, more lasting, or the reverse.

units.tr: So that he cannot escape the charge of falsehood, when he says on p. 19: Sylvius always puts forward the pancreatic juice as the most powerful and most violent thing, of which the example is to be seen in the corroding spirit of vitriol or of nitre. If this were so,

units.la: enda prorsus hominum sors & lugenda foret, quorum exta perpetuis dilaniarentur cruciatibus, aut adurerentur κau̇τποις. Sic nempe vivitur cum Flammifera Erynnis verbere excusso sonat Rogisq; adustas propius ac propius sudes In ora tendit.
units.tr: the lot of men would be wholly to be pitied and mourned, whose entrails would be torn by perpetual torments, or burned with cauteries. Thus indeed one lives, when the fire-bearing Fury cracks her whip and, ever nearer, thrusts the scorched stakes of the pyre into the face.

units.la: Peppis enim & tonsoribus notum, in ore, quod pari cum ventriculo & intestinis membrana vestitur, usu postulante, haud cohibendam excitari per Spiritum vitriolevi contactu ἰχάρ. Hęc scribere non dubescit. Ast tantum abest, ut Sylvius statuat omnem effervescentiam esse neam, ut ex professo doceat, nullam æter blandā effervescentiā in benè institutō humano corpore excitari: potę qui suæ praxeos p. 106. Non tantum, ait, quando è ventriculo ad Intestina propelluntur alimenta fermentata, fluunt quoque in tenue intestinum Bilis Succus Pancreaticus; verum continuo, F adeoadeoq; illo etiam tempore, quo nullum afsumtum, vel ad Intestina deductum est alimentum, eò feruntur, ac necessariò ibidem propter partium suarum dispositionem subcontrariam in concursu suo effervescentiam excitant, in Sanitatis quidem statu, h. e., quamdiu bene dispositus, temperatusq; est uterque, blandā & naturę amicā; ubiveròalteruter, aut uterq; intemperatus est & acrior, vitiosam & noxiam
units.tr: For it is known to bakers and barbers that in the mouth, which is lined with a membrane like that of the stomach and intestines, the spirit of vitriol, when lightly touched, excites a flow that cannot be checked, as the use requires [ἰχώρ]. He does not shrink from writing this. But Sylvius is far from holding that every effervescence is harmful, or from teaching professedly that no effervescence except a mild one is excited in a well-constituted human body. For in his practice, p. 106, he says: "Not only when fermented food is driven from the stomach into the intestines does the pancreatic juice flow with the bile into the thin intestine; but continually, and even at that time when no food has been taken or led down into the intestines, they are carried there and necessarily, in that place, on account of the subcontrary disposition of their parts, they excite an effervescence in their meeting: in the state of health, namely, as long as each is well disposed and tempered, a mild effervescence friendly to nature; but where either or both are intemperate and sharper, a vicious and harmful one."

units.la: Quod ut distinctiùs patescat, ostendit pag. 109. Hanc effervescentiam prosperæ valetudinis tempore admodum blandam esse vel inde patet, quòd nullus sit ejus Sanis sensus: qui tamen in ægris tàm sæpè tàm est manifestus & atrox, a per lancinationes, distensiones, tormina, frigora, æstus, ebullitiones, &c. tùm in regione lumbari, tùm in sinistro hypochondrio, tùm in universo quandoque abdomine prodens. Multifariè verò vitiosa existit prædicta effervescentia 1. rationè Bilis acrioris & Salinæ: unde sitim saepius augeri, atque Diarrhæam plerumque
units.tr: So that this may be set out more clearly, he shows on p. 109: "That this effervescence is very mild in the time of good health is evident from this alone, that the healthy have no sense of it. Yet in the sick it is so frequent and so manifest and fierce, showing itself by lancinating pains, distensions, gripings, chills, heats, bubblings, etc., sometimes in the lumbar region, sometimes in the left hypochondrium, sometimes in the whole abdomen." But the aforesaid effervescence turns out to be vicious in many ways: (1) by reason of a bile that is sharper and saline, whence I think thirst is more often increased and diarrhoea generally takes its origin;

units.la: originem trahere arbitror. · 2. Ratione ilis naturali Pinguioris, unde Ardorem regione lumbari tantum, aut in unierso praeterea corpore produci existimo.
units.tr: (2) by reason of a natural bile that is fattier, whence I think burning is produced only in the lumbar region, or moreover throughout the whole body.

units.la: Ratione Succi Pancreatici Acidioris acrioris; unde caeteris paribus Frigus citari puto plerumque in nominatâ imborum regione, ac postmodum in uniersum distribui corpus : quod manife- um est in omni penè Intermittentium ebrium principio. 4. units.tr: By reason of pancreatic juice that is more acid and sharper, whence, other things being equal, I think cold is excited mostly in the said region of the bowels, and afterwards distributed through the whole body, which is manifest in almost every beginning of intermittent fevers. 4. By reason of pancreatic juice that is astringent and bitter, to which I ascribe both the hypochondriac suffocation producing similar vapours and the origin of pains that twist and wrench the intestines wonderfully.
