So the man who on p. 78 says three times over the Belgian innovator might well be called the French old trickster.

units.la: Sedulò porrò investigemus quid efficiat illa humorum in tenui Intestini effervescentia. Sylvius Praxeos suæ pag. 107. ait: Censeo in illo binorum humorum confluxu dissolvi Pituitæ Intestini tenuis parietibus adhærentem partem Fluidiorem, eandemque cum maximâ Bilis, Succique Pancreatici coneffervescentium parte junctam penetrare in venas usque ad Cor: dum pars eadem Pituitæ tenacior & viscidior cum aliqua reliquorum Humorum parte itidem viscidiore pergit sensim ad Intestinum crassum, ibidemq; Alvinis Facibus adhæsta eadem viscidiores facit & flaviores. Primùm igitur Pituitam in intestino tenui contentam attenuat, ne videlicet illius infarctu fieret obstructio aliay occlusio meatuum illorum, per quos humores in Intestina ex ductu bilari, Intestinali, Pancreate, Stomacho aliisque meatibus profluant; vel etiam per quos Spiritus eo confluant; vel isto rum quoque per quos Chylus in reliquum corpus derivetur: vel etiam ne pituita illius abundantiâ Sensus aut motus Intestinorum amittatur, aut obtundatur, quò ad sequestrationem Chyli atque onerum Ventris excretionem segniores evadant, iisque impleantur & graveнтur, eorumque noxiis halitibus & vaporibus totum corpus inficiatur. quam pituitæ attenuationem Galenum necesse scium humoris Pancreatici, soli bili adscripsisse, suprà probavimus. Deinde ut attenuata illa Pituita bilis fluorem & acredinem temperet. Huic luci tenebras objiciens p.25,26,27. Primùm inquit, frigore nequaquam densari ho phlegma, quod tamen necesse est, si effer vescentiâ liquetur & contabescat.
units.tr: Let us next investigate carefully what that effervescence of the humours in the thin intestine produces. Sylvius says in his Praxis, p. 107: I think that in that confluence of the two humours, the more fluid part of the phlegm adhering to the walls of the thin intestine is dissolved, and this part, joined with the greatest part of the bile and pancreatic juice effervescing together, penetrates even into the veins as far as the heart; while the thicker and more viscid part of the same phlegm, together with some part of the other humours likewise more viscid, gradually passes on to the large intestine, and there, adhering to the faeces of the belly, makes them more viscid and yellower. First, then, he thins the phlegm contained in the thin intestine, lest by its obstruction there should be a blockage or occlusion of those passages through which the humours flow into the intestines from the bile duct, the intestinal, pancreatic and stomach ducts and other passages; or through which the spirits flow thither; or also of those through which the chyle is conveyed to the rest of the body; or lest by the excess of its phlegm the sensation or motion of the intestines be lost or dulled, so that they become sluggish in separating the chyle and in excreting the contents of the belly, and are filled and burdened with them, and the whole body is infected by their harmful exhalations and vapours. We have already shown above that Galen was obliged to ascribe this thinning of the phlegm to the pancreatic humour alone, and not to bile. Next, that the thinned phlegm may temper the flux and acridity of the bile. Casting shadows on this light, at pp. 25, 26, 27 he says: First, he says, phlegm is by no means thickened by cold, yet it must be, if it is liquefied and wasted by effervescence.

units.la: Cui sane plebejæ objectioni jàm udum alibi satisfactum. Nititur enim hypothesi, antea pag. 65. omninò diuta, omnemvidelicet effervescentiam esse calidam; cùm tamen eam quandoque calidam, quandoq; frigidam, quandoque moderatam, blandam & temperatam esse suprà abundè probatum sit. Adeò ut pituita illa liquidior reddatur & effervescentię, non quasi actio ea efficit calefactio ut supra p. 116. probatum, sed quatenus pituita effervescens à illâ præcipuè à spiritiosis & acidis articulis, velut totidem Lanceolis inditur & ulteriori motu rarescit. adeo que ea facilius segregatur atque ab intestinis separatur, naturaliter quidem, quousque id naturæ conducit, præternaturaliter verò, aut minùs aut etiam plurimùm: adeo ut non semel observatū erit intestina abrasa illa sua pituitosa tunica pellucida apparuisse. Hinc & dolores intestinorum illo suo vestimento privatorum; unde motus peristalticus augetur; inde fluxus alvi intempestivus stimulatis eo dolore intestinis ad excretionem eorum quibus onerantur atque tandem aliquando inde generari possunt intestinorū inflammationes, exulcerationes & dysenteriæ.
units.tr: This plebeian objection has indeed already been answered elsewhere. For it rests on the hypothesis, stated earlier on p. 65, which is entirely mistaken, namely that all effervescence is hot; whereas it has been abundantly shown above that effervescence is sometimes hot, sometimes cold, sometimes moderate, mild and tempered. So the phlegm is rendered more liquid and effervescent, not because that action produces heat, as shown above on p. 116, but insofar as the effervescing phlegm is struck, chiefly by the spirituous and acid particles, as if by so many little lances, and is rarefied by further motion. Thus it is more easily separated and detached from the intestines, naturally indeed, as far as this serves nature, but unnaturally, either less or even very much: so that it has not once been observed that the intestines, scraped of their pituitous transparent coat, have appeared bare. Hence also the pains of the intestines deprived of their covering; from which the peristaltic motion is increased; hence an untimely flux of the bowels, the intestines being stimulated by that pain to expel the contents with which they are burdened; and at last inflammations, ulcerations and dysenteries of the intestines can sometimes arise from this.

units.la: Ex quibus constat, ex mente Sylvii & rei veritate effervescentiā à valdè acri acido subtili sive spirituoso cū naturali bile excitatā, adeoq; naturali frigidiorē, de qua supra, magis attenuare pituitā quàm istam, quæ & naturalis est & calidior; unde dolores lancinātes, tormina, &c. acria enim ista instar strigilū intestina abradūt, atq; suâ acredine exedūt. Longè certè accuratius argumētatus fuisset si dixisset; Si effervescentia ab acido subtili & spirituoso cū sale volatili excitata pituitam attenuat atq; incidit, ergò effervescētia ab acido austero producta pituitā crassiorē reddit.
units.tr: From these points it is clear, both according to Sylvius's opinion and in the truth of the matter, that the effervescence excited by a very sharp, subtle or spirituous acid together with the natural bile is, for that reason, cooler than the natural kind mentioned above, and so it thins the phlegm more than the phlegm that is both natural and warmer. Hence the gnawing pains, the gripings and so on, for these sharp things scrape the intestines like scrapers and eat them away with their acridity. Certainly he would have reasoned much more accurately if he had said: If an effervescence excited by a subtle and spirituous acid together with volatile salt thins and cuts the phlegm, then an effervescence produced by a sour acid makes the phlegm thicker.

units.la: Melancholiâ enim hypochondriacâ Laborantium, ab acido austero pituitam coagulante, intestina scatent viscidâ cida & tenaci admodū pituitā. Adeò t Nobilis quispiam Schiedami morbo Hypochondriaco laborans, meæ cue commissus, excreverit per inferiora pituitam adeò viscidam, ut primùm utaverit sese intestini partem quamam,deinde verò se vermem immensę raffitiei excrevisse. Idem Lipsio acdisse refert Joannes Heurnius. quod aliis contigisse variæ Observationes medicorum protestantur. At verò D. eVasseur potentiarum & facultatum Hippocraticarū prorsus ignarus, nonsi frigoris & caloris, ut quispiam de ivio, ineptam mentionem facit. Si onsiderarepotuisset post effervescenam in intestinis fieri quandam, uti nuium humorum separationem, ita propterea crassiorum coagulatioem & velut præcipitationem, facile ncepisset, quî fiat, quòd quâdam piità soluta, alia quædam postea natuliter generetur, quæ denuò viscidior testinorum parietibus adhærescat.
units.tr: For in hypochondriac melancholy, the intestines of sufferers swarm with viscid and very tenacious phlegm, because a sour acid coagulates the phlegm. Thus a certain noble man at Schiedam, who suffered from hypochondriac disease and was committed to my care, passed through the lower parts phlegm so viscid that at first he voided a certain part of the intestine, and then he indeed expelled a worm of immense length. John Heurnius reports that the same thing happened to Lipsius, and various observations of physicians attest that it has happened to others. But D. le Vasseur, utterly ignorant of the Hippocratic powers and faculties, makes an inept mention of nothing but heat and cold. If he had been able to consider that, after effervescence in the intestines, a certain separation of humours takes place, and therefore a coagulation and, as it were, precipitation of the thicker ones, he would easily have understood how it happens that, once a certain phlegm has been dissolved, another kind is afterwards naturally generated, which in turn clings more viscidly to the walls of the intestines.

units.la: Ut autē videat viscida aliunde quàm à calore & frigore liquescere & condesari, Spiritûs ex.gr. Nitri dulcis parum misceat cum albumine ovi & oppidò illud attenuatum videbit. quod si condensare albumen ovi velit, alumen illi permisceat ; & è vestigio in consistentem pultem, insigne ad inflammationem præcavendam collyrium, concrescet.quam liquefactionē & concretionem non fieri vi caloris aut frigoris nemo negaverit: cùm in aëre calidior pariter & frigidiori succedant experimenta, sine mutatione caloris aut frigoris à solo spirituoso acido dulci , & illi opposito austero. Unde constat quia solius caloris & frigoris inentionem facit, quàm belle hic Doctor sui ægris , pituitosis morbis laborantibus consulat.Sed urget sol. 25.frigore nequaquam densari hoc phlegma , quod tamenecesse est, si effervescentiâ liquetur & contabescat, ostendam. εἰ ἂν ἔπηξε ἡ πέπε ψυχρὸν λύσει; ὅτω γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ ἀλλὰ ἔχει αὐτὸ
units.tr: So that he may see that viscous matters are liquefied and thickened by something other than heat and cold, let him mix a little sweet spirit of nitre with the white of an egg, for example, and he will find it considerably thinned. But if he wishes to thicken the egg white, let him mix alum into it, and at once it will set into a firm paste, an excellent eye-wash for preventing inflammation. No one will deny that this liquefaction and thickening do not come about by the force of heat or cold, since the experiments succeed equally in warmer and in colder air, with no change of heat or cold, through the spirituous sweet acid alone and its opposite, the astringent. From this it is plain how well this Doctor, who makes mention only of heat and cold, advises his patients who suffer from phlegmatic diseases. But he presses (sol. 25.): I will show that this phlegm, which must nevertheless be liquefied and wasted by effervescence, is in no way thickened by cold. If the cold has thickened it, will heat dissolve it? For in the same way [εἰ ἂν ἔπηξε ἡ πέπε ψυχρὸν λύσει; ὅτω γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ ἀλλὰ ἔχει αὐτὸ]

units.la: ἐναντ [?]ανλκων. i. e. Si igitur alterum incrassaerit, alterum liquabit; sic enim conraria erit caussa contrariorum, ut habet Aristoteles lib. iv. meteor. cap. vii. Ibi Aristotelis auctoritate probare contendit, quicquid altero contrario solvitur, altero debere concrescere. Inde infert; Si pituita dissolvatur calore, Ergò frigore debet densari. Sed primùm, apud Aristotelem verba, ab ipso citata non reperiuntur; quæ tamen aut fideliter recitanda aut retinenda fuissent. Hæc enim; εἰ ξὴν ἐπήξε [?]ἐπήξεν, ἐπήξεν λόγος, Si alterum incrassaerit, alterum eliquabit, non habentur in Textu. imò contrarium docet Aristoteles l. c. ita enim loquitur ἀπορώζατε [?]ἔχει ἡ τῆς ἐλαίας φύσις, &c. Olei autem natura perquàm ambigua existit. Nam si aqua haberet aquæ ut à frigore glaciei quodo cogeretur, oporteret. Sin verò terra, ab igni, perinde ut fictile, nunc autem neutro cogi, sed è regione ab utroque dissari videtur. Cujus rei caussa est, quod aëre aëre refertum sit. Quapropter & aquæ per summa insidet. etenim aër quem continet, sursum versus effertur. Frigus igitur, dum è spiritu, qui inter oleum est, aquam elicit, oleum spissescere facit. semper enim ubi aqua & oleum permista fuerint, quippiam utroque spissius exoriri assolet. Ab igni autem tractuque temporis albescit crassescitque. albescit quidem aqueo humore, si quis insit, evaporante; crassescit vero quòd marcescente calore, aër in aquæ vicem transeat. Utraque igitur ex parte, atque eandem ob causam, verùm non eodem modo eadem oritur affectio. Ergo opera utriusque spissari assolet.
units.tr: Contrary things [ἐναντίων]. That is: If the one thickens, the other will melt; for thus the cause of contraries will be contrary, as Aristotle has it in Meteorologica book 4, chapter 7. Here he tries to prove from Aristotle's authority that whatever is dissolved by one contrary must be congealed by the other. From this he infers: if phlegm is dissolved by heat, then it must be thickened by cold. But first, the words that he cites from Aristotle are not to be found there. They should have been quoted faithfully or else kept back. For these words, [εἰ ... ἐπήξεν] If the one has thickened, the other will melt, do not occur in the text. Indeed Aristotle teaches the opposite in the same passage, for he speaks thus: [ἀπορώτατα ἔχει ἡ τῆς ἐλαίας φύσις]: The nature of oil is most puzzling. For if it were water, it would have to be solidified by the cold, as ice is. But if it were earth, it would be hardened by fire, like pottery. Yet it seems to be solidified by neither, but to be dissolved by both alike. The cause of this is that it is filled with air. For this reason it also sits on top of the water, since the air it contains is carried upward. Cold, then, by drawing water out of the vapour that lies within the oil, makes the oil thicken. For wherever oil and water have been mixed, something thicker than either tends to arise. But by fire and the passing of time it turns white and thickens: it turns white from the watery moisture, if any is present, evaporating, and it thickens because, as the heat wastes away, air takes the place of water. Each of the two, then, produces the same affection from either side and for the same cause, though not in the same way. Therefore the work of both is usually to thicken it.

units.la: Quibus probat Aristoteles & ignem, & aquam elementa asymbola atque utraque qualitate contraria adeoque & calorem & frigus, oleum condensare. Et certè cornu mollescit frigido & humido, videlicet, aquâ; & calido & Sicco, videlicet, igne, illi è diametro contrario, & frigore itidem [?]calore siccari atque indurari fictia quis nesciat. Disat, si dubitat, Doctor Le Vasseur illud ex Aristotele citato cap. VII. lib. IV. Ubi inquit: hisce nonnulla frigoris etiam vehementiâ crassescunt, (uti diximus) exsiccantur: frigus siquidem non modo coit & desiccat, verùm etiam incrassat. Frigus igitur exsiccat, calor illi contrarius itidem. [?]ἀλλ' οὐχ ὡσαύτως, sed non eodem modo, uti diserte monet Aristoteles l.c. quod si percepisset & diversitatem modi agendi & subjectorum, considerasset, ni fallor, sequentia illa Aristotelis verba ad absurditatem quam probandam nunquam adduxisset.
units.tr: From these points Aristotle proves that fire and water, which are elements that do not mix and are opposed in each quality, and therefore heat and cold, both condense oil. Certainly horn softens under cold and wet, that is, water, and is hardened and dried under heat and dryness, that is, fire, which are diametrically opposed to it. Who does not know that the same thing is dried and hardened by cold as well as by heat? If Doctor Le Vasseur doubts this, let him see the passage from Aristotle he cites, Book IV, chapter VII, where he says: some of these thicken and dry under the great force of cold, as we have said, for cold not only gathers and dries but also thickens. Therefore cold dries, and heat, its opposite, does likewise. [ἀλλ' οὐχ ὡσαύτως] but not in the same way, as Aristotle clearly warns in the same place. If Le Vasseur had grasped this difference in the manner of acting and in the subjects, I think he would never have brought forward those words of Aristotle to prove an absurdity.

units.la: Contrariorum contraria sunt efsecta. Si enim illatio Doctoris Le Vasseur simpliciter vera foret, sequeretur, Si frigus exsiccat, uti probatum, ergò & calor humectat, atque itâ Aristoteles eò loci sibi & veritati titer contradixisset. Illi, ex quorum numero vult videri Le Vasseur, illam objectionem solvunt distinctione caussæ per se, & per accidens, adeoque ajunt frigus per accidens præter suam intentionem, vel si libet, præter opinionem & sententiam suam exsiccare, at verò quia omnis causa per accidês nugatoria est, orta ab inani hypothesi, quâ statuunt, rebus inesse quendam appetitū; existimamus in genere ventum & Solis radios esse causas discutientes humoris madefacti ex. gr. veli, atq; eatenus convenire, differre verò duntaxat modo. Sic & eadē est Solis facultas indurandi & condensandi glebam & emolliendi ceram, quamvis diversû opus in diverso subjecto producat. Absona igitur est illatio D. LeVasseur, Si calor liquefacit, ergò non condensat, notissimū enim est, præter statim allata exempla, calorē primùm liquefacere gelatinā ex glutine, deinde eandē cōdēsare.
units.tr: Contrary things produce contrary effects. If Doctor Le Vasseur's inference were simply true, it would follow that if cold dries, as has been proved, then heat also moistens, and so Aristotle would have contradicted himself and the truth at that point. Those whose company Le Vasseur wishes to be seen in answer this objection by distinguishing between a cause in itself and a cause by accident. They say that cold dries by accident, beyond its intention, or if you prefer, beyond its own opinion and purpose. But since every cause by accident is trifling, arising from an empty hypothesis by which they claim that things have a certain appetite, we hold that in general wind and the rays of the sun are causes that dissipate moisture soaked into, for example, a sail, and to that extent they agree, differing only in manner. So too the sun has the same power to harden and condense clay and to soften wax, although it produces a different effect in a different subject. Doctor Le Vasseur's inference, "If heat melts, therefore it does not condense," is therefore absurd, for it is very well known, apart from the examples just given, that heat first melts gelatine from glue and then condenses the same.

units.la: Sed & aliud non minus ficulneum argumentum veritati objicit pag. 27. absonum, inquit, videtur esse, muci intestinī [illegible, ~10 letters]stinalis ortum frigori imputare, cùm [illegible, ~10 letters]tius ex Philosopho constet, à coctione [illegible, ~10 letters]nia, & calore recipere, quod in-[illegible, ~10 letters]assentur. At verò Omniane à solo ca-[illegible, ~10 letters]re incrassantur ? perperàm igitur [illegible, ~10 letters]ippocrates lib. de Natura humana [illegible, ~10 letters] I. αὐξεται ἐν τῇ ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ φλέγμα χει-[illegible, ~10 letters]ῶν, &c. augetur pituita in homine [illegible, ~10 letters]eme, hæc enim hyemi maximè conve-[illegible, ~10 letters]t secundùm naturam, nam ex omnibus [illegible, ~10 letters] corpore existentibus, frigidissima exi-[illegible, ~10 letters]t. Utrumque ab Hipp. prolixè pro[illegible, ~10 letters]ntum videsis loco citato. addesis A-[illegible, ~10 letters]horism. 23. & 31. Sect. iii. Et Lib.[illegible, ~10 letters] Locis in homine xv. 10. πᾶν τὸ ὑγρὸν [illegible, ~10 letters]ῳ μαινόμενον λεπτότερον γίγνεται, &c. Omnis [illegible, ~10 letters]umor calefactus tenuior fit, & omne ce-[illegible, ~10 letters]ens fluit, maximè verò ubi valdè fuerit [illegible, ~10 letters]sflammatum, propter hanc fluit causam. [illegible, ~10 letters]ufficiat illi annotasse Galenum de [illegible, ~10 letters]brium differentiis Lib. ii. cap. 6. ita [illegible, ~10 letters]qui : Quicunque humor natura frigi-[illegible, ~10 letters]us atque humidus fuerit, hunc nos pi-[illegible, ~10 letters]uitam appellamus. Quin & expressis Aristotelis verbis eo ipso VII. capite quod modo pro sese citavit abunde refutatur, utpote qui verbis partim supra citatis ait; ex hisce nonnulla frigoris etiam vehementia (ut diximus) crassescunt ex siccanturque; frigus enim non modo cogit & desiccat verum etiam incrassat. Deinde quis unquam mortalium audivit frigus tantum attenuare: quod ex illius hypothesi verum erit, si, ut ait, à coctione omnia & calore recipiant quod incrassentur, argumento sententiae Hippocratis è diametro oppositō. Certe distinguere solet accuratiores Medici inter consistentiam eam, quæ est à coctione, & eam, quæ est à cruditate. Hinc cum requirunt quandam sanguinis tenacitatem, non eam exigunt, quæ est à pituita cruda, frigoris præsertim sobole, sed eam, quæ est à naturali humorum coctione. Pudéret sanè me rem nulli non compertissimam, frigus videlicet condensare, auctoritatibus velle probare; nam sola glacies vim frigoris coagulādi abundè demonemonstrat, nisi probandum suscepism Le Vasseur nunquam Sylvio conadicere, quin Hippocrati pariter iisque Veteribus contradixerit.
units.tr: But he also raises against the truth another argument no less worthless, on page 27: It seems absurd, he says, to impute the origin of intestinal mucus to cold, since it is more certain from the Philosopher that all things are thickened by cooking and heat, which they receive ... [...] But are all things thickened by heat alone? Therefore Hippocrates is wrongly quoted in his book On the Nature of Man [...] [αὐξεται ἐν τῇ ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ φλέγμα χειμῶνος], that is, phlegm in man increases in winter, for this season is especially in agreement with nature, since of all the bodily humours it is the coldest. You may see both points treated at length by Hippocrates in the passage cited, and add his Aphorisms 23 and 31, Section iii, and Book On the Places in Man, 15 [...] [πᾶν τὸ ὑγρὸν θερμαινόμενον λεπτότερον γίγνεται]: every moist thing becomes thinner when heated, and everything thick flows when it is heated, most of all when it is greatly inflamed, and for this reason it flows. It will be enough to note what Galen wrote on the differences of humours, Book II, chapter 6, as follows: whatever humour is by nature cold and moist, this we call phlegm. Indeed, Aristotle's own words in the same seventh chapter, which he has just cited, refute him thoroughly, for he says in words partly quoted above: some of these thicken and dry under the great force of cold (as we have said); for cold not only gathers and dries but also thickens. Next, who has ever heard that cold only thins? That would be true on his hypothesis, if, as he says, all things are thickened by cooking and heat, which is a direct argument for the opposite opinion of Hippocrates. Certainly the more careful physicians are accustomed to distinguish between the consistency that comes from cooking and that which comes from crudity. Hence, when they require a certain tenacity of the blood, they do not demand that which comes from raw phlegm, especially the offspring of cold, but that which comes from the natural cooking of the humours. I would indeed be ashamed to prove by authorities a matter known to nearly everyone, namely that cold condenses; for ice alone sufficiently demonstrates the power of cold to coagulate. Unless Le Vasseur had undertaken to prove that he never contradicts Sylvius, he would equally have contradicted Hippocrates and the ancients.

units.la: Porrò effervescentia illa promovet ἐδόσιν [?] distributionem, adde perficit imùm atque absolvit effervescendo oncoctionem cibi in stomacho ferentati, deinde distribuit: chyli au-, addo & spirituum, distributionem sariam juvat, primùm dissipatione, enim vi illius intestini motûs sive effervescentiæ, spiritus quidam minus gati dissipantur, & per Lacteas ves aliaque spiracula corpori reliuo, præcipuè cordi communicantur. einde etiam crassioribus cibi ferentati & effervescentiam passi parous veluti coagulatis & à chylo seegatis, ut caseus à Lacte, chylus on modò paratior est, ut inde discet, sed & eâdem illâ effervescentiâ omovetur, ipse & velut stimulis citantur intestina ad motum peri-stalftalticum, quo tùm segregatus & actu vi effervescentiæ chylus in venas Lacteas aliasque vias impellitur: tùm etiam Chylus, crassis excernendi intricatus, eâdem vi ex illis, veluti serum ex caseo exprimitur, atque in meatus modò dictos imprimitur; fortiùs quidem in Intestino jejuno ob motum peristalticum in illo talem quo, circulis illius Intestini continuo successu versus inferiora arctiùs contractis, ea, quæ in eo reperiuntur, vel deorsum secernuntur, vel in meatus intestinorum imprimuntur. Unde, quia raro quicquam in eo reperitur, Intestinum Jejunum appellatur. Quâ de re videfis Galenum lib. v. de Usu part. cap. III. & IV. Sed Sylvii sententiam ejus verbis describam:
units.tr: Moreover, that effervescence promotes the distribution [ἐδόσιν]. In addition, by effervescing it completes and finishes the cooking of food in the stomach, and then distributes the chyle and the spirits. It helps the distribution of the spirits in the first place by dissipation: for by the force of that intestinal motion or effervescence certain spirits, less fit, are dissipated and are communicated through the lacteal vessels and other pores to the rest of the body, and especially to the heart. Then also the coarser parts of the food, having undergone effervescence, are separated from the chyle like curds from milk, as cheese is separated from milk, so that the chyle is not only made purer, as one may learn from this, but is also moved by the same effervescence. The intestines themselves are as it were stirred up as by goads to peristaltic motion, by which the chyle, now separated and by the force of effervescence, is driven into the lacteal veins and other channels. Then too the chyle, entangled with the thick matter that is to be excreted, is pressed out from them by the same force, as whey is squeezed from cheese, and is forced into the passages just mentioned. This happens more strongly in the jejunum, because of the peristaltic motion in it, in which the circles of that intestine, contracting ever more tightly in succession towards the lower parts, either secrete downwards what is found in it or press it into the passages of the intestines. Hence the jejunum is so called, because very little is found in it. On this matter you may see Galen, On the Use of the Parts, Book V, chapters 3 and 4. But I shall set out Sylvius' opinion in his own words:

units.la: Quoniam verò, inquit, pag. 107. secundum naturam semper observatur Pituita in tenui intestino consistens, atque à Saliva continuò deglutita originem suam ducens, cujus quoque nomine mu-
units.tr: Since, he says, on page 107, according to nature there is always observed phlegm residing in the small intestine, and deriving its origin from the saliva continually swallowed, which also undergoes some change by its name

units.la: tatioetionem aliquam patiatur prædicta Efrvescentia : censeo in illo binorum houmce humorum confluxu dissolvi Pituita testini tenuis parietibus adhærescentis rtem fluidiorem , eandemque cum maima Bilis , Succique Pancreatici conrescentium parte junctam penetrare in acteas venas usque ad Cor : dum pari usdem Pituita tenacior & viscidior im aliqua reliquorum Humorum parte idem viscidiore pergit sensim ad Inteinum crassum , ibidemque alvinis facius admissa easdem viscidiores facit & aviores. At verò hæc iterum DoctoLe Vasseur displicent 1. quia bilis antæ in corpore utilitatis sibi non vieatur. quin etiam , ut stulti , dum vint vitia , Bilem non modo ut inutile ondus contemnit , sed ut venenum amnat. Lubet illius discursum hùc ducere , ut constet ex quibus locis undamenta sua petat. pagina igitur 4. ita fatur : Cæterùm non dubito, quas rquatur partes , ubi quæritur, utrum bilis sit ad vitam incolumnè transigendan necessaria. Sed eum percellere debent Antiqui, ex quorum sententia vulgo credebatur, vacuitatem fellis hominem prolixiori vitâ beare. Aristoteles ex lib. 4. de part. animal. cap. 2. qui ut movit, sic gessit acriter hanc litem, unam calculum adjecit, argumento, ex solipedum cervorumque tribu deducto, qui felle carent, & diu vivunt. Unde Plinius scribit, fel hominum paucis non est, quorum valetudo firmior & vita longior. Ex eodem, in Euboeæ chalcide nullum pecori datum est; cui fidem facit alicubi Dioscorides. Nec Democritum hîc æquiorem habet, cum ait χλωρὴ δὲ ὑγλὴ αεῶς ἤπαλι μύσους, ᾧ ἀλφοφόρη σώματος ἀνθρωπίνου ἐπιβλύσεως γίνεται. βλα-βερὸς δὲ σώματος ἀνθρωπίνου, ᾧ ἀναφελὴς ὑποι-κὸς. Bilis verò flava, quæ circà Hepar versatur, corpori est exitio ubi ebullit. Est enim corpori humano gravius & nullo ejus commodo, domestica, epistola ad Hipp. Posse etiam proferre Paracelsum, ut r habeat ἐκ τῶ συμμάχων, ex Sociis, Syl-
units.tr: undergo some change through the said effervescence: I think that in the joining together of these two humours, the phlegm adhering to the walls of the small intestine is dissolved, and that the thinner part of it, joined with the bile and pancreatic juice that are thickening, penetrates into the lacteal veins as far as the heart; while the thicker and more viscid part of the same phlegm, along with some other more viscid part of the remaining humours, passes gradually to the large intestine, and there, mixed with the faeces, makes them more viscid and thicker. But these things again displease Doctor Le Vasseur, first, because he does not think bile has any use in the body. Indeed, like a fool, while he condemns vices, he not only despises bile as a useless burden but also loves it as poison. It pleases me to bring his argument here, so that it may be clear from what places he draws his foundations. So on page 4 he says: "Moreover, I do not doubt what parts are concerned where it is asked whether bile is necessary for living life in safety. But the ancients ought to disturb him, from whose opinion it was commonly believed that the absence of gall makes a man blessed with a longer life. Aristotle, in Book IV, On the Parts of Animals, chapter 2, who pursued this quarrel as keenly as he stirred it up, added one piece of evidence, drawn from the tribe of solid-hoofed animals and deer, which lack gall and live long. Hence Pliny writes that few men have gall, and those whose health is firmer and life longer. From the same source, in Chalcis of Euboea, no gall is given to cattle, which Dioscorides confirms somewhere. Nor does Democritus here have a fairer view when he says: [χλωρὴ δὲ ὑγλὴ αεῶς ἤπαλι μύσους, ᾧ ἀλφοφόρη σώματος ἀνθρωπίνου ἐπιβλύσεως γίνεται. βλα-βερὸς δὲ σώματος ἀνθρωπίνου, ᾧ ἀναφελὴς ὑποι-κὸς] "Yellow bile, which is around the liver, is the destruction of the body where it boils up. For it is more harmful to the human body and of no advantage to it," in his domestic letter to Hippocrates. I may also bring forward Paracelsus, so that Sylvius may have an ally [ἐκ τῶ συμμάχων], from his Allies, Sylvius

units.la: us, quo ἀναπολογήτως sileat. Sic enim ...othus ille spuriusque Theophrastus, est ...oc membrum in natura superfluum, ...r instar monstri: lib.2.de viríb.memb. ...p. II. paulò post; sic fel quoque, lo...um naturæ est, quod juxtà bonum ...ese insinuavit, non ad conservatio...em corporis, sed ejusdem destru...tionem. Ast tales τῆς βίς λυμεσῶνας vitæ ...estes, ut loquitur Basilius Magnus, alio...um probatorumque consortio dignari
units.tr: ...by which he is silent, without defence [ἀναπολογήτως]. For thus that spurious Theophrastus ... says that this member is superfluous in nature, ... like a monster: Book 2, On the Powers of the Members, p. II, a little later. So too the gall ... is a thing of nature, which he has hinted is good near ... not for the preservation of the body but for its destruction. But such destroyers of life [τῆς βίου λυμεῶνας], as Basil the Great calls them, ... to be thought worthy of the company of the good and the approved

units.la: Diruit, ædificat, mutat quadrata rotundis.
units.tr: It tears down, it builds up, it changes squares into circles.

units.la: ingit abundè faeces, infit, habemus enim ...nfitentem reum, succi triumviralis ef...eta magis & vieta pars, ac ebullientem ...s fluidam illius copiam, per Lacteas ve...as Lymphæ conjunctam, cor petere tra...it, incorrupto chyli nitido puroque can...ore. Quid errare vocas, si non insignis ...rronis hæc sit inconstantia? qui latet ...recor, inconspicua illa, ut cum cinisloni-
units.tr: It heaps up dregs in abundance, it begins, for we have the accused guilty party, the more conquered and defeated part of the triumvirate juice, and its boiling fluid in copious flow, joined with the lymph through the milky veins, makes for the heart, with the chyle's clear and pure colour uncorrupted. Why do you call it error, if this is not the notable inconsistency of an error? What lies hidden in the depths, that unseen tincture, as I may speak with the cinder-men, so confused with a delicate colour of juice, if an unworthy portion of it defiles the solid residues of food?

units.la: bus loquar, tinctura, tam delicati colorsucco confusa, si illaudabilis ejusdem portio solidas alimentorum reliquias tameimpurat? Huic συναπολογία venia utcunque concedi poterat, sunt etiam in Solenævi, boni sunt libri, in quibus quàmminimum mali. At toties eadem oberrat chorda, ut id ipsi excidisse minus persuasum habeam, quàm data opera erroremlitavisse. Hucusque Le Vasseur.
units.tr: Some pardon for this joint defence [συναπολογία] could be granted in some way; there are also in Solenaeus good books, in which there is very little bad. But the same string is so often out of tune that I am less persuaded that it slipped from him than that he played the error on purpose. Thus far Le Vasseur.

units.la: Bilem igitur non modo ad vitam incolumè transigendam non esse necessariam atque inutilem, sed etiam noxiam, perniciosam & pestiferam, palam asserit. Qui antea p. 11. Stentoriâ voce, ubi opus non erat, clamitabat, naturam nil frustra facere eamque refingere impossibile esse, hîc, tanto flagrat in Sylvium odio, non modo secum ipse dissidet, sed & ipsi naturæ litem movet, eamque corrigere satagit, atque seriò queritur Naturam destinatâ operâ non modo frustranea sed & nocitura producere. Hinc cassis votis otis humanum corpus , vana quadam etamorphosi, bile,humore ad vitam ftentandam necessario , privatum optat. Et quare ? proculdubio , ne lvius , risum teneatis amici , efferfcentiam in intestinis probare post. Quin potiùs exoptet sibi soli cebrum esse cæteros mente cassos , ne uis illius nugas carpere possit. Bim , Humorem scilicet inutilem & oxium ex Humano corpore exturbam cupit. Si illi concessa esset omnipotentia quanta majori Sapientia ilm moderaretur acutus stipes. Homines crearet ad imaginem suam, quis & mulis similes, quibus uti nulla ilis inest , ut asserit ex Aristotele , ita nullus intellectus, teste Dei verbo. Nemo amplius miretur Sylvii opuscum Momo displicere , qui ipsam naturam,accuratissimum Dei Opt.Max. pus, carpere non veretur. Hactenus itur Sylvii Naturae interpretio , jam erò Dei causam directè tu egris, cor cujus utique opera inculpata sunt perfectissima.
units.tr: Therefore he openly asserts that bile is not only not necessary and useful for living a healthy life, but also harmful, pernicious and deadly. He who earlier, at p. 11, cried out with a stentorian voice, where there was no need, that nature makes nothing in vain and that it is impossible to remake her, now burns with such hatred against Sylvius that he not only disagrees with himself, but also brings a lawsuit against nature herself, and strives to correct her, and seriously complains that Nature produces, with a purpose, things that are not only useless but harmful. Hence with idle and futile wishes he wishes the human body, by some vain metamorphosis, deprived of bile, a humour necessary for sustaining life. And why? Undoubtedly, so that he may prove, friends, hold your laughter, effervescence in the intestines afterwards. Would he not rather wish that he alone had a brain and that all others were empty of mind, so that no one could carp at his trifles? Clearly he wants the useless and harmful humour driven out of the human body. If he had been granted omnipotence, with how much more wisdom would that sharp stake have governed it! He would create men in his own image, who would be like mules, of which, as he asserts from Aristotle, no use is in them, so there is no understanding, as the word of God bears witness. Let no one wonder any more that the little work of Sylvius displeases Momus, who does not hesitate to carp at nature herself, the most exact work of God, Best and Greatest. Thus far the interpretation of Sylvius's Nature; now I will directly take up the cause of God against the sick, whose works are certainly blameless and most perfect.

units.la: Bilem igitur nobis esse naturalem id est, naturæ, sive perfectioni nostræ corporis apprimè convenientem, ut [?]ilem & necessariam vel inde sequitur, quia est illius pars ; cum alii enim humoribus sanguinem cæterasque humani corporis partes componit. Adeo ut vix ulla detur humani corporis pars, quæ, naturaliter disposita, non sit magis minusve bile tincta. Hoc ratio probat, quandoquidem similibus alimur. idem ostendit chymia, manifestâ resolutione. Idem denique docet Hippocrates Lib. iv. de Morbis i. 4. Habet, inquit, & mulier, & vir quatuor species humoris in corpore, à quibus morbi fiunt, qui non à violentia aliqua fiunt. Sunt autem species sive pituita, sanguis, bilis & hydrops, sive aqua. Et de his non minima, neque debilissima in semen procedit portio. Et ne quis cum Doctore e Vasseur ofcitanter hæc verba lens putet bilem humorem esse qui en nisi morborum sit causa, subdit, ia animal parentibus simile nascitur, humorum species & sanorum & mororum in se ipso habet. Et postquam b. de Natura humana text. viii. lem, pituitam, sanguinem & aquam, e diversa natura & discrepantis fatatis, textu sequenti addit, illa esse egenita. Quomodo enim, inquit, non nt congenita? primum enim manium est, hominem in se ipso hæc omnia vere quamdiu vivit. Deinde nata et illa ex homine omnia illa habentia, ea nutrita sunt in homine hæc omnia ente. Etenim ut dixerat Lib. iv. morbis Text. iii. in omnibus cibis potibus biliosi quid est. & aquosi, & guinei & pituitosi in alio plus in alio ius: quibus adde sis Lib. de Naa humana text: xi. i. 2. supra pag. citat.
units.tr: Therefore bile is natural for us, that is, most suited to nature, or to the perfection of our body; that it is necessary and useful follows from this, since it is a part of that body; for the blood and the other parts of the human body are made up of other humours. So much so that there is hardly any part of the human body which, when naturally disposed, is not more or less tinged with bile. Reason proves this, since we are nourished by like things. Chemistry shows the same, by a manifest resolution. Hippocrates finally teaches the same, in Book 4 of On Diseases, section 1, chapter 4: Man and woman alike, he says, have four kinds of humour in the body, from which diseases arise that do not arise from any violence. There are, moreover, the kinds: phlegm, blood, bile and dropsy, or water. And of these no small, nor very weak, portion goes into the seed. And lest anyone, with Doctor Le Vasseur, think carelessly that these words are idle, and that bile is a humour which is the cause of diseases alone, he adds: the animal is born like its parents, and has in itself the kinds of humours both of the healthy and of the diseased. And after On the Nature of Man, text 8, he says of phlegm, blood and water, of different nature and discordant constitution, in the following text, that they are inborn. For how, he says, are they not congenital? For first it is clear that man truly has all these in himself as long as he lives. Then, born from man, having all of them, they are nourished in man, all these being in man. For, as he had said in Book 4 of On Diseases, text 3, in all foods and drinks there is something bilious, and watery, and bloody and phlegmatic, in one more, in another less. To these add also On the Nature of Man, text 11, sections 1 and 2, cited above on the page.

units.la: Imò verò Text. v. 9. Libr: (in quo ex professo agit) de Natura humana, corpus, inquit, hominis habet in se sanguinem & pituitam & bilem duplicem flavam videlicet & nigram, atque hæc sunt ipsius corporis natura & pehæc & ægrotat & sanus est.
units.tr: Indeed, in text 5, section 9, of the book (in which he treats the subject professedly) On the Nature of Man, he says: the body of man has in itself blood and phlegm and bile, twofold, namely yellow and black, and these are the very nature of the body, and by these it is sick and it is healthy.

units.la: Quo verò constet quando bilis & eadem est cæterorum humorum ratio sanitatis aut morborum pars est & causa, sanus, inquit, l. c. textu v. equidem maximè est, ubi temperamentum hæc inter se habuerunt moderatum tum facultate tum copia: & ubi maximè fuerint permixta. quod & alibi non semel inculcat. Libro videlicet de Veteri Medicina Text. XLII. supra pag. 21. citato. & ejusdem libri Text. XXXIV. 21 supra pag. 18. descripto; uti & ibidem Text. XXXI. 19, quem pag. itidem 18 Sed quid prodesset idem infinitis aliis locis probasse. Pergit autem Medicorum summus libro citato de natura humana Text. VI. & VII. Ægrotat autem, inquit, cum horum quid minus aut amplius fuerit aut separatur in rpore & non fuerit reliquis omnibus intemperatum. necesse est enim cum id horum secretum fuerit, & per se terit (nisi in locis secretioni illorum natura destinatis) non solum eum lom unde secessit morbidum fieri. Sed am eum in quo stat, & in quem proer nimiam copiam diffusum est, dolore morbo vexari. Etenim, cum quid rum omnium extra corpus effluxerit amplius, quam redundat evacuatio ipsa dolorem exhibet. rursus itaque. Si idem us fecerit evacuationem & transitiom, ac ab aliis secretionem, geminatum dolorem exhibere necesse est, velut dium est: nempe unde discessit, & ubi eptum redundat. Dixi porro quæcune hominem esse dixero, semper demonaturum me esse quod talia sint καὶ ψ ἡ καὶ φύσιν, id est, secundum vilicet à Deo naturæ inditam; vel, Interpres loquitur, juxta receptum rem ac opinionem & juxta naturam.
units.tr: But as to how it is established when bile, and the same is the case for the other humours, is a part and cause of health or disease, he says, in the same passage, text 5: it is healthy especially when these have held a moderate temperament among themselves, both in power and in quantity, and when they have been most thoroughly mixed. He also insists on this elsewhere more than once: namely in On Ancient Medicine, text 42, cited above on page 21, and in the same book, text 34, described on page 18 above; likewise in the same place, text 31, on page 19, which is also on page 18. But what would it help to prove the same from countless other places? The greatest of physicians goes on in the book cited, On the Nature of Man, text 6 and 7: He is sick, he says, when any one of these is less or more, or is separated in the body, and the rest are not all intemperate. For it is necessary, when any of these has been separated and has gone off by itself (unless in the places destined by nature for its separation) not only the part from which it departed becomes diseased, but the part in which it stays, and into which it is poured forth in excessive quantity, is afflicted with pain and disease. For when more of any of them has flowed outside the body than the evacuation itself exceeds, it causes pain. Again, if the same evacuation and passage, and the separation from the others, is made, it must cause a doubled pain, as is evident: namely where it departed, and where it superabounds in an unfit place. Moreover, I have said that whatever I say about man, I will always show that such things are kata physin, that is, according to nature, namely as implanted in nature by God; or, as the translator puts it, according to the received opinion and according to nature.

units.la: Si igitur bilis cum cæteris humoribus necessariò requiratur ut corpus humanum sit ἰσόκρασον æqualiter temperatum utpote cujus intemperies consistit in concordi discordia , sive contrariorum harmonia. Si hæc humorum harmonia sive proportio constituit hominem, sive naturam humani corporis, quam Hippocrates bonum illius habitum vocat qui subsistere non posset, si (uti loquitur l. c. Textu iv.) calidum & frigidum humidum & siccum, moderate & æqualiter sese non haberent, sed alterum alterum multum præcelleret, & fortius debilius superaret. Auƈta enim bilis flava copia & acrimonia pituita imminuitur, & debilior redditur, eadem enim, refrigerata pituita augetur, unde frigidior totius corporis temperies. Uti docet Hippocr. Lib. de Natura humana xiv. Si igitur tota bilis ex sententia Doƈtoris Le Vasseur auferretur, dubio proculfrigus, liƈtor mortis imò ipsa morbis is hominis membra occuparet. deo ut fine illa non magis fubfiftee poffit quam macrocofmus fine gne. Hinc propter multiplicem bilis fum Galenus lib. v. de ufu partium n principio obfervat Naturam nouiffe bilem prope anum excerni, uod, inquit, factum fuiffet fi bilis untaxat ut inutile pondus excernena fuiffet, quae certe naturaliter conituta non chilificationi modo fed & ti loquuntur, sanguificationi atque ffervefcentiae fanguinis in corde atue confervationi Chyli & fanguinis nfervit. Hinc multiplici conftat exerientia nimiam bilis evacuationem on modo lipothymiae caufam fuife, fed & mortem aliquoties intulife. Teftes funt lethales ab acri bile iarrhaeae, cholerae, & à vehementiobus pharmacis hypercatharfes, quius ultra modum evacuatâ bile vires rofternuntur, atque Syncope imo & nors quandoque fubfequitur. Quo spectat historia, quam Doctus quispiam Medicus his verbis perscripsit Clariss. Moëbio. Magnopere, ait, Olim mihi lecta placuit hac tua de bile sententia, (est autem eadem cum sententia Cl. Sylvii, unanimi ut loquitur Moëbius, avorum judicio comprobata) & exinde animadvertere cœpi in promiscuum trivialium Medicorum votum, quod apud suos, quos misere divexabant ægrotos ingeminare soliti fuere; dum bilem educendam esse dicerent; Utinam omnem è corpore bilem exturbaremus! Verum quid inde mali evenit? Id nempe quod plurimi cachectici & hydropici fuerint demortui. Tres occubuere uni parenti filii, omnes tandem marasmo tentati, ultimum dissectioni meæ commisit Mœstus ille genitor. Nullum revera nec vel vestigium ullius bilis in vesicula adinveni, illæsis cæteris omnibus visceribus. hinc culpam omnem in diagridiata illa contuli medicamenta crebris illis defunctis exhibita. hunc enim. errororem nostros errare sæpiùs deprehendi [?] à vehementissimis quoque purgantius non abstinerent in tenera ista ætate deoque præmaturo committant funeri corpuscula longiore dignißima diæta. [?]
units.tr: If therefore bile, together with the other humours, is necessarily required so that the human body may be isokrason [ἰσόκρασον], equally tempered, since its intemperance consists in a concordant discord, or in a harmony of opposites; if this harmony or proportion of the humours constitutes man, or the nature of the human body, which Hippocrates calls its good habit, which could not subsist if (as he says in the same place, text 4) the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry, did not stand moderately and equally with one another, but one far excelled the other and overcame it more strongly and weakly. For when the yellow bile is increased in quantity and sharpness, the phlegm is diminished and made weaker; likewise, when phlegm is cooled, it is increased, whence the temperament of the whole body is colder. As Hippocrates teaches in On the Nature of Man, chapter 14. If therefore all the bile were removed according to the opinion of Doctor Le Vasseur, without doubt cold, the approach of death, and indeed disease would occupy the members of the man. So that without it he could no more subsist than the macrocosm without fire. Hence, on account of the manifold use of bile, Galen in Book 5 of On the Use of the Parts, at the beginning, observes that Nature knew bile to be excreted almost in the same way, which, he says, would have been done if bile had been excreted only as a useless weight; for that bile, rightly constituted, serves not only chylification but also, as they say, the sanguification and effervescence of the blood in the heart, and the conservation of the chyle and the blood. Hence the manifold experience establishes that excessive evacuation of bile has not only been the cause of fainting, but has also on several occasions brought on death. Witnesses are the lethal diarrhoeas and cholera caused by sharp bile, and the hypercatharsis caused by violent drugs, by which, the bile being evacuated beyond measure, the strength is prostrated, and syncope, and at last death, sometimes follows. To this belongs the history which a certain learned physician wrote in these words to the most distinguished Moëbius: I was greatly pleased, he says, to read long ago this your opinion about bile (it is the same as the opinion of the distinguished Sylvius, which, as Moëbius says, is approved by the unanimous judgment of the elders) and then I began to notice the common wish of the ordinary physicians, which they were accustomed to repeat among their own sick, whom they miserably harassed, while they said that bile must be drawn out: Would that we drove all bile out of the body! But what evil came of it? Namely, that very many cachectic and dropsical patients died. Three sons died, one after another, all attacked by marasmus; the last of them was committed to my dissection by that sorrowful father. Indeed I found no trace of any bile in the gall-bladder, all the other viscera being unharmed. Hence I attributed all the blame to those diagrydium drugs administered to those dead boys so often. For I have often observed that our people err in this error, not refraining from the most violent purgatives at that tender age, and so commit the little bodies, most worthy of a longer diet, to premature burial.

units.la: dem olim à Fernelio, aliisque annotatuin legimus. Sed hanc veritatem edarguens Le Vasseur, Nec ullus, inuit, inficias ibit infensissima quaque & terrima quodam tamen calore corpori deo blandiri, ut integra eorum emissio, quod etiam monuit Hippocrates lib. 6. ph. 27. Sit periculo proxima. Sed uis ferat dissolutam hujus Doctoris argumentationem; An ergò uti omnis illis ablatio semper homini nocet ita [?] omnis puris emissio. Indicare bis sui ablationem, uti pus, tota sua naira à corpore nostro abalienatum. Certè totam bilem auferendam non sse docet illius utilitas & necessitas upra abundè probata. pus verò omne uferendum esse indicat ejus inutilitas z noxia. Sed non vidit, uti opinor, Le Vasseur distinctionem inter evacuationem totius puris, quæ legitimo tramite fiat nunquam nocet, sed semper est instituenda & evacuationem totius puris quæ fit ἀώρόως qua magna puris copia simul profunditur, quam solam Hippocratis perniciosam vocat loco citato, inquiens, Quicunque Empyi aut hydropici utuntur, aut secantur ἐκρύεν]& ἓ πύς ἡ ἓ. ὑδα]& ἀρρέσ, si pus aut aqua universim effluxerit, omnino moriuntur. Non sine gravi causa Doctissimus Ballonius Ἀώρόον, inquit, καὶ Ἀρρόως magnam vim in arte nostra habere, cum quid dicitur aut fieri, aut excerni ἀρρόως: Item cum Ἀλλογωρημα ἀρρόον dicitur fieri. Verbi enim proprietas non pili facienda Ἀώρόως confertim affatimque verti debet: & ἀρρόον simul totum, ut sic dicam confertim, multum, agminatim, factum, effusum. Absolutè autem multum, non significat: nam Galenus in Libr: ad Glauconem Φυλακτίον ἀρρόας καὶ πολλὰς κενεώσεις: tempe-ranandum à confectis effusum & multis evacuationibus, sic πολὺ κ᾽ ἆρρέον distinguui videntur. Quicquid enim sit quan-
units.tr: ...we have read it noted by Fernelius and others. But Le Vasseur, refuting this truth, says: No one will deny that the most hostile and terrible things, through a certain heat, still flatter the body, so that their complete discharge is dangerous, as Hippocrates also warned in Aphorisms lib. 6. ph. 27. But let us put up with this Doctor's loose argument. Does it follow that, just as every removal of bile always harms a man, so every discharge of pus does too? Both bile and pus, when removed, show that they are wholly alien to our nature. Certainly its usefulness and necessity, already proved abundantly above, show that not all bile is to be removed. But its uselessness and harmfulness show that all pus is to be removed. Yet, I think, Le Vasseur did not see the distinction between the evacuation of all the pus, which when done by the proper course never harms but must always be undertaken, and the evacuation of all the pus which is done [ἀώρως] (unseasonably, all at once), when a great quantity of pus is poured out at the same time. Hippocrates, in the passage cited, calls only this kind harmful, saying: Those who undergo empyema or dropsy, or are cut, if pus or water flows out [ἀώρως] altogether, die outright. Not without good reason, the most learned Ballonius says: ἀώρως and ἀρρόως [ἀώρως] have great force in our art, when something is said to be done or discharged ἀώρως; likewise when a thing is said to happen ἀώρως. For the proper sense of the word must not be disregarded: ἀώρως should be rendered all at once and in a mass, as I may say, in a crowd, in a body, made, poured out. But "much" does not mean this in itself. For Galen, in his book to Glaucon, says one must guard against ἀώρως and many evacuations, to be tempered from what is poured out in a crowd and from many evacuations; so that πολύ and ἀώρως seem to be distinguished. Whatever the quantity may be...

units.la: aque quantitate, si simul, universum, totumque excernatur, ἆρρόως excerni di-
units.tr: ...if it is discharged all together, entire and whole, it is said to be discharged [ἀώρως]...

units.la: itur, non tàm enim magna copia, quàm repentinum aliquid & celeritas significatur. Ita Theocritus κατήρρηκεν ἐς μέλαν ὡς ἆρρόῳ in nigram aquam universus, frequens & confertus incidit, ac si dicas uno ictu hunc celeritatis nota &c. Non ergò nocet puris evacuatio quia totum excernitur, imò totum excernendum est. Sed nocet quando ἆρρέως totum confertim, celeriter & uno impetu excernitur. Bilis verò nullo modo tota excernenda est. quia pars quædam non utilis modo sed & necessaria est. adeo ut subsistere homo nequeat sive ἆρρόως sive βεχδέως tota emittatur quod tantum abest ut proterea cum putridis & penitus inutilibus excrementis conferatur, ut istud illi cum cæteris humoribus utilibus & par-
units.tr: For it signifies not so much a large quantity as something sudden and rapid. So Theocritus says he burst down into the black water all at once [κατήρρηκεν ἐς μέλαν ὡς ἆρρόῳ], crowded and packed together, as if you were to say with a single blow, this mark of speed, and so on. Therefore evacuation does not harm the pure, because the whole is discharged; indeed the whole ought to be discharged. But it does harm when everything is discharged at once, quickly, and in a single rush [ἆρρέως]. Yet bile must by no means be discharged entirely, because a certain part of it is not merely useful but necessary. So much so that a man cannot survive if it is all sent out, whether all at once [ἆρρόως] or violently [βεχδέως]. Far from its being compared with putrid and wholly useless excrements, this bile is shared with the other useful humours and with the principal parts of the human body,

units.la: Ioan. Gorraei Definitionum... (not printed on this page; omitted) & partibus humani corporis principibus commune sit, utpote quibus pariter ablatis totum interit. adeo ut bilis & puris petulans quaedam sit comparatio, quae Medicinae Doctorem dedecet. Certè fel Diis antiquitus offerebatur. bonique ominis dicebatur, si vel geminum occurrat, quod Divo Augusto contigit, quo die apud Actium vicit, Teste Plinio Historr: Nat. Lib. xi. cap. 37. Sic etiam Arato Sacrificanti idem cùm accidisset, aruspex vaticinatus est, conciliatum iri civium dissensiones, quòd eventu verissimo consequutum est. Teste Alex: ab Alex. Qui itidem refert fellis magnitudinem in extorum observatione fortunata omnia feliciaque promittere. Quae quantum absint à purulenta & saniosa colluvie nemo nescit.
units.tr: as Gorraeus, [Definitionum ... (not printed on this page; omitted)], and it is common to them, since when these are removed together the whole body perishes. So the comparison of bile with pus and filth is a wanton one, and unworthy of a Doctor of Medicine. Certainly gall was offered to the gods in antiquity and was called a sign of good omen, if even twin galls turned up, as happened to the divine Augustus on the day he won at Actium, according to Pliny, Natural History, book 11, chapter 37. Likewise when Aratus was sacrificing and the same thing happened, the haruspex prophesied that the civil dissensions would be reconciled, which followed in the most true outcome, according to Alexander ab Alexandro. He also reports that a large gall-bladder in the inspection of entrails promises everything fortunate and happy. How far all this is from a purulent and filthy mass, no one fails to know.

units.la: Sed rationis praesidio destitutus labentem causam humana auctoritate & crassa similitudine sive comparatione equi, qui, asini & hominis fulcire gestit. Ariftot. videlicet docuisset & Plinius Solipedes caeteris animantibus diuius vivere propter vacuitatem fellis, Ergò & homines. Suffecisset uti opinor si dixisset hæc Aristotelem testari, quandoquidem Plinius illa verboenus ex eo descripsit. Sed primum error est equos caeteris animantibus diutius vivere. Etenim non modo ifces quaedam plures annos vivere testis est ipse Plinius Natur: Hist. Lib. ix. cap. 53. referens ex Anneo Seneca Pausi Cypi in Villa campaniæ haud procul Neapoli in Cæsaris Pisciis à Pollione Vidio injectum piscem [?]exagesimum post annum expirasse. duous aliis æqualibus ejus ex eodem genere etiam tunc viventibus. Cum equus [?]quadragesimum, aut saltem Arist. Teste quinquasimum annum non excedat. & certè cornix Corvus, Psit-tacus quamvis felle non careant eos [?]etate superare nemo inficiabitur. ut maneamus in quadrupedum classe Elephanti eodem Plinio authore vivunt plerique quantum longævi homines quidam ad ducentesimum perveniant annum. Aristoteles vivere ducentis annis & quosdam trecentis existimat. Hinc Solinus vivere asserit in annos trecentos. Aldrovandus ex Philostrate recitat elephantum trecentos & quinquaginta annos vixisse post prælium , quod Alexander Magnus cum Poro Indiarum Rege gloriose invehat, cui Elephantus ille interfuerat ; Neque constitisse quot annorum fuerit antequam pugnatum esset. Non ergò solipedes cæteris animantibus diutius vivunt. Nec est quod dicas Elephantos etiam bile carere istud enim erroneum esse. Statim ex Aristotele probabitur. Nec minor error est solipedibus Vitam prolixiorem esse concessam quia bile carent. Unde Argutus scriptor, Thomas Broun Anglus erroribus vulgaribus us annumerat Lib. III. errorum poularium cap. 2. Sententiam, quâ qui bile carere dicuntur. quandouidem, inquit, beneficio anatomiae se invenisse membranosam quanam substantiam extrinsecus albicancm intrinsecus felleam. ego duplici facta experientia pelliculam illam reeri primum humore subacido, deine humore bilioso cum acido tempeato refertam. quae cum ductu heatico sese exonerabant in ductum communem, in quem itidem humor cidulus ex pancreate profluebat, atue inde in intestinum duodenum, ut iliosus humor eo loci facta primum fervescentia temperaretur, uti supra liquoties significatum. Admirabar magnitudinem hujus ductus commuis, utpote qui digitum auricularem acile capiebat, cujus magnitudini ariter respondebant ductus bilarius ommunis atque pancreaticus: capaitas horum ductuum prohibent ne generosum animal nimio ardore inflammatum in furorem incendatur: Inde etiam oritur frequentior, quae famelico isti quadrupedi accidit, alvi dejectio, effectum alterum liberioris bilis in intestina effluxus. An igitur Aristoteles & Plinius eum secutus errarunt. certe hos non semel lapsos esse nulli non uti opinor constat, atque si illorum mens sit solipedes omni prorsus bile carere, eam isti fabulae non inconcinne comparaveris, quae equae favonio vento concipere dicuntur eidem Plinio non uno in loco, videlicet libr. ii. cap. 21. & libr. viii. cap. 42. sed ventosos illos equos bile non caruisse, si vitae longitudo a bilis absentia penderet, ex eodem authore sequitur, postquam enim dixisset, constat in Lusitania circa Olyssiponem oppidum & Tagum amnem equas Favonio flante obversas animalem concipere spiritum, idque partum fieri & igni pernitiosissimum ita, sed triennium um vita non excedere, quem vento-
units.tr: But bereft of the support of reason, he props up his tottering cause with human authority and a crude comparison with the horse, the ass and man. Aristotle, of course, taught, and Pliny too, that solipeds live longer than other animals because they lack gall; therefore so do humans. It would have sufficed, I think, to say that Aristotle bears witness to these things, since Pliny wrote those words copied from him. But first the error is that horses live longer than other animals. For Pliny himself, in Natural History, book 9, chapter 53, bears witness that certain fishes live many years, reporting from Annaeus Seneca that a fish thrown by Pollio Vedius into the fishponds of Caesar, in the villa of Pansa Cypius in Campania, not far from Naples, died in its sixtieth year, while two other fish of the same kind were still living then. A horse does not exceed forty years, or at least fifty according to Aristotle. And certainly no one will deny that ravens, crows and parrots, though they lack no gall, surpass horses in age. To stay within the class of quadrupeds, elephants, according to the same Pliny, live as long as some men, and some reach two hundred years. Aristotle thinks they live two hundred years and some three hundred. Hence Solinus asserts they live up to three hundred years. Aldrovandus cites from Philostratus an elephant that lived three hundred and fifty years after the battle which Alexander the Great gloriously waged against Porus, king of the Indians, in which that elephant had taken part; and it was not established how old it was before the battle. Therefore solipeds do not live longer than other animals. Nor can you say that elephants also lack bile; for that is false, as will be shown at once from Aristotle. Nor is it a smaller error to grant solipeds a longer life because they lack bile. Hence the acute writer Thomas Browne, an Englishman, counts this among the common errors, in book 3, chapter 2 of his Pseudodoxia Epidemica, the opinion by which they are said to lack bile. Since, he says, by the benefit of anatomy he found a membranous substance, whitish outside and bilious within. By a double experiment I found that little sac filled first with a sourish humour, then with a bilious humour tempered with an acid; these discharged through the hepatic duct into the common duct, into which a sharp humour also flowed from the pancreas, and from there into the duodenum, so that the biting humour there might first be tempered by fermentation there, as I have often said above. I marvelled at the size of this common duct, which could take in a little finger, to whose size the bile duct and pancreatic duct correspondingly answer. The capacity of these ducts prevents the noble animal from being inflamed with excessive heat into fury. Hence also arises the more frequent evacuation of the bowels which happens to that starving quadruped, another effect of freer outflow of bile into the intestines. Did Aristotle and Pliny, following him, then err? Certainly it is agreed, I think, by everyone that they did not slip only once; and if their meaning were that solipeds lack gall altogether, that could fittingly be compared with that fable by which mares are said to conceive from the west wind, as the same Pliny says in more than one place, namely book 2, chapter 21, and book 8, chapter 42. But that those windy horses lacked no bile, if the length of life depended on the absence of bile, follows from the same author; for after saying it is established that in Lusitania, near the town of Olyssipo and the river Tagus, mares turned toward the west wind conceive a living breath, and that this produces offspring most deadly to fire, but they do not live beyond three years, he

units.la: um equorum conceptum Varro & Columella aliique recensent. eodem edit, quod Plinius libr. xi. cap. 37. narrat, Pecora in Euboea Chalcide fel non habere, & uti subdit, carent eo, qui absynthio vescuntur in Ponto, & quae sunt istius generis innumera; nisi huius Ariftotelem & Plinium ita velit interpretari, ipsos noluisse folipedes & cervos omni prorsus bile carere, sed vesicula duntaxat fellea destitui, ut sane hanc ipsorum mentem esse, vel hinc constat, quia Plinius equorum fel virulentum esse docet libr. xviii. cap. 9. inquiens, inter omnia communia animalium vel praestantissimi affectus fel est, vis ejus, excalfacere, mordere, scindere, extrahere, discutere. minorum animalium subtilius intelligitur, & ideo ad oculorum medicamenta subtilius existimatur. taurino praecipua potentia, etiam in aere, pellibusque colore aureo ducendis. & paulo post: damnatur equinum tantum inter venena, ideo flamini sacrorum equum tangere non licet. Nec alia est mens Aristotelis, qui libr. II. hist. Animal. cap. 15. prorsus idem in Elephanto videtur observasse, quod nos in equo, inquiens: Elephanto etiam jecur sine felle: sectione tamen facta circa eam partem, qua fel adhærere solet, ὑγεράς χολώδης humor felleus effluit plus minus, quemadmodum & paulo ante dixerat, cervus felle vacat, quamquam ejus intestinum amarum adeo sit, ut ne à canibus quidem attingatur. Deinde etiam ibidem notat, fel in omnibus animalibus non eodem modo colligi, ex quibus manifestum, Aristotelem fellis nomine intellexisse, folliculum fellis, quem equos non habere talem, qualem pleraque animantia abunde probatum. certe Hippocrates in equis bilem agnovisse constat, ostendens enim quomodo segregentur humores, quorum secretione ab invicem & singulorum
units.tr: goes on to list the wind-conceived mares as recorded by Varro and Columella and others. In the same way, what Pliny relates in book 11, chapter 37, is that sheep in Chalcis of Euboea have no gall, and, as he adds, they lack it, those who feed on wormwood in Pontus, and there are countless things of this kind. Unless one wishes to interpret Aristotle and Pliny thus: that they did not mean solipeds and deer to lack all bile whatever, but only to lack the gall-bladder. That this was their meaning is evident even from this, that Pliny teaches the gall of horses to be virulent, in book 18, chapter 9, saying: among all the common animals, gall is the most potent in the most excellent creatures; its power is to heat, bite, cut, draw out and disperse. In smaller animals it is understood more subtly, and so is thought more subtle for eye medicines. The bull has the chief power, even in bronze, and in giving hides a golden colour. And a little later: horse gall alone is condemned among poisons; for this reason it is not lawful for the Flamen of the sacred rites to touch a horse. Nor is Aristotle's meaning otherwise: in book 2 of the History of Animals, chapter 15, he seems to have observed exactly the same in the elephant as we have in the horse, saying: the elephant also has a liver without gall; yet when a section is made around the part where gall is wont to adhere, a bilious humour [ὑγεράς χολώδης] flows out more or less, just as he had said a little before, the deer lacks gall, although its intestine is so bitter that not even dogs touch it. Then he also notes in the same place that gall is not gathered in the same way in all animals, from which it is clear that Aristotle, by the name of gall, understood the gall-bladder, which horses do not have in the way most animals do, as has been abundantly proved. Certainly Hippocrates is agreed to have recognised bile in horses; for in showing how the humours are separated, by whose secretion from one another and by whose correction the diseases come about, he says that this thing has a likeness to what the Scythians make from mare's milk. For they pour the milk into hollow wooden vessels and shake it; while it is churned it foams and separates, and the fat, which they call butter, rises, while the light...

units.la: lorum rum correctione morbi fiant, habet, quit, hac res similitudinem ad id, quod hyta faciunt ex equino lacte. lac enim cava vasa lignea infusum concutiunt. Id autem dum turbatur, spumescit & ernitur, & pingue quidem, quod burum vocant, cum leve sit, in superficonsistit: grave vero & crassum, deorn sidit, quod etiam secretum siccant. ti vero concretum & siccatum fuerit, opacen ipsum vocant. At serum lactis medium locum tenet. Sic etiam in homine, dum turbatur humor, quicquid est in corpore, a principiis, qua dixi, separatur. Et in superficie quidem bilis consistit (levissima enim existit, & pasin cum butyro comparatur) secundo sanguis: tertio pituita. Gravissimus autem horum humorum est aqua. constitit itaque & ratione & experientia, & auctoritate eorum, quos a sese citaverat, solipedes & cervos le non carere, quod erat probandum. at vero etiam Democriti manes
units.tr: ...the correction of diseases occur. It has, he says, a resemblance to what they do with mare's milk. For the milk, poured into hollow wooden vessels, is shaken. While it is agitated it foams and separates, and the fat, which they call butter, since it is light, settles on the surface; but the heavy and thick part sinks down, which they also set aside and dry. When it has been thickened and dried they call it cheese. But the whey of the milk holds the middle place. So also in man, when the humour is agitated, whatever is in the body is separated from the principles I mentioned. And on the surface indeed bile settles (for it is the lightest, and in its floating it is compared with butter), second blood, third phlegm. The heaviest of these humours is water. It is thus established, by reason and experience and by the authority of those he had cited, that solipeds and deer do not lack gall, which was to be proved. But he also strives to raise the ghost of Democritus against Sylvius and against bile,

units.la: in Sylvium atque adversus bilem excitare satagit, quasi docuerit, bilem flavam humano corpori exitio esse verba ejus sic sonant: Bilis vero flava, quæ circa hepar versatur, corpori est exitio ubi ebullit. Est enim corpori humano grávis, & nullo ejus commodo domestica Epist: ad Hippocr. sed primo nihil tale loco à Le Vasseur citato reperitur: ignoscamus tamen illi hunc lapsum, secutus enim fuit citationem Mœbii, cujus vitula hoc loco aravit. Sed quæso, licet hæc à Democrito dicerentur, quid inde inferri posset? non enim ibi statuitur bilem semper esse corpori exitio, sed tantum ubi ebullit præternaturaliter videlicet sese habens, adeo ut Le Vasseur argumentetur à bile præternaturaliter se se habente, quam nocere Sylvius centies monet, eique in praxi suâ mederi studet; at bilem naturaliter dispositam, quam utilem nobis esse & necessariam supra demonstratum. ri certe ratione sanguis cum cæris humoribus, imo cor & cereum, & similia male disposita noint, quibus tamen bene dispositis care neutiquam possumus.
units.tr: as if Democritus had taught that yellow bile is destructive to the human body. His words sound thus: Yellow bile, which is found about the liver, is destructive to the body where it boils. For it is heavy for the human body, and of no domestic benefit (Letter to Hippocrates). But first of all nothing of the kind is found in the passage cited by Le Vasseur. Yet let us pardon him this slip, for he followed the citation of Möbius, whose heifer ploughed in this place. But I ask, even if these things were said by Democritus, what could be inferred from them? For it is not there laid down that bile is always destructive to the body, but only where it boils, that is, when it is in a preternatural state. So Le Vasseur argues from bile in a preternatural state, which Sylvius warns a hundred times is harmful, and for which he strives to provide remedies in his practice; but bile naturally disposed, which we have shown above to be useful and necessary. By the same reasoning, certainly, blood along with the other humours, indeed the heart and wax and similar things, are harmful when badly disposed, though we can by no means do without them when they are well disposed.

units.la: Sed quandoquidem Democritum stem suæ futilitatis infeliciter citat, idem litem hanc dirimat, qui Hippocratis judicio Philosophorumnimus est, & cujus Philosophia m parum abest à Cartesii placitis, huic visum fuerit operæ prætium doctrinam Democriti à sua data opedistinguere. Democritus igitur, i refert Hippocrates Epist. ad Daagetum, postquam respondisset sese cupatum esse circa causas insaniæ & lis naturam ac sedem, subdit num:
units.tr: But since he has unhappily cited Democritus as a witness to his own futility, let me settle this dispute in a way that is worth the effort. Hippocrates judged Democritus the most philosophical of men, and his philosophy differs little from the tenets of Descartes. So I have thought it worthwhile to distinguish the teaching of Democritus from the opinion given by Democritus himself. Democritus, then, as Hippocrates relates in his Letter to Damagetus, after replying that he was occupied with the causes of madness and its nature and seat, adds:

units.la: nosti enim hanc, videlicet bilem, roris causam esse, (an simpliciter? fit. sed) ubi nimium redundarit; in mnibus equidem à natura inest: sed in ibusdam minus, in quibusdam amius. at ἀμετρίη immoderatio ipsius morbi sunt, ipsa velut materia aliquando bona, aliquando mala subjacente. & ego, (respondet Hippocrates) Per Jovem, inquam, o Democrite, vere hæc & sapienter dicis. Non ergo Democritus bilem absolute damnat, quod perabsurde hinc voluit exsculpere Le Vasseur, sed illius excessum, quem nemo unquam laudavit.
units.tr: You know that this bile is the cause of madness (or simply? it happens, but) when it has excessively abounded; in all men it is indeed present by nature, but in some less, in some more. But immoderation [ἀμετρίη] and the disorders themselves are, as it were, the matter lying beneath, sometimes good, sometimes bad. And I (Hippocrates replies): By Jove, Democritus, I said, you speak truly and wisely. Therefore Democritus does not condemn bile absolutely, which Le Vasseur absurdly wished to extract from this, but its excess, which no one has ever praised.

units.la: Paracelsum denique invocat, qui sel absolute noxium & inutile dixerit. certe puerorum est ᾧεῖαν hinc inde compitantium sine delectu ex quibusvis authoribus excerpere, & citato quovis nomine, putare sese officio defunctum esse. Quænam quæso hæc est illatio, Paracelsus hoc ait, ergo verum est; aut si mavis, ergo Sylvius hæc concedere debet, qui Paracelsi nusquam vel minimam fecit mentionem. indubium est Paracelsum uti multa scripsit veritati consona, ita etiam varia à veritate aliena pro veris venditasse, quo loco habenda sunt verba rba à Le Vasseur citata Pag. 25. si solute sumantur: cum tamen Paralsus cap. sequenti xii. non omnem em, sed nimiam duntaxat ejus coam demere voluerit. Fellis enim, quit, consumendi, ita, ut, quanm ejus est inutile, aboleatur, prosus ipse est, ut omnes à felle prognati orbi tollantur, nec ab eo deinceps ulla vel ægritudo inducatur, quinetiam lestibus & potentibus humani corris partibus bilem annumerat, postiam enim dixisset libro, qui illi inribitur, Parenthesis intercausa liber 1. Pagoyum 3. tractatus de Ente narali cap. i. uti cælum cum omni suo mamento, constellatione & cæteris cundum & per se ipsum, sic homo quoe constellatus intra se & pro se erit tenter. & postea distinctius microsinum cum macrocosmo conferens, ptem planetis totidem humani corris partes respondere fingit, Cor gr. Soli, fel Marti & ita porro, quin etiam ibidem cap. x. quod eatenus omnino Hippocraticum est, quatuor complexiones humorum enumerat, aciditatem, dulcedinem, amaritudinem & salsedinem. & paulo post, si, inquit, amaritudo præcellit, cholericus est, si dulcedo phlegmaticus &c, ex quibus luce clarius constat Paracelsum revera nonnisi bilis excessum damnare, quamvis nostra nihil referat, quid Theophrastus Bombast alicubi dissolutius & per incogitantiam dixerit, aut etiam quid aliunde in illius scripta irrepserit, voluimus tamen & ipsum cum cæteris à D. Vasseur citatis testibus in ipsum Le Vasseur retorquere.
units.tr: Finally he invokes Paracelsus, who said that bile is absolutely harmful and useless. Certainly it is a boy's business to pick up [ᾧεῖαν] things here and there without discrimination from any authors, and, whatever name is cited, to think oneself to have discharged the duty. What, I ask, is this inference: Paracelsus says this, therefore it is true? Or if you prefer: therefore Sylvius must concede this, who never made the slightest mention of Paracelsus. It is beyond doubt that Paracelsus, as he wrote much that agrees with the truth, so also put forward various things alien to the truth as true. In this place must be counted the words cited by Le Vasseur on p. 25, if they are taken absolutely; yet Paracelsus, in the next chapter, 12, wished to remove not all bile, but only its excess. For the consuming of bile, he says, so that it is abolished as far as it is useless, is itself such that all diseases arising from bile are taken away, and no sickness is thereafter induced by it. Moreover he reckons bile among the most vital and powerful parts of the human body. For having said, in the book which is ascribed to him, Parenthesis (book 1), Pagoyum (3), treatise on the Natural Being, chapter 1: as heaven with all its constellations and other things, so man, constellated within himself and for himself, will be. And afterwards, comparing the microcosm more distinctly with the macrocosm, he imagines that as many parts of the human body correspond to the seven planets: heart to the Sun, gall to Mars, and so on. Moreover in the same place, chapter 10, which so far is wholly Hippocratic, he enumerates the four complexions of the humours: acidity, sweetness, bitterness and saltiness. And a little later: If, he says, bitterness predominates, he is choleric; if sweetness, phlegmatic, etc. From which it is clearer than daylight that Paracelsus in fact condemns only the excess of bile. Although it matters nothing to our case what Theophrastus Bombast may have said rather loosely and carelessly somewhere, or even what has crept into his writings from elsewhere, we wished nevertheless to turn him back against Le Vasseur himself, together with the other witnesses cited by Dr. Le Vasseur.
