units.la: Medici igitur officium est, bilem non minus, quam cæteros humani corporis humores in naturali statu conservare, eamque à sanitatis perfectione deflectentem corrigere, aut expurgare quandoque ejus copiam imminuendo, volatilitatem compescendo, crassitiem solvendo & diluendo, acrimoniam temperando, & obtundendo. vel etiam propter alias causas ejus quantitatem augendo, ejusque substantiam incrassando, vel etiam ejus volatilitatem incendio augendo, inertiam excitando, atque acrimoniam acuendo, quæ cum sint verissima Hippocratica, & ad veram praxin necessaria, uti ex supra dictis manifestum est, sequitur Doctorem Le Vasseur, qui bilem omnem eliminandam esse docere debet, si inutilis est, si noxia, si vitam breviorem reddit, eandem praxin exercere cum eo, qui Parentem optimum duabus filiis turpi sua inertia orbavit, de quo supra: ut necesse sit ipsum meliora Praxeos fundamenta ex Hippocrate & Sylvio sibi comparare.
units.tr: It is therefore the physician's duty to keep bile, no less than the other humours of the human body, in its natural state, and to correct it when it departs from perfect health, or sometimes to purge it, by diminishing its quantity, checking its volatility, dissolving and diluting its thickness, and tempering and blunting its acrimony; or even, for other causes, to increase its quantity by thickening its substance, or to increase its volatility by heat, arousing its sluggishness and sharpening its acrimony. Since these things are most true and Hippocratic and necessary for true practice, as is clear from what was said above, it follows that Doctor Le Vasseur, who ought to teach that all bile must be eliminated if it is useless, if it is harmful, if it shortens life, is pursuing the same practice as one who, by his shameful sloth, bereaved an excellent parent of two sons, as mentioned above. So it is necessary that he acquire for himself better foundations of practice from Hippocrates and Sylvius.

units.la: Sed totum quod ipsum à tramite abegit non est nisi crassa ignorantia eorum, quæ accuratè scire medici est; & solummodo Andabatarum more imimpugnat quod ignorat verbosus Medicus, intelligere enim non potuit L Le Vasseur; quomodo bilis, cujus utilitatem hactenus probavimus & defendimus, hos usus exerceat; quomodo videlicet crassiores & tenaciores ejus partes crassioribus sec ibus adhære[?] segregatis aliis partibus liquidioribus minus flavescentibus; Putat enim L. Vasseur p. 16. incorrupto chyli nitido puroque candore bilis partes cum e[?] simul ad cor venire; Absonum vero esse sane rustici nostrates ipsi committerent ad oculum simile quia fieri, cum ex lacte bovillo aut ovillo caseum conficiunt stercoris ovilli urore tinctum.
units.tr: But all that has turned him from the path is nothing but crass ignorance of the things which it is the physician's business to know accurately. Like the Andabatae, he merely attacks what the wordy physician does not know. For Le Vasseur could not understand how bile, whose usefulness we have hitherto proved and defended, exercises these functions: namely, how its thicker and more tenacious parts, adhering to thicker serous matter, are separated from the other, more liquid, less yellow parts. For Le Vasseur thinks at p. 16 that the parts of bile come to the heart together with the chyle in its unspoiled, bright and pure whiteness. It is absurd indeed, since our own country folk, when they make cheese from cow's or sheep's milk, produce something like this to the eye, tinged with sheep dung.

units.la: Etenim Acidum sive coagulum quod lacti in hunc finem permiscent & salsum seri, quod lacti natura inest post quandam pugnam sibi mutuo adhærescunt, atque inde illius seri partes redditæ sunt crassiores, quam ut occupare possunt interstitia crassiorum[?] & magis ramosarum particularum lactis, quæ anteà divisæ fero innatabant, unde partes illæ ramosæ sibi adhærescunt, earumque concretione sive coagulatione postea fit caseus, ex viridissimâ autem illâ coagulatâ massâ sive caseo, cui ovillorum stercorum tinctura intricata est, serum subalbidum profluit; nec aliam novi rationem quare Hippocrates Aphor: 72. Sect: iv. & alibi sæpè toties monet, nalum signum esse cum phreneticorum & melancholicorum urinæ pellucidæ sunt & albæ; quam quia bilis sanguinis ramosis particulis potius adhæret; sero pariter à salsi & acidi acrimoniâ crassiore reddito. quod, quia tum à sanguinis particulis rubicundis sive magis ramosis separatur; ut solitò plus mingatur, uti non semel in phreniticis observavi, unde sanguis duplici de causâ justo calidior & acrior redditus phrenesim producere potest: Ciniflones certè chymici gens
units.tr: For the acid or coagulant which they mix with the milk to this end, and the salt of the whey, which is naturally in milk, after a certain struggle cling to each other. Hence the parts of that whey have become thicker than they can occupy the interstices of the thicker and more branching particles of milk, which before, being divided, floated in the whey. Thence those branching parts cling to each other, and by their concretion or coagulation cheese is afterwards formed. But from that very green coagulated mass or cheese, into which the tincture of sheep dung is entangled, a whitish whey flows out. Nor do I know any other reason why Hippocrates, Aphor: 72, Sect: 4, and elsewhere very often warns that it is a bad sign when the urine of frenetics and melancholics is clear and white. This is because bile clings rather to the branching particles of the blood, the serum being likewise rendered thicker by the sharpness of salt and acid. Since this is then separated from the reddish or more branching particles of the blood, one passes urine more often, as I have observed in frenetics more than once. Whence the blood, rendered doubly and justly hotter and sharper, can produce phrensy. Certainly the chemists, a race of Ciniflones

units.la: H
units.tr: H

units.la: gens illa barda, uti loquitur pag: 77. ridentnostrum Doctorem,quod nunquam vel ullam limpidissimæ aquæ ex viridibus plantis destillationem vel præcipitationem quandam unquam observaverit. Creta in pulverem redacta & acescenti cerevisiæ permixta, ita per suam salsedinem acidis cerevisiæ partibus præviâ effervescentiâ adhærefcit, ut cum iis præcipitetur ad fundum, relicto superiùs liquore clarissimo, qui antea fuerat turbulentissimus. Sed quid multis? an non à coagulato sanguine non rubicundo modò, sed & sæpè atro-purpureo separatum est serum limpidissimum incorrupto, nitido, puroque candore? notius igitur est, uti opinor, ex dictis, quàm ut ulterioribus probationibus tempus pretiosum sit dilapidandum. Bilem ex orificio meatûs bilarii in Intestinum duodenum effundi, eam cum Succo Pancreatico ibidem profluente atque pituita intestinali misceri ceri ac effervescere : cibum per eanem viam intestinum videlicet sensim ransire , ut bili & Succo Pancreatico ermisceatur ; bilis partes viscidiores c crassiores , id est , flavedinis intenoris (quò enim ea dilutior est eò mi-us flavescit ) eadem post effervescenam coagulari , ac fæces , cum quibus lis arctior nexus est infici ; chylum bicantem , à tota denique illa massa, uæ ex Triumviratu & cibo in stomaho costo componitur,tenuiorem huorem, vi motus peristalticivelut seum ex caseo, secerni nitidum, purum c candidum , atque per venas Lacteas iasque vias ad Cor caeterasque humai corporis partes distribui. Easque ro diversitate suæ constitutionis aut aturaliter aut preternaturaliter affice-e , quæ quidem omnia tot manifestis rgumentis, rationibus & experimens demonstrata sunt, ut, qui hæc non atelligat,disciplinæ incapax videatur.
units.tr: that barbarous race, as he says on p. 77, mocks our Doctor because he has never observed any distillation or precipitation of the clearest water from green plants. Chalk reduced to powder and mixed with sour beer adheres, by its saltiness and after a prior effervescence, to the acid parts of the beer, so that it is precipitated to the bottom with them, leaving above the clearest liquid, which before had been most turbid. But why say more? Has not the clearest serum been separated from coagulated blood, not only reddish but often dark purple, and found incorrupt, bright and pure white? It is therefore, I think, better known from what has been said than that precious time should be wasted on further proofs. Bile is poured from the opening of the bile duct into the duodenum, where it is mixed with the pancreatic juice flowing in at the same place and with intestinal phlegm, and effervesces. Food passes gradually through the same route, that is, the intestine, and is mixed with bile and pancreatic juice. The more viscid and thicker parts of the bile, that is, its yellow substance (for the more dilute it is, the less yellow it becomes), coagulate after the effervescence and are contaminated along with the faeces, to which they are more tightly bound. The chyle, a thinner liquid, is secreted, clean, pure and white, from the whole mass composed of the triumvirate and food in the stomach, by the force of peristaltic motion, as whey is separated from curds, and it is distributed through the lacteal veins and other passages to the heart and the other parts of the human body. These parts are affected, according to the diversity of their constitution, either naturally or unnaturally. All of this has been demonstrated by so many plain arguments, reasons and experiments that whoever does not understand it seems unfit for the discipline.

units.la: Asserta igitur veritate vix videtur necesse reliqua minoris momenti dubia, quæ vel sua sponte collabuntur solvendo, meum & Lectoris otium minus necessariis terere. Ne tamen hic ansam acciperet calumniandi, strictim scrupulos illi eximam; Ex iis quæ hactenus demonstrata sunt, vel sua sponte sequitur quid respondendum sit ad quæstionem quartam & ultimam supra pag: 32. propositam, videlicet, an cor vi effervescentiæ intestinalis bene & male afficiatur, & speciatim febris à quodam illius vitio excitari possit? Cor bene vel male afficiî à naturali vel præternaturali effervescentiâ, tum quatenus spiritus & reliquæ partes subtiliores convenientes effervescentię intestinalis operâ ex cibo fermentato excitatæ in cor assurgunt, tum etiam quatenus halitus, vapores & quandoque flatus vehementiori forte intestinali effervescentiâ excitati per venas lacteas inprimis ad cor convolant; . . . . . . . . quamvis vero oculis corporeis inconpicuum sit; spiritus tenuia corpuscula, per poros corporis diffundi, hoc tamen si non contingeret, frustra epithemata, emplastra atque fomenta varia adhiberentur, quorum usus ab omnibus Medicinae Peritis commendatur, ut eorum spiritus sive tenuia corpora per cutis & caeterarum interiorum partium spiracula prorumpentent. Nec alia via venenum sive extrinsecus illatum, sive ore assumtum, quam per venas (unde nomen sortitum dicitur) ad cor diffunditur: ab effervescentia denique intestinali cormale aut bene afficitur, quatenus chylus probe aut vitiose dispositus efferve-scentiae in corde naturalis aut praeternaturalis causa est: atque ipse chylus sequenti concoctione, quae in corde peragitur, accurate aut minus accurate aut nullatenus in sanguinem convertí potest converti, quatenus vitium antecedentis concoctionis facile, difficulter
units.tr: The truth having been asserted, it hardly seems necessary to waste my own and the reader's leisure on the remaining doubts of lesser importance, which fall apart of their own accord once they are answered. Yet, lest he take from this an occasion for slander, I will briefly remove his scruples. From what has been demonstrated so far, it follows of its own accord what must be answered to the fourth and last question proposed above on p. 32, namely whether the heart is affected well or badly by the force of intestinal effervescence, and in particular whether fever can be caused by some fault in that effervescence. The heart is affected well or badly by natural or unnatural effervescence: both insofar as spirits and other subtler parts, excited from the fermented food by the working of the intestinal effervescence, rise up into the heart, and insofar as breaths, vapours and sometimes gases, roused by a rather violent intestinal effervescence, rush to the heart chiefly through the lacteal veins. ... Although it is not visible to the bodily eyes that thin spirits diffuse through the pores of the body, yet if this did not happen, poultices, plasters and various fomentations would be applied in vain, and their use is commended by all experts in medicine, so that their spirits, or thin bodies, may burst forth through the pores of the skin and of the other inner parts. Nor is poison, whether introduced from outside or taken by mouth, diffused to the heart by any other way than through the veins (from which it is said to have its name). Finally, the heart is affected well or badly by intestinal effervescence insofar as the chyle, rightly or faultily prepared, is the cause of natural or unnatural effervescence in the heart; and the chyle itself can be converted into blood by the following concoction, which is carried out in the heart, accurately, less accurately, or not at all, insofar as a fault of the preceding concoction is corrected by the following one easily, with difficulty, or not at all.

units.la: [Note: the transcription above contains uncertain readings; see notes.] culter, aut nullatenus sequenti corrigitur. Dico difficulter; labitur enim D. Le Vasseur p. 41. ubi absolutè negat, vitium primæ concoctionis sequentibus corrigi posse; at certè quandam cruditatem primæ concoctionis repetitis concoctionibus tandem ad maturitatem reduci nemo negaverit, qui accuratiùs intellexerit sanguinem non modò semel in dextro cordis ventriculo effervescere atque iteratò in sinistro, sed etiam eum per totum corpus diffundi atque in arteriis & venis velut balneo quodam præparari atque ad Cor reverti, ut tandem multiplici rectificatione sanguinis persectionem adipiscatur.
units.tr: culter, or not at all, is corrected by the following one. I say with difficulty; for Le Vasseur, p. 41, flatly denies that a fault of the first concoction can be corrected by those that follow. But no one who understands more accurately would deny that a crudity of the first concoction is at last brought to maturity by repeated concoctions, since the blood not only effervesces once in the right ventricle of the heart and again in the left, but is also diffused through the whole body and prepared in the arteries and veins, as in a kind of bath, and returns to the heart, so that at last, by manifold rectification, it attains perfection.

units.la: Sed resistit iterum rei manifestæ Le Vasseur, inquiens pag. 30. Dum igitur igneum ex ejus placito flumen, πoταμὸς οἵσι ἀρδεῖται τὸ ζῷον, i. e. flumina quibus corpus irrigatur; seu ἐναιμος νεῦρος i. e. nervos sanguifluos, venas dico, percurrit, ut ad cor tandem, ex ejus voto, oto, perveniat, quid ni venæ pulsant? Docet enim in corde ac arteriis, ἀλλαχῶ sola prætereuntium succorum copia & bullitione celebrari. Non solùm igitur descendens cava, Triumviratu facta turgidaque distendi deberet & pulsare; sed eò magis succussione arterias superare, quò uniuscujusque virtus, si nullâ additione vires acquirat eundo, circà cortum, ἰχνεγτέρη vegetior, & infraior existit.
units.tr: But Le Vasseur resists the manifest fact again, saying on p. 30: "While, according to his view, the fiery river [potamos] by which the animal is watered [ὁ ποταμὸς οἷς ἀρδεῖται τὸ ζῷον], that is, the rivers by which the body is irrigated; or the blood-bearing nerve [ἔναιμος νεῦρος], that is, the blood-carrying sinews, I mean the veins, runs through, so that at last, as he wishes, it reaches the heart, why do the veins not pulse? For he teaches that the pulse is produced in the heart and the arteries, and elsewhere by the abundance and boiling of the passing juices alone. Therefore not only the descending vena cava, made turgid by the Triumvirate, ought to be distended and pulsate, but it ought much more to surpass the arteries in throbbing, since the vigour of each, if it gains no strength from any addition as it goes, is more lively [ἰσχυροτέρη] and weaker the further it is from the heart."

units.la: Tantùm abest omnem effervescentiam esse igneam ut præter evidentis-simam rationem manifestissimo experimento, beneficio Thermometræ; e quo suprà, constet dari effervescentiam non calidam modò sed & frigidam, & blandam probetur. Quod ψῦχρον ψεῦδος, quantas illis peperit solicitudines, quantos labores! Sed quidnam illud est? Dum, inquit, aqueum ex ejus, putà Sylvii, placito, flumen venas percurrit &c. Si statuat Sylvii sententiam esse, quod ubique urget, effervescentes humores semper calidos esse, imò eos incendi & confagrare, uti pag. 41. 44. &c. injurius est in Sylvium qui, (uti vel ex ipso scripto Doctoris Le Vasseur constat) diserte docet pro ratione humorum effervescentium excitari effervescentiam frigidiorem, calidiorem & blandam, quod ut salsissimum, Sylvio sæpè exprobravit, supra non semel demonstrare coacti fuimus. si verò sententia Doctoris Le Vasseur, ex Sylvii hypothesi erronea sit obortâ nempè effervescentiâ calidâ venam cavam descendentem pulsare quod objicit Le Vasseur, certè magis magisque suam prodit famam, utpotè qui auctoritate cujusdam seductus palàm ostendit sibi prorsus ignotum esse quid sit Pulsus & quâ vi fiat. Etenim pag. 31. ex Galeno negat arterias, vi caloris & spiritûs à corde in eas influentis, dilatari: sed quâdam facultate quam arteriarum cordi continuarum tunicæ semper semper ab eo proficiscentem obtinent. qui locus iterum non legitur loco ab ipso citato, sed ex Lib. de Usu Pulsuum cap. 5. ubi Galenus adversus Erasistratum contendit, non dilatari arterias, quia implentur, sed impleri quia dilatantur, atque arterias perinde ut Cor seipsas movere, vicissim se attollentes submittentesque, idque eadem, quâ ipsum, vi. Respondet ad hunc locum Doctiss. Casp. Hofm, & quidem in apologia pro Galeno certe Galenus hîc uti à veritate ita & ab antiquitate discedit, uti vel ex textu citato liquet, cum Erasistratus quo fuit Aristoteli ex filiâ nepos sit ipso longe antiquior. Imò Aristoteles Galeno longè superior. expressis verbis contrarium docet Lib. de Respiratione cap. 20. [Greek] i. e. in ipso autem corde tumefactio humoris (id est, effervescentia sanguinis in corde) qui semper è cibo accedit, ultimam cordis tunicam elevantis, pulsum facit atque hoc semper sine ullâ intermissione facit. Unde in fine ejusdem capitis naturalem pulsum definiens, inquit, Φύξις ἡ δ᾽ ψυχῆς θερμαιν-νομένῃ πνεύματος. Pulsus est humoris concalescentis inflatio. Sed pudet sanè de antiquitate certare super re hoc nostro seculo accuratiùs repertâ. quâ vi Cor suâ diastole aperiat arterias atque distendat fibrarum ope, aut in quo consistat illa facultas arteriarum, quâ dilatato corde arteriæ ad extremitates digitorum usque distendantur: quomodo teretes & cavæ arteriæ fibris suis parietes suos diducant non facilius dixerit aut animo conceperit, quàm quomodo ter tria fiant decem. Cùm contrà facilè intelligatur sanguinem ex corde prorumpentem in arterias sanguine plenas, totum sanguinem, qui iis continetur; propter continuitatem, & rerum cunctarum plenitudinem eodem momento debere impelli, cujus ex corde expulsi sanguinis effectum & indicium est Pulsus, ejusque differentias vel ex sanguinis copia vel ex pulsus vehementia vel frequentia, vel duritie vel ex signis his contrariis vel denique & ordine defumi norunt, qui quicquam. Præter rationes experimentum dabimus, ut oculis suis credat, qui rationi diffidens alienis opinionibus mavult adhærescere quàm rationi. Læsa Arteria sanguis ex ea singulis pulsibus novà prorumpit vehementiâ. quod non fieret si arteria diastole sese dilataret; quin potius in Systole sive earum contractione sanguis ex iis impetuosius exprimeretur. Sed accipiat tubulum vitreum eique si vel guttam stando indat, statim liquor omnis eo contentus magno licet intervallo distitus simul impelletur. Si mihi cum pueris res esset intestinula quædam illi tubulo annecterem quò illorum
units.tr: So far is every effervescence from being fiery that, besides the most evident reasoning, it is shown by a most manifest experiment, with the help of the thermometer, from which it is established above that there is an effervescence not only hot but also cold, and that a mild one is proved. What a cold falsehood [ψῦχρον ψεῦδος] has caused them, how many anxieties, how many labours! But what is it? "While, he says, the watery river, according to his, that is Sylvius's, view, runs through the veins, etc." If he takes the view of Sylvius to be, as he presses everywhere, that effervescent humours are always hot, indeed that they burn and set on fire, as on pp. 41, 44 and elsewhere, he does Sylvius an injustice, who (as is clear even from Doctor Le Vasseur's own writing) plainly teaches that, according to the nature of the humours, a cooler, warmer or mild effervescence is excited. Since he has often reproached Sylvius with this as most absurd, we have been compelled more than once to demonstrate above that it is false. But if Doctor Le Vasseur's view is right, that the descending vena cava pulsates from the erroneous hypothesis of Sylvius of a hot effervescence, which Le Vasseur objects to, then he certainly betrays his own reputation more and more, since, led astray by the authority of another, he openly shows that he is wholly ignorant of what the pulse is and by what force it is produced. For on p. 31 he denies, following Galen, that the arteries are dilated by the force of heat and spirit flowing into them from the heart, but that they possess a certain faculty which the coats of the arteries, continuous with the heart, always derive from it. This passage is not read again in the place he cites, but in Galen's book On the Use of the Pulses, chapter 5, where Galen contends against Erasistratus that the arteries are not dilated because they are filled, but are filled because they are dilated, and that the arteries, just as the heart, move themselves, raising and lowering themselves in turn, by the same force by which the heart itself does so. The most learned Caspar Hofmann answers this passage in his apology for Galen. Certainly Galen here departs from the truth and from antiquity, as is clear even from the text cited, since Erasistratus, who was the grandson of Aristotle through his daughter, is much older than Galen. Indeed Aristotle is far superior to Galen. In plain words he teaches the opposite in his book On Respiration, chapter 20: "but in the heart itself the swelling of the humour (that is, the effervescence of the blood in the heart) which always comes from food, lifting the innermost coat of the heart, produces the pulse, and it does this always without any interruption." Hence, at the end of the same chapter, defining the natural pulse, he says: [Φύξις ἡ δ᾽ ψυχῆς θερμαινομένῃ πνεύματος]. The pulse is the inflation of the humour growing warm. But it is truly shameful to dispute about antiquity over a matter discovered more accurately in our own age: by what force the heart, by its diastole, opens the arteries and distends them by the help of their fibres, or in what that faculty of the arteries consists by which, when the heart is dilated, the arteries are stretched out even to the tips of the fingers. How round and hollow arteries spread their walls by their fibres would not be easier to say or conceive than how three times three makes ten. On the contrary, it is easily understood that the blood bursting from the heart into the arteries, which are full of blood, must impel the whole blood contained in them at the same moment, on account of continuity and the fullness of all things. The effect and indication of this blood expelled from the heart is the pulse; and those who know anything about it derive its differences from the amount of blood, from the vehemence, frequency or hardness of the pulse, or from these contrary signs, and finally from order. Besides reasons, we shall give an experiment, so that he may believe his own eyes, if he distrusts reason and prefers to cling to other men's opinions rather than to reason. When an artery is wounded, the blood bursts out of it with fresh force at each pulse. This would not happen if the artery dilated itself in diastole; rather, in systole, or its contraction, the blood would be squeezed out of it more violently. But let him take a glass tube and put a single drop into it while standing: at once all the liquid contained in it is driven forward together, even at a great distance. If I had to do with boys, I would attach to that tube some little intestines, so that the cause of the pulse, or the distension of the arteries, might be made plain to their eyes. Besides this there is also another manifold reason why he ought not to have said that the chyle in the descending vena cava excites the pulse, both because it is not established that the chyle travels to the heart through that branch of the vein, and also...

units.la: oculis causa pulsûs sive distensionis arteriarum palàm innotescceret. præterea & alia multiplex ratio subest, quare dicere non debuisset Chylum in vena Cava descendente, pulsum excitare, tum quia illi non constat chylum per illum venæ ramum contendere ad cor tum etiam quia licet chyli quædam portio per eam ad cor ascenderet pulsus tamen nullus excitaretur; uti nec pulsus in ascendente venæ cavæ ramo, tum quia chylus atque sanguis in illum non impetu quodam & confertim uti sanguis ex corde in arterias prorùit, sed per parvos varios canaliculos & exiguos poros. Hanc itidem causam esse propter quam venæ pulsus sunt expertes, quamvis sanguis ex arteriis in eas profluat, quia videlicet sanguis ex arteriis capillaribus in capillares venas & ex iis in ampliorem concavitatem diducitur ea vehementia sanguinem in venas non prorumpere, quà ex corde in arterias, erias, utpote qui modo plane contrario ex eo in amplissimas arterias & ex iis in minores & tandem minimas prorúit. Taceo effervescentiam in descendente venæ cavæ ramo tam facile non excitari quia causæ effervescentiæ inter quas uti supra visum etiam enumeratur humorum acidorum & falsorum contrarietas, in ea tanta non est, quanta quidem datur in sanguine ascendente & descendente chylo & lympha sibi commissis. quibus accedit, majorem illum, qui est in corde, calorem atque spirituum vibrationem requiri ut sanguis ita moveatur, elevetur, rarescat: & modo supra explicato augeatur aut potius auceri videatur, ut ex corde prorumpat; neque quod ferio notatum velim effervescentia pulsum facit, (alias enim ille in intestinis observaretur) sed ruptio sanguinis è corde in arterias effervescentiæ, unde sequitur licet venæ cavæ ramis quædam accidaret effervescentia uti accidit in febri cujus efficacia omnem humani corporis sanguinem effervescere constat, non tamen inde majori probabilitate sequitur eas debere pulsare, quam cæteras venas quæ tamen præter alia signa etiam pulsu propter rationem modo recitatas ab arteriis discernuntur.
units.tr: for the sake of the eyes, the pulse or distension of the arteries would be made plainly evident. Moreover there is another, manifold reason why he ought not to have said that chyle in the descending vena cava excites the pulse. First, because it is not certain that chyle makes its way through that branch of the vein to the heart. Second, because even if some portion of the chyle were to ascend through it to the heart, no pulse would nevertheless be excited; nor is there a pulse in the ascending branch of the vena cava. Third, because chyle and blood do not flow into it with any rushing force and all at once, as blood bursts from the heart into the arteries, but through small, various little channels and tiny pores. This is likewise the reason why the veins are free of pulse, although blood flows from the arteries into them. Blood is led from the capillary arteries into the capillary veins and from these into a wider cavity, so it does not burst into the veins with the force with which it bursts from the heart into the arteries, since it moves in the exact opposite manner, from the heart into the very large arteries and from these into smaller and at last very small ones. I pass over the point that effervescence is not so easily excited in the descending branch of the vena cava, because the causes of effervescence, among which, as was seen above, is the contrariety of acid and salt humours, are not there as great as they are in the blood, ascending and descending, with the chyle and lymph entrusted to them. To this must be added that the greater heat that is in the heart, and the vibration of the spirits, are required if the blood is to be so moved, raised and rarefied, and augmented, or rather seems to be augmented, by the method explained above, so that it bursts forth from the heart. Nor do I wish it to be noted that effervescence makes the pulse (otherwise it would be observed in the intestines), but the rupture of blood from the heart into the arteries is an effervescence. From this it follows that, although some effervescence might occur in the branches of the vena cava, as it occurs in fever, whose power is known to make all the blood of the human body effervesce, it does not follow with any greater probability that they must pulse than the other veins, which nevertheless are distinguished from the arteries, besides other signs, also by the pulse, for the reason just recited.

units.la: Sed & aliud veritati objicit: non vidit quomodo acidi vapores vi effervescentiæ ex intestinis ad cor possint depelli, cum acida maxima sui parte fixa sint, uti urget pag. citata 63.
units.tr: But he also objects to the truth in another way: he did not see how acid vapours can be driven by the force of effervescence from the intestines to the heart, since acids are for the most part fixed, as the cited page 63 insists.

units.la: Unde certe testatum facit se nunquam oculis medicis hoc negotium scrutatum fuisse: si enim unquam nares adhibuisset fermentationi aut effervescentiæ humorum, nunquam eo de re dubitare potuisset, signum enim illud à chymicis observari sufficientis fermentationis quando acor fermentescentis materiæ nares ferit, vel tyrones norunt. Certe quotiescunque cervi cerevisia in cellis coctorum fermentescit, omnia acidis halitibus repleri nemini latet. Quod si acria etiam in frigidiori aëre vel leviter fermentescentia atque effervescentia aciditate quadam nares vehementer feriunt, quanto magis illud accidit in intestinis calidis, uti experimento supra relato tot studiosis spectatoribus re ipse probatum fuit. Si minus fidat naribus & dubitare pergat an acidus vapor à materia fermentescente atque effervescente separetur ex. gr. cucurbitæ vitreæ, in qua fit humorum effervescentia vel fermentatio applicet reortum aliquem tubulum, cujus orificium inferius applicetur ollæ cui lac dulce insit & videbit aliquanto tempore post cum coquitur, coagulari lac actili argumento acidos vapores ex a materia effervescente fuisse disturbatos. Ructus & halitus acidi quos à idorofis tam serio non distinguendos docerent hippocratici medici, ex sto-macho macho per os non ascenderent. u hyperbolicè illius rhetoricationes, i[?] est, vana fallacia aqueisque coloribu[?] picta halitibus illis sponte disperiant.
units.tr: Whence he certainly attests that he never examined this matter with medical eyes. For if he had ever applied his nostrils to the fermentation or effervescence of humours, he could never have doubted it, since the sign by which chemists recognise sufficient fermentation, when the sharpness of the fermenting matter strikes the nostrils, even apprentices know. Certainly, whenever beer ferments in the vats of the cellars, no one is unaware that everything is filled with acid breaths. But if sharp things, even slightly fermenting and effervescing in cooler air, strike the nostrils vehemently with a certain acidity, how much more does that happen in hot intestines, as was proved in fact by the experiment related above before so many studious spectators. If he trusts his nostrils less and still doubts whether acid vapour is separated from fermenting and effervescing matter, let him, for example, attach to a glass cucurbit, in which the effervescence or fermentation of the humours takes place, some bent tube, whose lower opening is applied to a pot containing sweet milk. He will see some time later, when it is cooked, that the milk has curdled, a sure proof that acid vapours were driven off from the effervescing matter. The belches and acid breaths, which the Hippocratic physicians taught should not be so seriously distinguished from ..., do not rise from the stomach through the mouth. Let his hyperbolic rhetoric, that is, vain deceit painted in watery colours, vanish of its own accord along with those breaths.

units.la: Mirum igitur nulli, uti opinor, co[?] hominis diversimode affici ab effervescentia diversa diversorum effervescentium humorum, quorum halitus [?] spiritus, flatus, vapores in ipsum co[?] illabentes illud suaviter demulcet vel illius contenta depravat, accendit atque ad vehementiorem agitationem incitat, vel contra illorum motum impedit atque vel plane vel fere suffocat: vel alia quadam pravitate eadem imbuit qua cor vel minus vel magis ad motum stimulatur. Hæc autem omnia utpote naturalem sanguinis & spirituum in corde generationem turbantia non parum sanitati obesse qui non vidit lucem odisse videtur.
units.tr: It is no wonder, I think, to anyone that a man is affected in different ways by the different effervescence of different effervescing humours. Their breaths, spirits, blasts and vapours, falling into him, either gently soothe the heart or corrupt its contents, kindle it and incite it to more vehement agitation, or on the contrary impede its motion and nearly or wholly suffocate it, or imbue it with some other defect by which the heart is stimulated to motion less or more. All these things, however, disturbing the natural generation of blood and spirits in the heart, are not a little harmful to health. Whoever does not see this seems to hate the light.

units.la: Sua sponte igitur hinc profluit febrem ex devitiata illa effervescentia trium illorum humorum in intestinis exexoriri posse. Quod ultimo suscepimus probandum.
units.tr: Therefore it follows of its own accord from this that fever can arise from that faulty effervescence of those three humours in the intestines. This is what we undertook to prove last.

units.la: In plurimarum febrium intermittentium paroxysmis ita abdomen ut plurimum distenditur ut si quis linteo quodam intermissionis tempore menturam crassitiei corporis ea parte perperit, experiatur ipsum tempore accessionis febrilis octava parte crassiorem evasisse. tumque anxietates, murmura, dolores, ructus, borborygmi, &c. excitantur; quae si non intelligat Le Vasseur experiatur audiat & intelligat hippocratem sect. 4. aph: 73. sect. 5. aph: 64. & sect. vi. aph: 40. & alia : videatque D. Le Vasseur quantum à veritate, auctoritate omniumque experientia, (propriis praejudiciis obcaecatus) aberraverit.
units.tr: In the paroxysms of most intermittent fevers the abdomen is for the most part distended, so that if anyone, during the intermission, measures the girth of the body at that part with a linen cloth, he will find it to have grown an eighth thicker at the time of the febrile attack. Then anxieties, rumblings, pains, belchings, borborygmi, and so on, are excited. If Le Vasseur does not understand these things, let him try, listen and understand Hippocrates, Section 4, Aphorism 73, Section 5, Aphorism 64, and Section 6, Aphorism 40, and others; and let Dr Le Vasseur see how far he has strayed from truth, authority and the experience of all, blinded by his own prejudices.

units.la: EPILOGUS.
units.tr: EPILOGUE.

units.la: Satis superque Doctrina de febrib; Sex dictis elucescit; plura verò qui de[?] sideret, adeat Caput XXVII, & se[?] quentia de febribus praxeos Medic[?] Clarissimi & Experientissimi Viri D[?] Francisci de le Boe Sylvii Praxeo[?] Medicæ Professoris primarii; & bre[?] (annuente Divino Numine) tractulu[?] de febribus, hisce dictis fundamentis in[?] nitentem, studiosis Lectoribus dabimus.
units.tr: Sufficient, and more than sufficient, is the doctrine of fevers; it becomes clear from the six points already stated. Whoever wants more should turn to Chapter XXVII and the chapters that follow it on fevers in the Practice of Medicine of the most distinguished and most experienced man, Dr. Franciscus de le Boë Sylvius, chief professor of the practice of medicine. Briefly, by the favour of the Divine Power, we will give the studious reader a short treatise on fevers, resting on the foundations just laid down.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
